Regarding the position of reflection (*pratibimba*), however, it must be argued that since the reflected space is observed even while the natural space existing within the water is present, its occurrence as a doubling in one place is logically established. For even in the case of reflection, it must be stated that the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*) therein belongs only to that which is not contained within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and not a total reflection according to the analogy of the moon in water; because a portion situated inside that adjunct cannot possibly be reflected there.

For indeed, just as there is no reflection in water of the sky or light delimited by clouds—even though they are within the water—nor is there a reflection of the face and so forth when submerged in water, as there was while it remained outside; therefore, just as the sky and clouds are not inside the water with respect to their reflection therein, so too the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cannot be the locus of the reflection for that which is not contained within them. Since it is impossible for the original object (*bimba*) to exist in another modification (*vikāra*), the absence of an "inner ruler" (*antaryāmin*) in the Lord is the same as the absence of such a one in the case of the ignorant person mentioned in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*.

By this, the objection that if the individual soul (*jīva*) were defined by limitation (*avacchinna*), there would follow the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*)—because the portions of consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) differ in each respective instance of agency and enjoyership—is refuted.

Even in the view that [the self] is a reflection, since it must be stated that the reflection of a portion of consciousness—which is not contained within itself but is in proximity to it—is cast upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there arises an equality of defects; for as the internal organ moves from place to place, the original object (*bimba*) changes, and consequently, its reflection must necessarily change as well. Nor can it be argued that although the equality of defects applies to the position that "the individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection in the internal organ," this does not apply to the position that "the individual soul is the reflection in ignorance (*avidyā*)."

And in the view that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which moves from place to place, is like the reflection of the water of a great cloud pervading a body of water, where the spreading and intense light above it is the cause for the manifestation of specific [reflections] here and there—this fault does not apply. For it cannot be argued that because the internal organ moves, while ignorance (*avidyā*) does not, there can be no diversity of reflections; for the same applies to the theory of limitation (*avacchedapakṣa*), since it is possible to accept that the individual soul (*jīva*) is that which is delimited by ignorance.

Furthermore, even in that case, since one must ultimately resort to the unity of the individual soul (*jīva*)—in order to avoid defects such as the loss of what was performed (*kṛtahāna*) by asserting that agency belongs to one part of the soul while enjoyment belongs to another part—it is possible to dispel those very defects even under the view that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). This is because, by that same logic, one must admit that what is determinative is the actual unity of consciousness and the unity of the limiting adjuncts that delimit it.

Furthermore, in the view that [the soul's plurality] is due to limitation (*avaccheda*), there is no contradiction with the Śruti and Sūtra: "Just as this one luminous self, the sun, entering into various waters, appears divided in many ways; even so, this unborn Self, though one, is made to appear as diverse by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) within the fields [of bodies]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3), and "And for this very reason, there is the analogy of the sun and so forth" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.18).

By the sūtra immediately following the one cited—"But [the Self] is not like that because of the non-apprehension [of the reflection] as in the case of water"—it is stated that there is no possibility of a reflection, since there exists nothing whatsoever separated from the all-pervading Self that is capable of producing a reflection, unlike the case where the colored water, which is distant from the Sun, is perceived as being suitable for the arising of the Sun's reflection due to its own color. Then, by the subsequent sūtra—"In this way, there is consistency for both because of the inclusion [of the reflection] within [the medium], despite the variation in increase and decrease"—it is explained as follows:

The sun reflected in water appears to increase when the water increases, to decrease when the water decreases, and to move when the water moves; thus, its participation in increase, decrease, and so forth, according to the water, is merely superimposed (*ādhyāsika*). Similarly, for the Self, due to its delimitation by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), its participation in increase, decrease, and so forth, according to those adjuncts, is likewise merely superimposed. Since there is thus consistency between the illustration and the thing illustrated, there is no contradiction; for the author of the Sūtras himself has stated their intended meaning regarding these two in the context of the theory of delimitation (*avacchedapakṣa*): "Just as the space enclosed within a jar [appears to move] when the jar is being carried..."
A jar may be carried away, but not the space within it; likewise, the individual soul is like the sky.

Furthermore, because the position of limitation (*avacchedapakṣa*) alone is adopted by both scripture and aphorism in the statement, "A part [of Brahman], on account of its being designated as manifold" (*aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt*), they favor the view that "the individual soul (*jīva*) is limited," since it is necessary that the all-pervading consciousness must necessarily be delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that the individual soul (*jīva*) is neither a reflection nor a limited portion [of Brahman]. Rather, just as one who is a son of Kuntī may also be Rādheya, it is Brahman itself—remaining unmodified—that assumes the state of an individual soul through ignorance (*avidyā*). This is because it is established in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya* by means of the analogy of the prince brought up in the family of hunters: "Brahman alone transmigrates through its own ignorance and is liberated through its own knowledge.
Upon the recovery of his memory, the prince's status as a hunter ceases.
In the same way, for this ignorant self, [realization arises] from such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi).
And because of this statement in the Vārttika:

"Thus, since Brahman itself, having attained the state of a *jīva* through its own ignorance, is the imaginer of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), they declare that even Īśvara—along with attributes such as omniscience—is imagined by the *jīva*, like a deity perceived in a dream. (6)
Now, is this individual soul (jīva) one, or is it many? The cleansing of the mire of the doubt just mentioned must be performed with the very stream of water from the analogy of the dream.

However, others, finding no mental conviction in this doctrine of a single body and a single soul (*ekaśarīra-ekajīvavāda*), maintain—based on such sūtras as "But [the Lord is] distinct because of the mention of difference" and "But [His] sport is like that of the world, being absolute"—that the Lord alone, who is superior to the individual soul (*jīva*), is the creator of the universe, not the *jīva*. They argue that even though He has no purpose since His desires are fulfilled, the creation of the universe occurs solely for the sake of His sport (*līlā*). Considering this to be a contradiction, they hold that Hiraṇyagarbha alone, as the primary reflection of Brahman, is the principal *jīva*.

Others, however, maintain the doctrine of a single soul in multiple distinct bodies, asserting that the appearances of living beings—which are like reflections of that [one soul] and comparable to the reflection of a cloth placed upon human forms painted on a canvas—participate in saṃsāra and other such states.

Others, however, considering that there is no determining factor as to which specific Hiraṇyagarbha possesses the primary status of being the *jīva* given the difference in Hiraṇyagarbhas at every kalpa, maintain that there is only one *jīva* who presides over all bodies without distinction.

Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of mutual recollection of pleasure and so forth across different bodies—just as there is none between the different parts of a single body—since it is established that the difference of bodies serves as the cause for the non-recollection [of experiences], as seen in the fact that one does not recollect the pleasure and so forth of another birth.

However, since for a yogin the continuous connection with a manifold body, bliss, and so forth, is based on the power of yoga—just like the perception of objects that are spatially remote—that [example] is not applicable; thus, they favor the doctrine of a single soul inhabiting multiple bodies without distinction.

However, others—finding that even here the absence of a distinction between the bound and the liberated is equal, and thus seeing that the scriptural passage, "Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he indeed became that," as well as the commentary in the section beginning with "If it be said [there is no liberation] because of prohibition, no, because of the body," which establishes the state of being bound and liberated, would otherwise lack consistency—do not accept this; rather, by admitting that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), they resort to the doctrine of manifold souls (*anekajīvavāda*) and thereby establish the distinction between the bound and the liberated.

Among them, some say as follows: "Even though ignorance has only pure Brahman as its locus and object, and liberation is indeed the destruction of that [ignorance], nevertheless, since ignorance possesses parts (sāṃśatva) by virtue of the admission that a trace of ignorance persists in one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), that very ignorance is removed in part upon the arising of the realization of Brahman in a certain limiting adjunct (upādhi), while it continues in other limiting adjuncts through its remaining parts just as before."

Others, however, hold that according to the view of the Nyāyaikadeśins, when the absolute absence of a jar exists on the ground, the absence of the conjunction with a jar is the restrictive factor; thus, while the absolute absence of the jar exists in conjunction across many locations containing it, it does not remain in conjunction in a particular location where the conjunction with a jar has arisen and thereby the absence of that conjunction has ceased.

Thus, since the mind is the regulator of the activity of ignorance within consciousness, ignorance—which exists by being conjoined with those specific regions [of consciousness] through that limiting adjunct (upādhi)—is, upon the cessation of the mind according to the manner described in the statement "the knot of the heart is broken" due to the arising of the vision of Brahman in a certain place, no longer conjoined [with consciousness]. Elsewhere, it remains as before. And they say that bondage and liberation consist precisely in the conjunction and non-conjunction with ignorance, respectively.

Others, however, say that ignorance does not reside in pure consciousness, but rather resides in the individual soul (jīva) and has Brahman as its object. Therefore, just as a genus exists in all individuals—here, the individual souls which consist of reflections in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—by residing in each one individually, it abandons a particular soul in whom knowledge has arisen, just as a genus leaves behind a perished individual; that itself is liberation. It then takes up another soul as its substrate as before; thus they explain the systematic order (vyavasthā).

Others, however, having accepted a distinction in ignorance for each individual soul, justify the distinction between the bound and the liberated based on the persistence or cessation of that [ignorance].

If it is asked, "In this view, by whose ignorance was the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) created?", [the answer is: due to the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamakābhāvāt*), it is created by the ignorance of all [individuals], like a cloth woven from many threads. Upon the liberation of one person, when that person’s ignorance is destroyed, there is the destruction of the phenomenal world common to them, just as a cloth is destroyed when one thread is removed. At that very moment, just as another cloth is produced by other existing threads, another phenomenal world common to all others is produced by the ignorances and so forth of the rest—so say some.

Like the illusory silver produced by various instances of ignorance, and like the duality produced by various relative cognitions (*apekṣābuddhi*) according to the Nyāya school, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of ether and so forth, created by various forms of nescience (*avidyā*), is distinct for each individual. Others, however, maintain that it is merely a delusion of identity, as when one says, "The very same silver that you saw in the mother-of-pearl is what I have seen too."

Others hold that *māyā*, which is distinct from the mass of ignorance (*avidyā*) residing in individual souls (*jīva*), resides in the Lord (*īśvara*) and is the cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). They maintain that the ignorances of the individual souls, however, serve only for concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and are employed even in the production of illusory appearances (*prātibhāsika*), such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. ||7||
The nature of being the material cause (*upādānatva*), along with its relevant corollaries, has been determined. Now, what is the nature of agency (*kartṛtva*)?

Some say that, based on the scriptural declarations, "It thought; it desired; it made itself by itself," agency consists in possessing knowledge, volition, and effort conducive to the effect, just as in the Nyāya system.

Others, however, maintain that since there would be the consequence of an infinite regress if one were to require further desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*) and volition (*kṛti*) in order to sustain the Brahman’s status as an agent characterized by desire-to-act and satisfaction, the Brahman’s agency consists solely in possessing knowledge conducive to the effect. Nor does this same consequence apply to knowledge itself, because it is of the very nature of Brahman and is therefore not an effect.

Thus, they argue that the statement in the *Vivaraṇa* regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) being the agent of pleasure and so forth, as well as the statement in the *Kalpataru*—that the ether and other elements are "observed" (*vīkṣita*) because they are accomplished by mere observation, whereas the material elements are "smiled upon" (*smita*) because they are accomplished through greater effort involving observation via Hiraṇyagarbha—are both consistent with this view.

Others, however, maintain that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in possessing a cognition in the form of a creative deliberation conducive to the effect, and not merely possessing a cognition conducive to the effect. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the individual soul (*jīva*) is an agent even in cases such as the illusion of silver in mother-of-pearl or dreams, since it possesses the knowledge of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*) conducive to superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Nor is this a desired conclusion.

It should not be argued that the individual soul (jīva) is the creator of the dream-phenomenon because the scripture itself states, "Then he creates chariots, horses for the chariots, and roads; for he is the creator," and so forth. For the commentators have explained this as being merely a figurative attribution of agency—just as one says "the plow draws the oxen"—based on the fact that the soul is the cause of the manifestation of the chariots and other objects. Thus they say. ||8||

By this very fact of being the creator of the entire cosmic manifestation, the omniscience of Brahman is established as a matter of course; this has also been demonstrated by its being the author of the Veda in the section beginning with "Because [Brahman] is the source of the scripture" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).

Now, how is the omniscience of Brahman consistent? For, like the individual soul (jīva), in the absence of an internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), even the status of being a knower would be impossible. In this regard, the position of Bhāratītīrtha and others has already been shown previously: the Lord (Īśvara) is conditioned by ignorance (ajñāna) colored by the impressions (vāsanā) of the cognitions of all living beings regarding all objects; therefore, His omniscience consists in His being the witness (sākṣin) of those impressions concerning all objects.

The authors of the *Prakaṭārtha* say: Just as for the individual soul (*jīva*), the transformations of its own limiting adjunct, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), are recipients of the reflection of consciousness, and through connection with them it possesses the status of a knower; so too, for Brahman, the transformations of its own limiting adjunct, Māyā, are recipients of the reflection of Consciousness. Thus, by means of the manifestations reflected therein, there is omniscience due to the indirect apprehension of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) existing in the three periods of time.

The authors of the *Tattvaśuddhi*, however, maintain that omniscience is established as follows: by the aforementioned method, since Brahman is capable of producing the entire manifest world existing [within it], and since recollection is possible due to its possessing the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced thereby, the manifestation of all past objects is proven. Furthermore, because prior to creation, Māyā undergoes a phenomenal transformation (*vivarta*) in the form of the manifestation of all objects to be created, in accordance with the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of individual souls (*jīva*), Brahman—being the witness of that process and having that Māyā as its limiting adjunct—is also established as the agent of that manifestation; thus, the cognition of future objects is possible, and in this way they justify its omniscience.

The followers of Kaumudī, however, maintain that Brahman’s omniscience arises from its very nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*), since it illuminates everything with which it is connected. This is because even the past and the future exist within ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), like a painted image that has been contemplated but not yet manifested; thus, their connection [with Brahman] is also logically possible. But its omniscience does not arise through the cognitions produced by mental modifications (*vṛtti-jñāna*).

Because it would contradict the restrictive scriptural statement, "Everything shines only after Him who shines," and because—given the restriction that "in the beginning there was one only, without a second"—the dissolution of even the subtle modifications of knowledge (vṛttijñāna), just like the great elements, must be admitted; this would entail that Brahman lacks omniscience at that time, and consequently, it would follow that He could not possess the power of seeing (īkṣaṇa) as the initial transformation of Māyā, nor the power of creation regarding the great elements and so forth which precede it.

If it is argued that this being the case, Brahman would possess omniscience only in the sense of being of the nature of knowledge regarding all objects, and not in the form of omniscience as the status of a knower (*sarvajñātṛtva*), we reply: True. Brahman is indeed of the nature of knowledge regarding all objects, but it does not possess the status of a knower in the form of being the agent of all cognitions. For this very reason, the Commentators stated in the section beginning with "On account of the connection of the sentences" (*vākyānvayāt*) that the status of being a knower (*vijñātṛtva*) is a characteristic mark of the individual soul (*jīva*). Even scriptural passages such as "He who is omniscient" (*yaḥ sarvajñaḥ*) should be interpreted solely with the intention that [Brahman] is of the nature of knowledge.

Although Brahman, by its very nature as pure consciousness, is the illuminator of all things through its intimate connection with them, nevertheless, even though it is not an effect in its essential form, it is an effect of Brahman insofar as it is delimited by the objects of perception; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever even with the scriptural statement, "He who is omniscient," which speaks of Brahman as the agent of the production of knowledge—so say the teacher Vācaspati Miśra. 9.

Now, one might ask: why does the individual soul (jīva), like the Lord (īśvara), not manifest objects by its own essential consciousness (svarūpacaitanya) alone, without depending on mental modifications (vṛtti)?

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "The consciousness of Brahman, having attained identity with all things by virtue of being the material cause of everything, manifests all that is in contact with itself; the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva*) does not. Although the latter is omnipresent due to its adjunct of ignorance (*avidyā*), it lacks the nature of a material cause and is therefore non-attached. Just as the universal 'cowness,' though omnipresent, naturally comes into contact with an individual possessing a dewlap despite lacking contact with individuals such as horses, so too the individual soul, though non-attached to objects, naturally comes into contact with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)."

And thus, when a modification (*pariṇāma*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), in the form of a mental mode (*vṛtti*), issues forth through the gateway of the eyes and other senses, and having quickly transformed into the shape of a long beam of light like a ray of vision, pervades the object, it then ascends that [mode] and makes that object its own sphere of perception. Just as grass and the like, which cannot be burned by fire alone, are burned by fire mounted upon an iron ball, so too it is logical that objects such as a jar, which cannot be illumined by the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) alone, are illumined when they have ascended onto a modification of the internal organ.

Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is limited by virtue of having the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); therefore, due to the absence of contact, it does not manifest objects such as a jar. However, when there is the manifestation of non-difference from the Brahman-consciousness delimited by an object that has come into contact [with the internal organ] through the medium of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it illuminates that object.

Or else, although the *jīva* is all-pervading, because it is veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*), it does not manifest objects since it is itself unmanifest; yet, through the influence of a mental modification upon a particular object, the veil is removed right there, and being manifested in that very place, it illuminates that specific object.

And thus, whether by way of the purpose of coloring consciousness (*cid-uparāga*), by way of the purpose of manifesting the non-difference between the object and consciousness (*viṣaya-caitanya-abheda*), or by way of the purpose of overcoming the veil (*āvaraṇa-abhibhava*), the limited knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*) is also established, because it illuminates only that object with which [the internal organ] is in contact, depending upon the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*). ||10||

In this regard, according to the first position, what kind of coloring by an object could there be for an all-pervading soul that depends upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*)? For even by means of a modification, it is impossible to bring about either identity or conjunction between the already established and inactive consciousness of the object and the consciousness of the soul.

Others, however, argue that if the function (*vṛtti*) were merely the regulator of the relationship between object and subject, then even an internal sensory function would regulate that relationship without leading to over-extension; thus, the admission of its external emergence would be rendered useless. Therefore, they maintain that this is not what is intended. Rather, when the function—which has attained identity with the living consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) present at the location of the object—comes into contact with the object, a mediated, indirect connection (*paramparāsambandha*) is established for the consciousness as well through that medium. It is precisely this "coloration by consciousness" (*ciduparāga*) that is intended.

Others, however, maintain that since pleasure and the like are observed to be immediate precisely because they are in direct contact with immediate consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), a direct contact must be admitted in the case of an immediate object. Therefore, when the mental modification (*vṛtti*) comes into contact with the object, it acquires the limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) consisting of that modification; by means of that limitation, a "contact-born-contact" (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) is possible for the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of that modification.

They argue that this is appropriate because, by parity of reasoning, just as the contact between an effect and a non-cause follows from the contact between a cause and a non-cause, so too the contact between a cause and a non-cause may be accepted from the contact between an effect and a non-cause.

However, for the proponents of the "partial reflection" (ekadeśin) view, what is intended by the term "superimposition on consciousness" (ciduparāga) is precisely the attainment of identity with the object, achieved through the manifestation of non-difference between the consciousness that illuminates the object—conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—and the Brahman-consciousness which has attained identity with that object.

Even though the individual soul (jīva) is omnipresent and thus in proximity to all objects, its manifestation of those objects cannot occur in that [omnipresent] form, because such a form would be common to all persons, making it impossible to establish the restriction of direct perception to a specific individual. Therefore, the soul manifests objects only insofar as it is conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). And in this way, the established conclusion (siddhānta)—that the superimpositional relationship (ādhyāsika-sambandha) is the regulator for the direct perception of objects—is also consistent. Nor does this lead to a confusion with the second position;
for they say that the first position holds when the soul is omnipresent, while the second holds when it is limited, and thus there is a distinction between the two. ||11||
Now, regarding the second position, what is this "manifestation of non-difference" (*abhedābhivyakti*)?

Some say: just as the waters of a pond and a field become one through a canal, so too the manifestation of non-difference is the unification of the consciousness delimited by the object and the consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by means of a mental modification (*vṛtti*). And thus, although it is the very Brahman-consciousness delimited by the object that illumines the object, nevertheless, because it attains the state of being the individual soul (*jīvatva*) through its unification with the modification, the illumination of the object by the individual soul is logically established.

Others, however, say that the unification with the *jīva*, which is the reflection of Brahman delimited by the object (the *viṣaya*) that stands as the prototype (*bimba*), does not mean the manifestation of non-difference; for as long as the distinguishing adjunct (*upādhi*)—like a mirror—is present, the unification of those two is impossible.

If, through the manifestation of non-difference by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*), Brahman delimited by an object were to attain the state of being a *jīva*, then since Brahman would at that time lack contact with that object, it would be impossible for it to be its perceiver; consequently, Brahman’s omniscience would be compromised. Rather, the consciousness of Brahman delimited by an object projects a reflection that illumines the object onto the foremost part of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) conjoined with that object; it is this reflection that becomes one with the *jīva*.

In this way, the non-confusion of the cognizer, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—consisting of the consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), its modifications (*vṛtti*), and the object—is also established. Nor should it be argued that if consciousness conditioned by the modification (*vṛttyupahita-caitanya*) is the cognizer of the object, then, because it lacks the illusory superimposition (*adhyāsika-sambandha*) with the object—unlike the consciousness which is the substrate of the object (*viṣayādhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*)—the illusory superimposition could not be the necessary factor for the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of the object.

This is because the very consciousness that is the substrate of the object, when delimited by the object, is reflected in the modification; thus, through identity with that [reflection], the connection with the object exists.

Others, however, say that it is consciousness itself, which has the object serving as its reflected image (bimba) and which resides in the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), that directly manifests the object by virtue of attaining an illusory (ādhyāsika) connection with it. Thus, although there exists a distinction between that [consciousness] in its form as the reflected image and its specific substrate, the manifestation of non-difference is the unification [of them] in the nature of consciousness as characterized by those two. And this being so, there is no confusion between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, nor is there any contradiction with the omniscience of Brahman, because Brahman remains exactly as before in its nature as the original image (bimba). ||12||

Now, regarding the third position, what indeed is this "overpowering of the veil" (*āvaraṇābhibhava*)? If it is the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna*), then one might object that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which has ignorance as its root, would cease to exist through the knowledge of a jar alone. To this, some say: the overpowering of ignorance—which veils pure consciousness—is either (1) its partial destruction by knowledge, like the dispelling of great darkness by the light of a lamp in a specific location; or (2) its being rolled up like a mat; or (3) its receding like a frightened soldier.

Others, however, maintain that the aforementioned form of suppression is not possible; for if ignorance were destroyed in one part, it could not sprout again there due to the absence of its material cause (upādāna), which would entail the consequence that there would be no veil even at a later time once [the knowledge] has occurred once. Furthermore, since that which is inactive cannot undergo displacement or contraction, such suppression is impossible. Therefore, suppression is simply the inherent nature of ignorance—which, though veiling pure consciousness—to not veil that consciousness as delimited by an object when it is in a state conjoined with a mental modification (vṛtti) having that particular form.

Nor should it be doubted how it is possible for ignorance—which resides by depending on the consciousness of the object like a veil covering the object—to not obscure that very object; for they say that, through the cognition "I am ignorant," one does not perceive its obscuring nature precisely because it has as its substrate the very consciousness that is manifest in the experience of the "I."

Others, however, maintain that what is experienced in the form "I do not know the jar"—as being opposed to the knowledge of the jar, and as being sublated when the knowledge of the jar arises—is not the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). This is because it is impossible for that [root-ignorance] to have the pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*) as its object or to be sublatable by the knowledge of that [consciousness]. Rather, it is another form of ignorance, consisting of a specific state (*avasthābheda*) of the root-ignorance, which has the consciousness delimited by the jar (*ghaṭāvacchinnacaitanya*) as its object; thus, its destruction alone constitutes its suppression.

And it is not the case that, when ignorance is destroyed by one cognition, other cognitions having the same object would fail to overcome the veil; for they maintain that there are as many instances of ignorance as there are cognitions. This is what they say.
Some maintain that these forms of ignorance corresponding to the various states, like fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), are beginningless because they are of the nature of ignorance.

Sleep, which covers the empirical world and individual soul and projects the dream-world and dream-soul, is a specific state of ignorance (*ajñāna*) by virtue of its association with the powers of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*). Likewise, the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and other faculties have dissolved, is also a specific state of ignorance experienced during the time of deep sleep—just like root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)—as evidenced by the subsequent reflection: "I slept happily; I was not aware of anything. Furthermore, because these two states arise only when the karma that provides experience in the waking state has ceased, they are considered to have a beginning (*sādi*). Others maintain that other forms of ignorance consisting of such states are likewise beginningless.

Now, one might object: "In the view that [ignorance] is beginningless, the destruction of all ignorance regarding a jar would occur by the very first cognition produced with respect to it; for there is no criterion for selection (*vinigamanā-viraha*), and because if all ignorance obscuring the consciousness delimited by that [jar] were destroyed, the manifestation of the object would be impossible. Therefore, the fact that subsequent cognitions do not overcome the veil remains exactly as it was. To this, some say: "Just as even though there are many prior absences (*prāgabhāva*) of a cognition, when a single cognition arises, only one prior absence is removed."

Even though other forms of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) exist as veils due to their capacity to generate doubt and the like, there is still the manifestation of the object. Similarly, upon the arising of a single cognition, only that one ignorance (*ajñāna*) is removed; even while other ignorances persist, there is the manifestation of the object.

Others, however, maintain that the direct perception of what is veiled is contradictory [to its being veiled]. They hold that when a single cognition arises, although there remain other prior absences (*prāgabhāva*), the veil—which consists of the aggregate of absences regarding all particular cognitions—is removed by that particular cognition. They argue that whenever ignorance veils something, it is destroyed by that very cognition; yet it does not veil everything at all times, as that would be purposeless. Rather, when the veiling ignorance is destroyed by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), upon the cessation of that modification, another ignorance veils [the object].

Nor does it follow that, at the time of the arising of the realization of Brahman, there would be the undesirable consequence of those ignorances (*ajñāna*) which existed as non-obscuring [factors] not being removed even then; for although they lack direct opposition to that realization, their removal is established because they are dependent on the root-ignorance which is itself removable by it—just like the connection with ignorance and so forth. It is precisely for this reason that their dependence on it is accepted, insofar as they consist of different states (*avasthābhedas*) of that [root-ignorance].

Others, however, maintain that because ignorance has as its very nature the possession of an object, it invariably veils everything at all times. They do not think that it can be argued that its status as a veiler is untenable before the emergence of an object due to the absence of anything to be veiled; for even then, it exists in a subtle form. Thus they imagine: just as a thunderbolt falling upon the head of one person in a place crowded with many people also sweeps away others.

Or, just as a single medicine that pacifies a combination of humors (sannipāta) eliminates one humor while also driving away other humors, so too knowledge, in destroying one instance of ignorance, also sets aside other instances of ignorance. And this setting aside consists in the obstruction of the power of concealment for as long as that knowledge persists.

But if this were the case, then in the instance of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika*), the second and subsequent mental modifications would be useless, since the veil would be overcome merely by the first cognition through its removal and suppression of the obstruction.

On this point, they say: even ignorance that has been set aside by a mental modification (vṛtti) covers [the object] again once that modification ceases, just as darkness that has been set aside by a lamp returns when the lamp is extinguished. However, at the moment the modification ceases, if another modification arises, the ignorance remains set aside in that very same way, just as darkness remains dispelled when another lamp is lit at the moment the first lamp is extinguished.

And thus, in accordance with the general definition for preserving prior non-existence—namely, "that in whose presence another exists in the subsequent moment, and in whose absence it does not exist, that [latter] is produced by that [former]"—the second and subsequent occurrences of the effect are also obtained as being the results of non-obstruction; therefore, that [non-obstruction] is not futile.

The authors of the *Nyāyacandrikā*, however, say: "By a particular cognition, there is simply the destruction of a particular ignorance, but not the suppression of other veiling ignorances. Thus, even the second and subsequent cognitions in a continuous stream (dhārāvāhika) are purposeful, as each destroys one specific ignorance."

Nor does it follow that there would be a failure to perceive objects even when knowledge arises, because of the possibility of obscuration [remaining]. For the various forms of ignorance (*ajñāna*) are of the nature of states that obscure the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as characterized by their respective times; and cognitions (*jñāna*) are the destroyers of those ignorances that obscure the objects as characterized by the time of the cognition itself. Thus, when a particular cognition arises, since the ignorance obscuring the object of that specific time is destroyed, and because the other existing ignorances obscure objects belonging to other times, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the manifestation of the object belonging to that specific time.

Just as the time of rain is indicated by the fruit of the *kārīrī* sacrifice even when that time is imminent, so too, in the case of objects such as a jar—which fall within the domain of ignorance—the subtle distinctions of time do not enter into the category of the object as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the cessation of ignorances through a continuous stream of second and subsequent cognitions, which do not apprehend those subtle temporal differences.

However, some maintain that only that ignorance which is sublated by the first cognition is the concealer of the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Those sublated by the second and subsequent cognitions, on the other hand, have as their objects [the self] qualified by various attributes such as place, time, and so forth. For this very reason, when the perception of Caitra—which has the form of a certainty regarding existence and serves to remove ignorance—occurs even once, the concealment of the essential nature (*svarūpāvaraṇa*) in the form "I do not know Caitra" is no longer experienced; rather, there is only the concealment of specific attributes, in the form "I do not know where he is now," and so on.

If, in the case of those prone to forgetfulness, a concealment of one's own nature is observed—such that even when something has been seen once, they say "I do not know"—let it be so in that instance. In other cases, however, regarding objects perceived only once, both ignorance and knowledge pertain exclusively to specific attributes.

It should not be argued that, this being the case, the second and subsequent cognitions in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika*) would lack the capacity to remove ignorance; for while the ignorance qualified by gross time is removed by the first cognition alone, it is impossible for the ignorance qualified by subtle time—which is distinct from the preceding and succeeding cognitions—to be removed by the second and subsequent cognitions which do not have that [subtle time] as their object. This is because, in the case of a continuous stream, it is possible for the very same mental modification (*vṛtti*) that arose first to persist for that duration, and thus no difference between successive modifications (*vṛttibheda*) is admitted.

Even if that [position] were accepted, since it is possible for there to be five or six cognitions persisting over a long duration, it is logically consistent that they have as their objects distinct qualifiers such as gross time and so forth, which are mutually exclusive. Furthermore, even if one accepts that cognition consists of a continuum of multiple occurrences arising at every moment, there is no loss [of the theory's integrity], because subsequent cognitions—having as their object only what has already been apprehended—lack validity and thus do not remove the veil [of ignorance]. For validity does not consist merely in the non-sublation of the object.

For since there is no difference in the absence of sublation (*abādha*) regarding the mountain and the fire residing therein—which are both objects of inferential cognition—there would follow the undesirable consequence that the inferential cognition is valid in both cases alike. Nor is this an acceptable conclusion, because we do not observe such usage as "the inferential cognition regarding the fire is valid," while simultaneously observing "the inferential cognition regarding the mountain is also valid."

Furthermore, in the *Vivaraṇa*, it is stated that although ignorance—which is established by witness-consciousness (*sākṣisiddha*)—may be the object of inference and other means of knowledge for the purpose of conveying its exclusion from non-existence, it is nonetheless not known through [ordinary] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, since subsequent mental modifications (*vṛtti*) lack the status of being means of valid cognition, there is no loss even if they do not remove ignorance—just like the modifications involved in meditation (*upāsanā*) and the like—because it is only those modifications that are means of valid cognition which are accepted as having the power to remove it.

If it is objected that even this rule is not absolute, because [ignorance] residing in the remote object does not remove ignorance since it does not emerge [into the mind], some here say in response: Ignorance that veils the object is of two kinds. One is located in the object, such as the rope [in the case of a snake-illusion], which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the projection (*vikṣepa*) and is to be inferred from its effects. The other is located in the person, being experienced as "I do not know this. Since it is impossible for that which resides in the person to be the material cause of a projection that is mixed with the object, and since it is impossible for that which resides in the object to have contact with the light in the form of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*) expressed as "I do not know this," both types are necessary.

And thus, in the case of an imperceptible object, although there is no emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) [into the object], even when one perceives a specific dimension of a distant tree through the words of a reliable person, and despite seeing a discrepancy regarding its dimension, there is indeed a cessation of the ignorance residing in the person, even though the ignorance residing in the object has not ceased. This is because we experience the cessation of the ignorance previously felt as "I do not know the meaning of the scripture" immediately after its instruction.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tattvadīpana* that the meaning of the *Vivaraṇa* passage, "the exclusion of deep sleep with respect to the inferable and so forth," is the cessation of the ignorance regarding that object.

Others, however, maintain that ignorance (*ajñāna*), which veils the object, resides solely in the person (*puruṣa*), like a cataract on the eye; there is no evidence for an ignorance residing in the object itself apart from that. Nor can it be argued that it is impossible for that which resides in the person to undergo the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of projection (*vikṣepa*) toward the object. Or, even if such a possibility were granted, one might argue that once ignorance is removed by a perceptual cognition of the size of a distant tree, a projected erroneous perception of a different size could not occur. To this it must be replied: [this is not so]. For just as a cataract on the eye is removed by the application of medicinal collyrium, so too is the ignorance residing in the person removed by the rise of valid knowledge (*pramā*). Furthermore, since the transformation of the mind (*citta*) consists in its assuming the form of the object, it is possible for the mind to project an erroneous form even when the object is not present. Moreover, just as a cataract on the eye does not cease merely because the person sees clearly at a distance, so too the ignorance residing in the person does not cease merely through the perception of the object's true nature from afar. Therefore, the removal of ignorance occurs only when the object is directly perceived, and the manifestation of error occurs when the object is not directly perceived. Thus, the theory that ignorance resides in the object is untenable. Consequently, it is established that ignorance resides in the person. And since ignorance is the cause of bondage, it follows that liberation is attained through the cessation of that ignorance. This is the view of the followers of the *Vijñānavāda*. However, this is not accepted by the followers of the *Sāṃkhya*. For they hold that the mind (*citta*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), and therefore cannot be the locus of ignorance. Since the mind is insentient, it cannot be the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*); rather, the enjoyer is the pure consciousness (*caitanya*). Ignorance, being the cause of bondage, must reside in the enjoyer. Hence, it is established that ignorance resides in the person. And since the cessation of that ignorance constitutes liberation, it follows that liberation is indeed attained. This is the view of the followers of the *Sāṃkhya*. Thus, the doctrine of the *Vedāntins* is refuted. Therefore, it is established that liberation is attained through the cessation of ignorance. According to the view of Vācaspati Miśra, since the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman as made the object of ignorance residing in the individual soul (*jīva*), it follows that [illusory objects] such as nacre-silver are likewise illusory manifestations of Brahman as made the object of ignorance residing in a person. Furthermore, they argue that even when one state [of ignorance] is removed by indirect cognitive function (*parokṣavṛtti*), the projection of a contrary dimension (*viparītaparimāṇa-vikṣepa*) is possible through another state [of ignorance]. Thus they say.

Others, however, argue that because the theory of the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of nacre, silver, and so forth is more consistent, it is ignorance residing in the object itself—like a cloth enveloping the object—that constitutes its veil. Nor should it be objected that if this were the case, there would be the impossibility of illumination from that [object] due to the ignorance’s lack of contact with the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), nor the impossibility of its being removed by indirect mental modification (*parokṣavṛtti*); for even though the ignorance in the form of a particular state (*avasthārūpa-ajñāna*) lacks contact with the witness, the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) which is in contact with it is indeed manifested as "I do not know the nacre."

Since even the mother-of-pearl and other such objects are non-different from the consciousness that is the object of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), there is no contradiction in experiencing them as objects [of that ignorance].

Furthermore, in the *Vivaraṇa* and other texts, in the context of establishing root-ignorance, the perception "I do not know this" is presented as the proof; therefore, it is precisely the general experience of ignorance, namely "I am ignorant," that has root-ignorance as its object.

Even if one accepts a specific [subordinate] ignorance as the object of the experience "I do not know the mother-of-pearl," because there is no difference between the state and that which possesses the state, the subordinate ignorance residing in the object is logically established as being within the scope of the witness (sākṣin). This occurs either through the connection of the root ignorance with the witness, or through the real identity between the witness and the consciousness that is the object.

They say that even though indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) does not remove ignorance (*ajñāna*), the experience of its removal following such knowledge is possible because it is a delusion based on the non-apprehension of the mental modification (*vṛtti*)—which is indirect, takes the form of a certainty regarding existence, and acts as an obstacle [to direct perception]. This is because they accept the rule that only direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) removes ignorance.

If it is objected: "Is this not also an over-strict rule? For it is not admitted that the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), egoity (*ahaṃkāra*), pleasure, pain, and their attributes possesses the capacity to remove nescience (*ajñāna*)," we reply: No. Since the direct perception of ignorance and so forth is of the nature of the Witness (*sākṣin*), the rule that immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) removes the veil does not fail to apply here. ||13||

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kūṭasthadīpa*: the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*), which serves as the substratum for the two bodies, is called the "Witness" (*sākṣin*) because it directly perceives its own limiting adjuncts—the two bodies—and because it is devoid of modification. Indeed, even in the world, witness-hood is well-known to consist solely of neutrality and awareness.

Although the individual soul (jīva) possesses mental modifications (vṛtti) that manifest the two bodies, nevertheless, the two bodies—which are always slightly illumined by the immutable consciousness (kūṭastha-caitanya) delimited by itself as it extends everywhere—are manifested by the cognitive modifications (vṛtti-jñāna) arising from the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which contains the reflection of the nature of the jīva-consciousness, as these modifications emerge one after another. During the intervals between them, however, they are manifested solely by the immutable consciousness together with the absence of modifications.

For this very reason, because the ego (ahaṃkāra) and other such factors are always in contact with the Light, they do not become objects of doubt and the like. Furthermore, there is the retrospective recollection of the ego occurring during a stream of other cognitions, in the form: "For all this time, I was indeed perceiving this. Nor should one raise the objection: "How can empirical activity, memory, and so forth belong to the individual soul (jīva) when [the ego] is illuminated by the Immutable (kūṭastha)? For, through mutual superimposition, the identity of the soul is attained, and thus the Immutable is internal to the individual soul.

Nor should it be argued that the conscious living self (jīvacaitanya) itself may be the witness (sākṣin), rendering a changeless one (kūṭastha) unnecessary; for since that agent of worldly and Vedic transactions cannot possibly be an indifferent observer, it lacks the status of a witness as described in the scripture: "The witness, the cognizer, alone and devoid of qualities. Furthermore, the witness who is of the nature of indifferent luminosity is taught separately from the living self, the enjoyer of the fruits of action, in the passage: "One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating."
In the *Nāṭakadīpa* as well, the Witness is distinguished from the individual soul (jīva) by means of the illustration of a lamp situated in a dance hall; for it is said:
"The lamp standing in the dance hall [illuminates] the master, the audience, and the dancer."
It should be kindled without distinction; even in its absence, it shines.

Likewise, illuminating the *jīva*—which consists of the *ahaṃkāra* qualified by the reflection of consciousness—as being like a master dancer due to its possession of joy and dejection caused by the conceit of either the completeness or deficiency of experiencing objects; illuminating the objects as being like the audience members because, although situated in the vicinity of that [master], they lack those [emotions]; and illuminating the intellect (*dhī*) as being like a dancer because it exists within various modifications; [the Self] shines even during deep sleep and other such states when the *ahaṃkāra* and the rest are absent.

The Witness (sākṣin) is the immutable consciousness (kūṭasthacaitanya), which serves as the substratum for the illusion of the individual soul (jīva) whose nature is the ego (ahaṃkāra) qualified by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). Thus, this Witness, distinguished from the individual soul, does not belong even to the category of Brahman; rather, it is said in the *Kūṭasthadīpa* to be the consciousness that is untouched by the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord.

In the *Tattvapradīpikā* as well, it is stated that because the qualification "alone, devoid of qualities" (*kevalo nirguṇaḥ*) would be untenable with respect to the Supreme Lord who is qualified by *māyā* and possesses attributes, the pure Brahman—which is the inner self of all—is established as the Witness through its non-difference from the individual soul (*jīva*).
In the Kaumudī, however, it is said:
"The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."

"Supervisor of karma, the abode of all beings, conscious, solitary, and devoid of qualities"—from such scriptural passages as these, it follows that there is a certain modification of the Supreme Lord Himself known as the "Witness" (sākṣin), who is indifferent and merely the permissive observer of the activity and cessation of the individual soul (jīva). Because He is not the locus of attributes such as causality, He is directly perceived; and by illuminating the ignorance and other states belonging to the jīva, He is its innermost essence. Furthermore, during deep sleep and similar states, when the body and its organs have ceased their functions, He is designated as "Prājña," the manifester of the mere ignorance residing in the jīva.

"Just as one embraced by a beloved woman knows nothing external nor internal, even so this person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātmā), knows nothing external nor internal"; and "Mounted by the conscious Self, he goes forth emitting [the breath]"—by these two scriptural passages, the Supreme Lord is established as distinct from the individual soul (jīva) in the states of deep sleep and departure. Thus, it has been described that the determination of the *Suṣupti-utkrānty-adhikaraṇa* also concerns the Witness (sākṣin).

Even in the *Tattvaśuddhi*, this very position is supported by stating that, just as in the case of the error "this is silver," the "this" portion (*idamaṃśa*), although in reality included within the category of mother-of-pearl, appears phenomenally as the category of silver; so too, the Witness (*sākṣin*), who is actually of the nature of Brahman, appears phenomenally as the category of the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, the Witness is utilized for the soul's empirical dealings with pleasure and the like.

However, some maintain that the *jīva* itself, conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopādhika*), is the witness (*sākṣin*) because it is directly the seer. For even in the world, being a witness is well-known to consist in being a seer while remaining a non-agent. And this is possible directly only in the *jīva*, whose nature is unattached, indifferent, and luminous; for although the *jīva* undergoes the superimposition of agency and so forth through its identification with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it is itself inherently indifferent. The mantra "The one God" (*eko devaḥ*), moreover, establishes the witnesshood of Brahman with reference to its state as the *jīva*.

They say that there is no contradiction whatsoever: the mantra "dvā suparṇā" refers to both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) according to the principle of the Guhādhikaraṇa, or it refers to both the individual soul and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) in the manner explained in the Paiṅgirahasya-Brahmaṇa as cited in the commentary on the Guhādhikaraṇa.

Others, however, maintain that it is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*) alone who is the witness (*sākṣin*), and not in its form as the all-pervading one conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*). For if that were the case, the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth belonging to one person would also result in being perceived by another person, since there is no difference in their contact with the witness who illumines each respective internal organ. Nor can it be argued that this consequence does not arise because the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) differs according to the difference in internal organs; for when the internal organ and other such objects are illuminated by the witness, the difference between cognizers is irrelevant as long as the witness remains non-different across all instances.

Therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the witness (*sākṣin*) by virtue of being conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Consequently, because there is a distinct witness for each person, it is logical that the internal organs and other factors belonging to one person do not manifest to another person; this is either due to their lack of contact with that other person's witness or due to their inherent unfitness [to be perceived by it]. Even during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), since the internal organ exists in a subtle form, the witness conditioned by it certainly persists even then. Nor should it be argued that what is conditioned by the internal organ cannot be the witness because it possesses the status of a cognizer (*pramātṛ*), and that a distinction between the two must necessarily be asserted on the grounds that the witness exists while the cognizer is absent in deep sleep.

They say that since the distinction between a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is accepted in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the distinction is thus justified: the knower (*pramātṛ*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as qualified (*viśiṣṭa*), while the witness (*sākṣin*) is that same organ as limited (*upahita*). ||14||

If it is objected: "Since the witness (sākṣin), whose nature has been described, is necessarily veiled by ignorance (ajñāna) which obscures pure consciousness (caitanyamātra), how can there be the manifestation of ignorance, the ego (ahaṅkāra), and so forth, when [the witness] is thus veiled?"—[we reply: There is no fault here, because this is a conceptual construction based on experience, according to which ignorance veils consciousness only after setting aside the witness-consciousness that illuminates ignorance, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and its attributes. Therefore, because they are always in contact with an unobscured light, they do not become objects of ignorance, erroneous cognition, or doubt.

If it is argued that since the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is unobscured, its very nature—bliss (*ānanda*)—must also be manifest, we say no; for this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). This is because we observe self-regarding love (*nirupādhikaprema*) toward the Self, which is prompted by the manifestation of its blissful form. Furthermore, the *Vivaraṇa* states: "The happiness characterized as being the object of supreme love is indeed manifest. (15)

It might be argued that even now, during the manifestation of the bliss of the witness (*sākṣin*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of no distinction between liberation and transmigratory existence. If it is replied: "Indeed, although the bliss of the witness—which possesses imagined difference—is manifest, there is still a distinction because the unconditioned bliss of Brahman remains unmanifest during the state of transmigratory existence due to being veiled," we say: No. This is because the aspect of non-limitation within bliss is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), and because the mere immediate intuition (*aparokṣa*) of bliss exists even now. If it is further argued: "The bliss of the witness, when conditioned, is indeed subject to gradation; for we experience a superiority in worldly pleasures over the bliss common to deep sleep, which is neither very clear nor superior."

If it is argued that the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) is indeed unsurpassed and unlimited because the *Ānandavallī* concludes its description of the progressive hundredfold increase in human bliss and so forth with the bliss of Brahman, we say no. For in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since the bliss of the witness (*sākṣyānanda*), the bliss of the object (*viṣayānanda*), and the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) are in reality one, any distinction of superiority or inferiority is impossible. If you ask, "Does the Śruti not state that there is a progressive increase from human bliss onwards?"—who indeed says that the Śruti does not state it? However, what is being said is that such an explanation is untenable within the non-dualist (*advaita*) system.

If it is argued that—just as a single solar light exhibits differences in the degree of its manifestation depending on the specific manifesting conditions such as the palm of the hand, crystal, or a mirror—it is likewise logical for bliss (*ānanda*) to possess degrees of excellence or deficiency in the form of varying intensities of manifestation, due to the influence of different manifesting mental states (*vṛtti*) of pleasure—even though bliss is one—this is not so, because the illustrative example is unestablished.

Just as the light of the sun, which spreads everywhere in the sky and appears indistinctly without contact with the palm of the hand or similar objects, becomes more intensely bright when its movement is obstructed by contact with the palm—due to its becoming concentrated like water spreading on a low-lying surface—and becomes even brighter than that when its movement is obstructed by contact with a polished mirror or the like—due to its concentration and the blending of its own radiance—it is because one does not admit a gradation in manifestation based on the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that manifest it.

Furthermore, if the analogy were accepted, it would follow that the bliss of liberation—which is uninterrupted like sunlight spreading across the sky—is indistinct, whereas the bliss of transmigratory existence—which is delimited by mental modifications such as those occurring in the palm of the hand—is more intensely manifested; thus, saṃsāra would become more desirable than liberation.

By this, the following view is also refuted: "Although bliss shines forth during the state of saṃsāra, it appears indistinctly—like the light of a lamp tossed by a violent wind—due to being distracted by false knowledge and its latent impressions; whereas in liberation, because of the absence of those [obstacles], it manifests as it truly is. For if the bliss of the nature of the Self, devoid of distinctions, is shining forth, it is impossible for there to be an excellence associated with liberation that remains unmanifest due to the defect of distraction. Therefore, the hypothesis that the witness-bliss is unenveloped is untenable.

On this point, the masters of Advaita-vidyā say: just as when the reflection of a single, supremely excellent white form appears in many mirrors possessing varying degrees of tarnish, a corresponding diminution of whiteness is superimposed upon each respective reflection due to the varying degrees of tarnish in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi); so too, in the state of being the bliss of the witness (sākṣyānanda), the one, unsurpassed essential bliss (svarūpānanda) is reflected in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

Because it is reflected in a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*)—which takes the form of pleasure and is characterized by degrees of purity consisting of the increase or decrease of *sattva* induced by contact with specific objects dependent upon the perfection of past meritorious deeds—and because it exists in the state of objective bliss (*viṣayānanda*), a degree of inferiority is superimposed upon it through the defect of the varying degrees of turbidity caused by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of the quality of *tamas*. Thus, even though bliss is manifest during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no satisfaction because it is subject to gradation due to the superimposed degrees of inferiority.

The dawning of knowledge results in the fulfillment of all duties because it brings about the cessation of the superimposition of all deficiencies and the removal of the objectivity attributed [to the Self]; thus, since it manifests as the object of unconditional love, the witness-consciousness (sākṣyānanda) is indeed unobscured.

Others, however, maintain that bliss, even while being manifest, is indeed veiled because of the experience of concealment in the form: "Bliss does not exist in me; it does not manifest. This is because, even though there is only one witness (*sākṣin*), there can be a distinction between forms imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, there is no contradiction between its being unobscured in its nature as consciousness and being obscured in its nature as bliss. Furthermore, since the manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) serves to remove obscuration, obscuration is not incompatible with that which is manifesting. Moreover, obscuration is observed precisely when something is manifest, as in the thought: "I do not know the meaning of what you have said."

Nor should it be argued that in that case, what is experienced is precisely the concealment of the particular (viśeṣa) through the delimitation of the unobscured universal form (sāmānyākāra); for if the concealment of one thing were to appear through the delimitation of another, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of such a principle. Nor should it be argued that the relation of universal and particular (sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva) serves as the restrictive factor, thereby avoiding the over-extension; for since there exists no relation of universal and particular distinct from the relation of pervader and pervaded (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva), it would follow that one could experience the ignorance concealing smoke in the form, "I do not know fire."

Therefore, that which is delimited by ignorance appears; thus, it is precisely that which is veiled. Consequently, it is logical that ignorance persists even while [the object] is manifesting. And just as ignorance veils consciousness (caitanya) while leaving aside its witness-portion (sākṣyaṃśa), so too does it veil bliss (ānanda) while leaving aside only those portions of bliss that have been swallowed up by their respective mental modifications (vṛtti) in the form of pleasure. This very process constitutes the sublation of the veiling of objective bliss.

And this overcoming of the veil occurs at the time of dawn, like the overcoming of external veils, by virtue of a specific modification [of consciousness] induced by a specific cause, manifesting in degrees of intensity (tara-tama-bhāva). Therefore, they say that the mutual distinction between the bliss of one's own nature (svarūpānanda), the bliss of the object (viṣayānanda), and the various pleasures derived from objects is established. However, in every respect, since the witnessing consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) is unobscured, it is the same [in both cases]: the manifestation of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth occurs by that [consciousness] without depending on a mental modification (vṛtti) for the purpose of overcoming a veil. ||16||

But if this is so, how can there be the synthesis of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and so forth? For it is impossible for a latent impression (saṃskāra), which consists of the subtle state of cognition, to be deposited by the eternal witness (sākṣin), since that [witness] does not come into contact with cognition.

Regarding this, some say: the ego (ahaṃkāra), which is always illumined by the Witness (sākṣin) through its own association, is also illumined by the Witness as delimited by its own transformation into the form of various objective modifications (*vṛtti*) such as those of a jar and so forth. Because it is thus non-eternal, the deposition of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is possible for it, just as it is for an object like a jar. For there is no rule that the deposition of a latent impression regarding its own object occurs only by means of the Witness as delimited by a modification having that [object] as its form; if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-remembrance of a modification due to the impossibility of a latent impression regarding that modification itself.

This is because an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has been refuted by the rejection of a further cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) directed toward a cognition that is itself an object of a [prior] mental modification (*vṛtti*). Rather, the rule is simply this: whatever is manifested by consciousness delimited by a particular mental modification (*vṛtti*), that very modification deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding its own object. In this way, cognitions, pleasures, and so forth—which are also modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—are illuminated by the Witness (*sākṣin*), which is non-eternal and delimited by each respective [modification], just as sparks emerging from a red-hot iron ball are illuminated by the fire delimited by themselves. Thus, it is logical that a latent impression is deposited even in those cases. As for that which...
The consciousness residing in the cognition of the single form of a jar would manifest only that jar.
The cognizedness of the jar is manifested by the consciousness of Brahman. ||4||

Thus, there is the position stated in the *Kūṭasthadīpa* that knowledge, as qualified by its object, is manifested by the Brahman-consciousness delimited by that object; and subsequently, there is the position stated in the *Tattvapradīpikā* that knowledge, volition, and so forth, are manifested by the eternal witness (sākṣin) which is the undelimited, pure consciousness. In both cases, since consciousness is of the nature of immediate manifestation (*aparokṣa*) with respect to what it is in contact with, its connection with the mental modification (*vṛtti*) must necessarily be asserted. Therefore, because there exists an impermanent form [of consciousness] conjoined with that [modification], there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the production of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) within those [modifications].

Others, however, in order to establish the continuity of the connection with ignorance and so forth even during deep sleep, accept an imagined mental modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance in the form of "I" and thereby account for the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the referent "I. Nor does this position entail the impossibility of the continuity of the referent "I" at a time when there is a stream of other cognitions—such as the recollection: "For all this time, I remained seeing this very thing"—because, just as pleasure and pain can coexist through a difference in their limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*), there is no contradiction in two mental modifications coexisting; thus, even during a stream of other cognitions, a continuous flow of mental modifications of ignorance in the form of "I" is possible.

Others, however, maintain that the mental state (*vṛtti*) consisting of the form "I" is indeed a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Nevertheless, it is not knowledge (*jñāna*), unlike the modifications involved in meditation (*upāsanā*) and the like, because it is not produced by the established causes of such [knowledge]. For in this case, the definition of perception through the eyes and so forth is not possible, nor are there any inferential marks (*liṅga*) and the like. This is because the apprehension of the "I-notion" is observed even in one who is devoid of the recollection of inferential marks and so forth. Nor is the mind (*manas*) the instrument (*karaṇa*), since its status as an instrument is nowhere established, given that it functions as the material cause (*upādāna*) [of cognition].

If it is argued that, in that case, the recognition of the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) would also not be a cognition (*jñāna*), we say no. For although that [recognition] lacks the nature of cognition with respect to its "I"-portion (*ahamaṃśa*), it possesses the nature of cognition with respect to its "thatness" (*tattā*)-portion, because it is produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) established as the instrument of memory. They say that there is no contradiction between being a cognition and not being a cognition within a single cognition—just as there is no contradiction between being indirect (*parokṣatva*) and direct (*aparokṣatva*), or between being valid (*pramātva*) and invalid (*apramātva*).

Others, however, maintain that even the egoic mode of existence (*ahamākārā*) is indeed knowledge, because of the experience "I know myself. Nor is there an impossibility of a means (*karaṇa*); for, in accordance with experience, one may postulate that the internal sense-organ (*antarindriya*), namely the mind (*manas*), serves as the instrument as well. Thus they say. ||17||

This being the case, it follows as a settled rule that only those mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which are immediate with respect to external objects possess the capacity to sublate the veil [of ignorance].

Now, one might object: "Even this rule is not absolute, because in the case of a mother-of-pearl shell appearing as silver, the modification in the form of 'this' (*idamākāra-vṛtti*) does not sublate ignorance; otherwise, since there would be no material cause (*upādāna*), the production of silver would be impossible. If you say this:

On this point, they say: although the ignorance regarding the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) is removed by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this," the ignorance regarding specific attributes such as "mother-of-pearl-ness" (*śuktitva*) is not removed; therefore, that very [ignorance] remains the material cause (*upādāna*) of the silver. This is because it is experienced that the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver occurs when there is ignorance of mother-of-pearl-ness, and that it does not occur when that [mother-of-pearl-ness] is known. For in the *Vivaraṇa*, a commentary on the *Bhāṣya* on the section concerning superimposition, it is stated that only that ignorance which is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is the material cause of the superimposition of silver and so forth.

For this very reason, the "mother-of-pearl aspect" (śuktyaṃśa) is the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), while the "this-aspect" (idamaṃśa) is the locus (ādhāra). As explained in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, the substrate is the object of ignorance accompanied by its manifestation (savilāsājñānaviṣaya), whereas the locus is that which, though not of that nature, appears in the form of that [superimposed object] within the cognition of superimposition (āropabuddhi). Thus it is analyzed.

Others, however, maintain that for silver—which is perceived as being mixed with the "this" portion in the cognition "this is silver"—the very ignorance regarding the "this" portion is the material cause (*upādāna*). Even though its power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) is removed by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this," it continues to exist along with its power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti); therefore, there is no impossibility of its being the material cause.

They say that even when there is the superimposition of the uprightness and downwardness of trees reflected in water, and when the superimposition of the phenomenal world persists even for one liberated while living, although the obscuring power (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) has been removed immediately after the direct realization of the substrate in its entirety, ignorance (*ajñāna*) alone—devoid of its power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*)—is accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*).
