However, Nṛsiṃhabhaṭṭopādhyāya, the sovereign of poets and logicians, considers the inquiry into whether that [vṛtti] can or cannot remove ignorance to be baseless, on the grounds that apart from the erroneous mental modification (vṛtti) in the form "this is silver," there is no vṛtti at all in the form of "this" prior to the production of the silver.

For instance, first of all, no mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this" is established by experience apart from the modification in the form of error. Nor can it be postulated as an effect—that the knowledge of the general nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the cause of superimposition—since there is no evidence for its being the cause thereof. Furthermore, the non-arising of silver and so forth in the absence of contact with the substrate is not proof [for such a claim]; rather, this leads to the conclusion that contact with a defective sense organ alone is the cause of superimposition.

Nor can it be argued that while association (*samprayoga*) does not pervade all instances of error, the manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-sphuraṇa*), however, by itself pervades even the superimposition of the ego (*ahaṅkāra-adhyāsa*) upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*) which is self-luminous; for even that [manifestation of the substrate] does not pervade the superimposition of jars and the like. This is because, prior to the perception of a jar or similar object, a visual modification (*cākṣuṣa-vṛtti*) cannot possibly have as its object the formless Brahman which serves as the substrate for those objects, since the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa-prakāśa*) is veiled.

It cannot be argued that the mere manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), whether veiled or un-veiled, is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) because it is common to both cases; for since the manifestation in the form of consciousness delimited by that [substrate] exists even before the contact with the "this-aspect" (*idamaṃśa*) of the mother-of-pearl—though it is then veiled—superimposition would result at that time as well. Nor can it be said that the general manifestation of the substrate is the cause for superimposition in general, while the manifested manifestation of the substrate is the cause for illusory (*prātibhāsika*) superimposition (and thus there is no over-extension), because it is more appropriate for the general to be the cause of the general and the specific to be the cause of the specific.

Even so, this [definition] fails to encompass superimpositions such as the illusory yellowness of a conch-shell or the blueness of water in a well; for since visual cognition cannot occur without being conditioned by color, there is no perception of the whiteness residing in the conch-shell at that time, and thus it is impossible for a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the formless substrate (the conch-shell, etc. to exist prior to the superimposition.

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of apparent (prātibhāsika) objects, such as silver, let there be only the aforementioned specific cause for superimposition; for if that were so, since one must necessarily state that the contact of a defective sense organ is the cause for the superimposition of a yellow conch and the like—prior to the actual contact—in order to avoid the undesirable consequence of such a superimposition occurring then, it would follow by parsimony (lāghava) that this very [defective contact] is established as the general cause for all apparent superimpositions. Consequently, the occasional nature of the superimposition of silver would be accounted for by that alone, and the status of the manifestation of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) as a cause of superimposition—whether in a general or specific sense—would remain unestablished.

Now, even if similarity is not the cause in other types of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) that are independent of it, it must necessarily be stated that in the case of the superimposition of silver and the like—which does depend on similarity—the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which consists in the cognition of the object qualified by specific attributes such as the particular color that constitutes the similarity to silver, is the cause. For if mere contact with a defective sense organ were the cause, it would follow that silver would be superimposed upon a piece of coal just as it is upon mother-of-pearl.

Nor should it be argued that even similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not a cause [of superimposition] by virtue of being a defect of the object; for superimposition occurs even when there is an error of similarity regarding a dissimilar thing, as seen in the case of attributing the nature of a dark stone slab to the mass of water in the ocean from a distance. Nor is it correct to say, on the grounds of the maxim "the cause of that [effect] alone," that the causal complex for the cognition of similarity itself should be the cause of superimposition; because a causal complex of cognition is never observed to be a direct cause of an external object, and because the status of being a cognition of similarity is simpler (and thus more parsimonious) than that.

Nor should it be argued that, just as there is a fixed rule that the superimposition of blueness occurs only in clear water—even when that water is naturally white and contained within a bright silver pitcher—and not in a pearl, so too the superimposition of silver occurs on mother-of-pearl due to the very nature of the object, and not on glowing coals and the like, rather than because of a dependence upon the cognition of similarity.

For even though the state of being a lotus bud is not superimposed upon a piece of cloth by its own nature, we observe that such a superimposition occurs precisely when that same piece of cloth has been fashioned into that shape through cutting and other processes; from this, it is certain that the occurrence of such a superimposition depends upon the presence or absence of the cognition of similarity, rather than following the intrinsic nature of the object itself. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of that superimposition occurring at that place at any other time as well.

It is replied: Even on the view that knowledge of similarity is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), its causality must be asserted only in cases of superimpositions such as silver, which are obstructed by the perception of specific features (*viśeṣadarśana*). It is not, however, [asserted] in cases of superimpositions such as a yellow conch, which are not so obstructed, because [the causality of similarity] is impossible there. Furthermore, since it is a rule that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of an obstructing cognition necessarily acts as an obstructor in cases obstructed by the perception of specific features, the causal complex of the perception of specific features itself must necessarily be admitted as the obstructor. Since all systematic distinctions are thus established from that alone, what is the point of postulating the causality of knowledge of similarity?

For instance, when the eye is in contact with charcoal and the like, there is no superimposition of silver because the causal complex for perceiving its specific qualities, such as blueness, is present. Even in the case of mother-of-pearl, when the eye is in contact with the blue portion that pervades it, there is no such superimposition because that [perception of the specific quality] exists. Superimposition occurs only when there is contact with a merely similar part, because in that case the perception of the specific quality is absent. If it is argued: "Even then, since the causal complex for perceiving the specific quality of 'mother-of-pearl-ness' (*śuktitva*) is present, there would be the undesirable consequence of no superimposition," we say:

No. At the time of superimposition, there is an absence of the perception of "mother-of-pearl-ness"; therefore, you too must admit that prior to that [superimposition], the causal complex for such perception was absent.

If it is argued that at that time there is an admission of the absence of the causal conditions for perceiving the "shell-ness" (śuktitva) due to the obstruction caused by the defect (doṣa) consisting of the superimposition (adhyāsa) in the form of the cognition of similarity to me, and that such an admission on your part results in the "dawn at the very house where one was working at night" (ghaṭṭakuṭīprabhāta), we say: no.

Immediately after approaching one's own location, while the glittering appearance (cākacikya) consisting of a resemblance to silver is still being perceived, the nacre-ness (śuktitva) is apprehended; thus, it is not established that this [glittering appearance] acts as an obstacle to its [the nacre-ness] causal complex. Alternatively, one must state that the absence of that causal complex is due either to an obstruction caused by defects such as distance, or to the non-coincidence of the perceivers of the manifesting factors, such as the blue back-surface and so forth.

Thus, in the case of the ocean water, due to the defect that causes the superimposition of a fixed blue color, and because of the absence of the proximity of waves and other factors that manifest its watery nature at a distance, there is an absence of the causal complex for perceiving specific qualities such as whiteness or its being a mass of water; consequently, there occurs the superimposition of [solid] rock-surface-ness and the like. On a wide cloth, however, because the causal complex for perceiving specific qualities such as its breadth exists, there is no superimposition of the bud-like form of a white lotus; yet, when it has been fashioned into that shape through cutting and so forth, because that causal complex is absent, that superimposition does occur.

If it is objected: "In that case, why does the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver not occur upon a piece of iron touched by the hand, since there is an absence of the causal conditions for perceiving its specific blue color and because similarity is not required? [The answer is: It certainly does occur. However, due to the absence of the causal conditions for perceiving the specific features that distinguish it from copper and other metals, it is not fully realized through that superimposition; thus, in some instances where multiple superimpositions are possible, it becomes an object of doubt. In other cases, however, such as in a treasury room where silver is commonly found, the superimposition of silver alone occurs.

In some cases, such as with mother-of-pearl and the like, even when there is a cognition of similarity, the superimposition (adhyāsa) does not arise at times due to the absence of defects in the instruments [of perception] and so forth; likewise, even when there is no superimposition, there is no loss [to our position].

Therefore, this mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this" is not to be inferred from its effect, nor is it to be inferred from the cause—the unimpeded contact with the object "this"—since we maintain that this very modification of "this" has as its object silver existing at the same time as itself, which is a transformation of ignorance (*avidyā*) agitated by the contact of a defective sense organ.

And in that case, since the silver—which arises simultaneously with the cognition and exists merely as a mental appearance—shares its identity with that [substratum], it is possible for it to be perceived by the eye through the very contact (*saṃprayoga*) with the object "this" (*idam*), even though there is no prior contact with that [silver]. This is because the illusory silver is experienced as being visual, as in the perception, "I see the silver with my eyes," despite the absence of any direct contact between the eye and that [illusory] silver.

Nor is it the case that this [perception] is not visual simply because of the absence of contact with the eyes as a subverting factor, nor is it produced by a defective sense-organ contact at the same time as the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of "this-ness. This is because sense-organ contact, which is the cause of knowledge, is not established as being a cause of the object itself. Rather, it occurs immediately after the modification of "this-ness," is produced by it, and is manifested by it through superimposition upon the Witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), thereby becoming its object.

It must be stated that the experience of visuality [in the case of a yellow conch] depends on the eye only indirectly, by virtue of generating the "this-ness" (idam-vṛtti) which manifests the consciousness that illuminates itself. For if that were the case, it would follow that the eye is not required in the error of a yellow conch. This is because there is no requirement for the eye in the apprehension of the conch itself—since a mere conch cannot be grasped by the eye without its color—and nor is there a requirement for the apprehension of yellowness, as it is not admitted that the superimposed object (the yellow color) is perceived through the senses.

Nor should it be argued that yellowness is not superimposed by its own nature, but rather that only the contact with the conch is superimposed upon the yellowness of the bile located in the eye which is being experienced; for if that were the case, it would follow that both the conch and its contact are not objects of perception. This is because those two cannot be manifested by the witness-consciousness through a connection with a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that has the form of the bile's yellowness located in another place. Furthermore, one does not admit a single mental modification whose object is the conch as conjoined with yellowness.

Nor can it be maintained that the superimposition of contact [of yellowness] upon the conch shell is not accepted because of the defect of the yellowness of bile situated in the region of the eye; rather, it must be said that the superimposition of contact occurs there because that [bile], having gone out along with the rays of the eye and pervading the object, [comes into contact]. For it is possible [to say] "it is saffron-colored like [a cloth] dyed with kusumbha," or that there is contact with the Witness (sākṣin) manifested by a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of that [object]. If that were the case, then when a conch shell is being viewed by one whose eyes are afflicted by bile—as if it were coated in gold—there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the cognition of yellowness for others as well.

Nor can it be argued that once the yellowness has been apprehended in close proximity, it cannot be apprehended at a distance—just as a bird flying high in the sky cannot be caught by others nearby—because for others as well, if they direct their eyes toward the vicinity of that [object], the apprehension of the yellowness would be unavoidable due to the presence of its proximity.

Even so, since it is impossible to speak of a superimposition (āropa) being experienced in the case of the superimposition of blueness upon the water of a clear river flowing over a bed of extremely white sand, or the superimposition of the blueness of the sky, or the superimposition of blueness upon red garments at night under the moonlight, one cannot avoid the unavoidable consequence that the eye would be useless there if one does not admit a visual modification (cākṣuṣavṛtti) whose object is the locus as conjoined with blueness.

Furthermore, this is because the *Pañcapādikā* establishes that for a child who has never tasted a bitter flavor, the appearance of bitterness in what is sweet is caused by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from experience in another life; it thereby clarifies that the bitter flavor being superimposed in its own nature is indeed perceptible through the senses. Otherwise, the dependence on the operation of the sense of taste in that case would be inexplicable.

Therefore, in the instances of superimposition such as the aforementioned blue color, it must be admitted that the superimposition arises simultaneously with the visual modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward its object, solely through contact with the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and that it is the object of that modification; thus, its visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) is to be accepted. For, in the absence of color, if there were no modification directed toward the substratum alone, there would be no manifestation of the consciousness of the object, and consequently, water and the blue color superimposed upon it could not be manifested by it.

In the case of the superimposition of a bitter taste, however, because the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) and the superimposed object (adhyāsa) are not both graspable by a single sense organ, the manifestation of the consciousness delimited by that [taste] occurs through a mental modification (vṛtti) directed toward the substrate produced by the sense of touch. Then, due to the contact of the tongue with the bile-affected [object], the superimposition of the bitter taste and the gustatory modification (rāsanavṛtti) having that [taste] alone as its object arise simultaneously; thus, the bitter taste must also be admitted to be an object of gustation.

Since even indirectly there is no utility for the sense of taste regarding the bitter taste—which is manifested by the consciousness revealed through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is the substrate produced by the tactile sense—it is impossible to justify the experience of its being tasted (*rāsanatva*) in that instance by any other means whatsoever. Likewise, since the silver [in the illusion] can also be established as visual (*cākṣuṣatva*), the experience "I see" is not to be sublated.

Nor should it be argued that if non-associated silver were visual, there would be a violation of the established rules regarding cause and effect—namely, that "in all perception, sense-object contact is the cause" and "in the perception of silver, conjunction with silver is the cause"—because the first rule is unestablished, as there is no single, common property of "contact-ness" (*sannikarṣatva*) that subsumes conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the other types of contact.

Regarding the second rule, according to the Nyāya school, since it is possible for the superimposition of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) to occur even upon some non-substantial entity that is unfit for conjunction—just as in the case of darkness—the third rule is not established. This is because, from the perspective of empirical usage, the cognition of "substance-ness" in illusory silver is accepted as being a superimposition of the substrate's own "substance-ness," just like its "this-ness" (*idantva*), and thus there is no contradiction with the second rule. Furthermore, apart from the general causal relationship in the form of the second rule, the postulation of a specific causal relationship is refuted by the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*), and thus the third rule remains unproven.

Even regarding the principle that "whatever is the cause for a general category is the cause for its particular instance," this principle applies only to cases such as seeds and sprouts where one accepts a general causal relationship; for in those cases, there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that another sprout would arise from another seed. Since that is the scope [of the principle], a specific causal relationship distinct from it—which would be like a fleshy protuberance on a goat's neck—is not established.

Nor should it be argued that even here there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), such that by accepting the general rule alone—"in the perception of a substance, conjunction with a substance is the cause"—the perception of one substance would result from conjunction with another; for we accept the specific rule: "in the perception of a particular substance, conjunction with that very substance is the cause. Otherwise, even under a third rule, the over-extension would be unavoidable. Therefore, there is no contingency of violating an established rule.

Furthermore, there is no fault here even in the violation of an established rule, because such unerring experiences as "I see this silver" and "I see blue water" cannot be accounted for without assuming a restriction of rules—such as "in all perception, sensory contact with the object is the cause"—to the domain of empirical reality (*vyāvahārika*), even if those rules were previously accepted as universal.

And this being the case, since the possibility of a restrictive assumption—namely, "we do not say that sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is the cause of valid cognition"—cannot be maintained, there would follow the superimposition here of silver located in another place without any sensory contact; this would result in the advocacy of the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*). This is because it is impossible for silver located in another place—which is devoid of the veil of manifested consciousness—to be directly perceived. Furthermore, it is established by the impossibility of [otherwise accounting for] the appearance and sublation of the error that the object of the delusion is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).

Nor should it be argued that if one accepts the perceptibility of the illusory object based merely on its conjunction with the substrate, then why would the redness (*raṅga*)—which is to be superimposed there at a later time—not also be visual at the very moment of the superimposition of silver upon the mother-of-pearl? For although there is no difference in the perception of the glittering luster common to both redness and silver at the time of the silver-superimposition, there is no superimposition of redness there at that time due to the absence of personal defects such as passion (*rāga*); for that very reason, I accept the non-arising of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward that [redness].

Therefore, there is only one single modification (vṛtti) produced by the sense organ, which has as its object silver as permeated by the "this" aspect; it is not the case that there is a separate modification in the form of "this" prior to that. Thus, the inquiry into whether this [modification] possesses the capacity to remove ignorance or not should not be undertaken here alone.

Others, however, hold that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form "this" (*idamākārā*)—which serves as the cause for superimposition by means of the knowledge of the substrate—is sufficient; for since the manifestation of the silver superimposed thereon is possible through the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) manifested by that very [modification], and since the depositing of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the object silver is established by that same "this"-modification which manifests the witness that illumines it, they consider a separate mental modification in the form of silver (*rajatākāravṛtti*) to be purposeless.

According to some, in the view that there are two cognitions (*jñāna*), the first cognition, "this" (*idam*), is the cause of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*); the second cognition, "this is silver" (*idaṃ rajatam*), has as its object the silver that is superimposed, but it does not have as its object the superimposed alone apart from the "this" aspect. This is because one experiences that cognition as having as its object silver that has attained identity with the "this" object, as in the awareness: "I know this silver."

Others, however, hold that just as the ignorance (*avidyā*) residing in the consciousness delimited by the "this" portion (*idamaṃśa*) undergoes illusory transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of silver, so too the ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*) whose object is the "this" portion undergoes illusory transformation into the form of the appearance of the cognition of silver; it is not the case that there exists a cognition of silver that is non-superimposed, like the mental modification directed toward the "this" portion.

And thus, just as the silver possesses the manifestation of the relation with "this-ness" residing in its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is logical that the cognition of silver also possesses the manifestation of the relation with the status of being an object of "this-ness" residing in its substrate; therefore, it need not be admitted that this cognition itself has "this" as its object.

Nor should it be argued that, because the superimposed relation between "thisness" (*idantva*) and silver—just like "silver-ness"—is within the scope of the cognition of silver, its counter-correlate, "thisness," must also be admitted as an object of that cognition; for since the locus of its identity-in-itself (*tādātmya*) is already the object "thisness," there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in admitting that relation as an object of that cognition.

Nor should it be argued that the object of a single mental modification (*vṛtti*) must be asserted, because the *Bhāṣyavivaraṇa* establishes that there is no possibility of a rule for the simultaneous manifestation of both the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the superimposed object (*adhyāsya*) within a single cognition. For they say that even when the modifications are distinct, the manifestation of those two occurs within a single witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) that is made manifest by the modification having the form of "this" (*idam-ākāra-vṛtti*). ||18||

Now, since the manifestation of all objects is possible through the grace of the Witness alone, what is the use of a mental modification (*vṛtti*)? Even if one accepts its necessity for the sake of establishing impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding objects such as jars, the admission that it must go out [of the mind] is useless; for even in the case of an object like a jar, its manifestation can be accounted for by the Witness itself as delimited by a modification that has not gone out, just as in the case of indirect (inferential) cognition.

Nor does this result in the impossibility of distinguishing between the direct and the indirect, for that distinction is established simply by the difference in the types of modifications produced by specific instruments, just as in the case of verbal testimony and inference.

On this point, some say: in the case of perception, it is consciousness (caitanya) as delimited by the object itself—by virtue of the object being the locus—that constitutes the manifestation of the object. Since a direct relation in the form of identity is possible, it is improper to postulate a relation of essential nature (svarūpa-sambandha) or any other kind; therefore, the admission that the mental modification (vṛtti) goes out [of the mind] is appropriate for the purpose of manifesting that [consciousness].

In the case of an imperceptible object, such as fire situated at a distance, since there can be no connection with the mental mode (*vṛtti*), and because—unlike the sense organs—one does not perceive any gateway for the exit of the mode that would possess positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one is compelled to accept, by necessity, that the consciousness delimited by the non-emerged mode itself becomes directed toward the object through its own essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

Furthermore, a clarity is indeed experienced when something is perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa) as compared to what is understood through verbal testimony or inference. For even if the specific fragrance of a mango tree and so forth has been taught by a reliable person a hundred times, there is no such clarity as when it is perceived through direct perception; for even after that, the inquiry "How is that? persists.

Nor should it be suspected that, even when sweetness alone is understood from a word, there can be no apprehension of sweetness as qualified by a specific uncommon genus (asādhāraṇajātiviśeṣa) through the word, because of the absence of a word denoting a specific subordinate genus within the function of the mango’s sweetness; or, even if such a word existed, because its relation [to the object] has not been grasped by the ear. This is because from the word, "There is a specific excellence of sweetness in the mango that surpasses all," there is indeed an apprehension of even the specific subordinate genus residing therein.

For this word denoting a particular (*viśeṣa-śabda*) does not, setting aside the particular residing in that [object], convey a particular residing elsewhere; for that would result in a loss of its validity (*aprāmāṇya*). Nor can it be argued that it conveys the particular residing in that very object merely as a "particular" in a general form, and not as a specific one, because of the resulting desire to know (*jijñāsā*); for even in the case of perception, since the specific quality of sweet taste—which is a particular of the genus *jāti*—is apprehended only in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), and other particulars residing in that specific genus are not apprehended, there would follow the consequence of a continuous persistence of the desire to know.

Therefore, one must accept the following distinction: clarity, which is capable of terminating the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), arises because that which is grasped by perception is enveloped by consciousness (*caitanya*)—which is of a single flavor with manifest immediacy (*aparokṣya*); however, in the case of that which is known through words and so forth, there is a lack of clarity due to the absence of that [envelopment]. For this very reason, pleasure and the like, which are known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), possess clarity. Furthermore, even in the case of Brahman, which is known through a verbal modification (*śābdavṛtti*), there is a lack of clarity as long as ignorance has not been removed prior to reflection (*manana*) and so on; once that ignorance is removed thereafter, clarity occurs. Thus they establish the necessity for the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛttinirgama*).

But surely, even by this much, it has been stated that the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is for the purpose of removing the ignorance that veils the object. That is incorrect; for even if one accepts that the ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the object is removed by a modification that has not emerged [from the internal organ], there is no over-extension of the principle.

Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the knowledge of Devadatta’s pot would entail the cessation of Yajñadatta’s ignorance regarding that same pot, since they share the same object; for while knowledge and ignorance residing in the consciousness whose substrate is the "I" (the self) are contradictory because they have different substrates, having a common substrate is not a necessary factor for their opposition.

Even if one accepts that the condition for the contradiction between knowledge and ignorance is having the same locus and object, and even if one admits the emergence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains unavoidable; for the mental modification regarding a jar belonging to Devadatta and the ignorance regarding a jar belonging to Yajñadatta would both result in having the same locus in the consciousness delimited by the jar (*ghaṭāvacchinna-caitanya*). Therefore, since the condition for contradiction must be stated separately as "the ignorance which obscures an object for a particular person is removable by the manifestation of that object for that very person," the requirement of a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*) is unnecessary.

On this point, they say: if one does not admit the emergence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it is indeed difficult to determine the very factor that constitutes the contradiction between knowledge and ignorance. If it is argued that this is already stated in the passage beginning, "the ignorance which [subsists] with respect to which person," we say no; for then it would follow that even indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) would remove the ignorance residing in the object. If it is argued that "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) is also a qualification of the subverting knowledge, then what is this immediacy? It cannot, first of all, be a universal (*jāti*).

If that [ignorance] were present even in the aspect of the staff in a visual cognition whose object is a person qualified by a staff—brought forth by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) "this man was possessed of a staff"—then it would follow that ignorance residing in the object is removed in respect to that [staff] as well. Furthermore, it would entail the experience of immediacy (*āparokṣya*) even in that aspect, such that one would think, "I am directly perceiving the staff."

Even if there is no actual experience [of the object], if one were to postulate a contact (*sannikarṣa*) as a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) and thereby accept a conceptual immediacy (*kālpnikāparokṣya*) in that case because it is produced by sense-contact, then one would also have to accept such a thing for inference and so forth by postulating a contact such as the knowledge of the logical mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, if there were no immediacy with respect to the aspect of the staff, it could not be a universal (*jāti*), because a universal is necessarily pervasively present (*vyāpyavṛtti*). Even if that rule were not fixed, it could not be a non-pervasively present universal, since no distinct limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) could be specified for it.

Nor can it be a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because such an adjunct cannot be defined. If it is argued that the defining characteristic is "being produced by a sense-organ" (*indriyajanyatva*), we say no; for this fails to encompass perception by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*). Furthermore, it over-extends to the perceptual cognition of a jar qualified by weight and so forth—which are brought to mind through inference or verbal testimony—since it would apply to the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*) as well. This is because, in the absence of any other instrument, the sense-organ itself acts as the producer even regarding that portion which is otherwise indirect (*parokṣa*), due to the power of the auxiliary factor of mental presentation (*upanaya*). Moreover, since no inclusive determinant of being produced (*janyatāvacchedaka*) is apprehended, it is difficult to establish "being produced by a sense-organ" across multiple instances.

Furthermore, since that very [object] which was first perceived can be established as having a direct (*aparokṣa*) form upon its apprehension, it is impossible to postulate that the state of being direct—which is incompatible with the nature of perceptual experience—belongs to something produced by the sense organs. By this, the following objection is also refuted: "Directness consists solely in being produced by sensory contact; and in the case of the indirect portion produced by the senses aided by *upanaya* (mental presentation), there is no production by sensory contact, because *upanaya*, being common to other means of knowledge, is not a sensory contact since it functions as the manifestation of what is presented (*upanītabhāna*) even in inference. This is so because there is a lack of uniformity (*ananugama*) among the various types of sensory contacts, such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the rest.

If it is argued, "Let that very immediacy (*aparokṣya*) which you accept also belong to me," we say no. For that [immediacy], which is to be established in the context of defining verbal immediacy, must be shown there itself to be produced by the cessation of ignorance; therefore, it cannot logically serve as a qualifying attribute that causes that cessation. Consequently, because the knowledge of Brahman—heard in the scripture, "The knower of the Self overcomes sorrow"—is necessarily associated with Brahman, the material cause of all things and the substratum of root-ignorance, it brings about the cessation of that root-ignorance.

Accepting the rule that "sensory functions arise as conjoined with the consciousness delimited by their respective objects precisely through the capacity of the contact between those specific sense organs and those objects," one must state that the defining characteristic of the sublating knowledge is its necessary conjunction with the consciousness that is the substratum of ignorance. Thus, it is established that the factor determining the opposition between knowledge and ignorance is this: "Whatever ignorance obscures a particular object for a particular person, that [ignorance] is removable by a knowledge whose very existence is necessarily dependent on its conjunction with the consciousness that is the substratum of that ignorance regarding that object for that person. This explains the causal basis for the contradiction between knowledge and ignorance.

And this being the case, it does not follow that even verbal knowledge whose object is the nature of the channels (nāḍīs) and the heart would have the capacity to remove ignorance. For although such verbal knowledge may sometimes involve a connection with a real entity—either the channels or the heart—since it can also arise without a connection to its object, it lacks the property of having its very existence necessarily dependent upon that connection. Therefore, in order to account for the opposition between knowledge and ignorance, the emergence of the mental modification (vṛtti) must be asserted.

Others, however, say that because it is simpler to establish that ignorance residing in the object is sublated by ignorance co-located with it, the emergence of the mental modification (vṛtti) follows as a necessary consequence.

Others, however, say that since it is observed that external light removes external darkness only when there is co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the emergence of the mental modification (vṛtti) is established in accordance with this analogy.

However, some say that even if there is no need for the outward extension of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) for the purpose of overcoming the veil (*āvaraṇa*), it is nevertheless required either for the purpose of the reflection of consciousness (*ciduparāga*), or for the purpose of manifesting the non-difference between the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛcaitanya*) and the consciousness of Brahman which illumines the object.

Now, by what means of knowledge is this non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman established, which is manifested through [spiritual] transformation (*vṛtti*)? The proclamation is: "It is established by the Vedānta as its authority. When all the Vedāntas are examined through the marks of purport (*tātparya*), such as the uniformity of their opening and concluding passages, they are seen to be in complete harmony (*samanvaya*) with the non-dual Brahman, who is non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*). That this is the case has been elaborated upon in the very scripture itself in the chapter on "Harmony" (*Samanvayādhyāya*); it is not demonstrated here for fear of excessive prolixity. ||19||
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Siddhāntaleśasaṃgraha*.
|| The Second Chapter ||

Now, if it is asked: "How can there be a systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with a non-dual Brahman, given the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge?"—the answer is: no. This is because, through the scriptures and reasonings cited in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, the world (*prapañca*) as apprehended by perception and the like is understood to be false, being a mere illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman. But surely, it cannot be established by scripture or reasoning that the world is false, because this contradicts perception and other means of knowledge which apprehend the reality of jars and so forth, such as in the cognition "the jar exists" (*ghaṭaḥ san*).

Regarding this, the authors of the *Tattvaśuddhi* say: "Perception does not grasp the jar, the cloth, and so forth, nor their existence; rather, it grasps pure Being (*sanmātra*) which inheres in the jar and other objects as their substrate. Thus, even perception is indeed conducive to the establishment of the non-duality of Brahman, whose nature is Being. If that were so, perception would take the form 'Being, Being,' and not the perception 'the jar exists' and so forth, which conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organs. To this we reply: No.

Just as in illusions the "this-portion" (idamaṃśa), which is the substrate, is apprehended through perception, and the positive and negative concomitance of the sense organs is exhausted in that alone; whereas the silver-portion, which is superimposed, appears through delusion—likewise, in all cases, pure Being (sanmātra) is apprehended through perception, and the operation of the sense organs pertains to that alone. This is because it is accepted that the appearance of distinct objects such as jars and the like is due to delusion.

If it is argued that, just as in that case, the acceptance of such [non-duality] here is groundless because no sublation is observed, we say: no. For even in the absence of observed sublation, the very basis for this is the fact that the reality of distinctions such as jars and the like is unfit for perception, just like objects separated by space and time.

For instance, a jar or the like, which is perceived immediately following the operation of the sense organs, is perceived as being distinct from everything else; this is because at that time, no doubt or error regarding the difference of the jar and so forth is observed. Even in cases where there is a doubt concerning a post or the like—such as whether it is a person—there, the distinction from things other than that [post] certainly manifests, since it is neither doubted nor erroneously inverted. Furthermore, the perception of difference, which is necessarily co-apprehended with its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*), is not possible through direct sensory perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is argued that—since even remote counter-correlates (pratiyogins) can exist due to separation by space and time—the cognition of difference must be of the nature of memory with respect to its aspect as the counter-correlate because it requires a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), just as recognition is of the nature of memory with respect to its aspect of "that-ness" (*tattā*)—we say no; for even so, there is an absence of such [memory-nature] regarding the aspect of the counter-correlative's qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) inherent in the difference.

Furthermore, since Mount Meru (Kanakācala) is not the counter-correlate of difference because it is a real entity (*vastu*), the possibility of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding that [counter-correlate] arises through an inference whose object is the qualification of the counter-correlate within the difference. This is because, in the absence of knowledge of the difference, no inference could occur, which would lead to the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Moreover, when there is an error regarding the non-difference of the subject, the probandum, the reason, or the "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*), inference does not proceed due to the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); therefore, knowledge of the difference between them is required to dispel the knowledge of their non-difference.

If it is argued that perception occurs with respect to the aspect of the counter-positive’s qualification just as it does with respect to the aspect of difference, we say no; for if the counter-positive is not perceived, perception of its qualification is impossible, since the perception of a relation cannot occur without the perception of both relata.

Therefore, since the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) that is unfit for direct perception appears only as an illusory form, both difference—which is necessarily known through the same cognition as its correlate—and the jar and so forth—which are necessarily known through the same cognition as the distinct entity—are objects of illusion alone; thus, perception is conducive to the establishment of non-duality (advaita), which grasps only undifferentiated existence.

The author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, however, says: even though jars and the like are perceptible by the senses, there is no contradiction because [cognitions] such as "the jar exists" (*san ghaṭaḥ*) involve the superimposition of the substrate’s existence (*sattā*). If it is asked, "In that case, why could [cognitions] such as 'the jar is blue' (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*) not likewise involve the superimposition of the substrate’s blueness?"—[the answer is: No. Since the Veda declares that the reality whose nature is Being (*sad-rūpa*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, this is accepted by all without contradiction; therefore, since the appearance of [cognitions] such as "the jar exists" is accounted for through the superimposition of that [Being] alone, it is cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate the existence of Being in the jar and so forth as well.
Because that [space] is devoid of color and other qualities, blueness and so forth must be attributed only to the jar and such; thus, there is a disparity.

The teachers of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, however, say: although perception grasps the existence of jars and the like, since perception and other means of knowledge directed toward external objects lack the validity characterized by revealing reality (*tattvāvedakatva*), there is no suspicion of sublation of the non-duality of the Upanishads and similar texts on account of such contradiction. For a means of knowledge is that which makes known what was previously unknown. Now, there is no state of being unknown for jars and the like, which are the objects of perception and so forth; because in an insentient object, there is an absence of the function of veiling (*āvaraṇa*), it is not admitted to be the object of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

Since Brahman alone possesses a manifestation that is necessarily present by virtue of its self-luminosity, it is Brahman itself that is the object of ignorance; therefore, only that which makes it known is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that reveals reality (*tattvāvedaka*). That [Brahman] alone is the object of true cognition (*pramiti*).

For this very reason, the Śruti also restricts the status of being the object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) to the Self alone in the passage: "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen. By the word "is to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*), an act of seeing is not being enjoined, because such an act, being dependent upon a valid means of knowledge, cannot be the object of an injunction; rather, it means "the Self is worthy of being seen. Thus, it is established that because of its being unknown, it is the Self alone—and nothing else—that appropriately possesses the status of being the object of knowledge.

However, some maintain that although the validity of perception—which apprehends the existence of jars and other objects—is not deficient in its capacity to cognize Brahman, the "existence" (sattva) grasped by it must ultimately resolve into one of three possibilities: either as the universal "Being" (*sattājāti*) due to the uniform cognition [of existence]; or as the relation to specific space and time, because of the perception of connection with place and time in such cognitions as "the jar exists here and now"; or as the intrinsic nature of the jar and so forth, because of the perception of the negation of the jar's own nature in such cognitions as "the jar does not exist. And this [apprehended existence] is not contradicted by its own falsity.

For even by the proponent of falsity (mithyātvavādin), neither the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of a jar or the like, nor its relation to space and time, nor the universal (jāti) and so forth residing therein, is denied; rather, what is denied is their non-sublatability (abādhyatva). Nor should it be argued that existence (sattva) should simply be defined as non-sublatability and apprehended by perception (pratyakṣa); for they say that it is impossible to grasp through perception—which grasps only the present—the idea that "there is no sublation of this [object] even throughout the three periods of time."

Others, however, maintain that although truth in the form of non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*) is indeed graspable by perception, the Śruti passage—"The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are truth; of them, this [Brahman] is the Truth"—indicates a gradation of excellence and deficiency in the truth of the entire phenomenal world (characterized by the mention of the primary vital breaths) and of Brahman. For if truth consists in non-sublatability, then there would be no such gradation as "non-sublatable at all times" versus "non-sublatable for some time," were it not for the distinction between "the king of kings" and "the destroyer of the god of love."

They say that because there is no possibility of superiority or inferiority—such as having more or fewer objects—in qualities like the capacity to govern the intended meaning of words beginning with "and so forth" (ityādi), or in beauty and the like; and even if such superiority or inferiority were possible in another way, they would ultimately resolve into the aforementioned [absence of] superiority and inferiority due to the consistency with other scriptural passages stating that the world is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, the reality of jars and other things perceived by the senses consists in their being unsublated until the knowledge of Brahman arises, and thus there is no contradiction with the scriptures on illusoriness (*mithyātva*).

Others, however, maintain that even though there is a contradiction between scripture (*śruti*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*)—the former grasping the falsity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) and the latter its reality—scripture alone is more powerful. This is because perception, being subject to the suspicion of defect due to its prior occurrence, is superseded by scripture, which is free from defect and is subsequent according to the logic of the "supersession" (*apacchedanyāya*). Furthermore, this is supported by the traditional rule: "The superiority of scripture over those three [perception, inference, and verbal testimony] is remembered as inherent by nature. Nor is this traditional rule restricted solely to matters cognizable through the Veda alone; for since the suspicion of contradiction with perception does not arise in such cases, it is appropriate to state the superiority of the Veda regarding the meaning of the Veda precisely when there is a suspected contradiction with perception.
The sky appears as level as a palm-leaf, and the firefly shines like a sacrificial flame.
The sky has no floor, nor is a firefly a flame. ||1||
Therefore, it is proper to examine even an object that has been perceived by direct perception.
One who makes known matters after having examined them does not fall away from dharma. ||2||

Thus, in the section on witnesses (*sākṣiprakaraṇa*) in the *Nāradasmṛti*, it is established that even what is directly perceived must be examined through the instruction of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, because one cannot place trust in direct perception alone. Indeed, the perception of the blueness of the sky cannot be sublated by other means of knowledge such as perception, without the instruction of scripture (*āgama*) which establishes that among the five qualities of the sky—sound and the rest—it possesses only the single quality of sound. Nor can there be a sublation of that [perception] by the certainty that "the cognition of blueness at a distance is produced by the defect of distance, since blueness is not perceived when one is near," for [that certainty itself] depends upon the aforementioned scriptural authority.

Furthermore, the non-perception of that blueness when near—despite its perception from a distance—is possible as being caused by the defect of proximity, just like the non-perception of something enveloped in frost; moreover, it is logically established on the strength of experience that the blueness of the sky is not omnipresent (avyāpyavṛtti).

Nor is there a sublation by perception of the absence of that cognition of blueness for a person who has approached nearby at the very same portion of space near the earth where the cognition of blueness occurred for him when he was at a distance; for it is logically consistent that the blueness belongs only to what is above—such as clouds or stars—and that its appearance as being near the earth is due to the defect of distance. As for odors and other qualities perceived as mixed with the earth and so forth, if some unskilled persons should say that they perceive odor in water, one should know that it resides in the earth alone, while water and air are merely mixed with it. (1)

Since the determination [of the matter] must be stated through such scriptural authorities (*āgama*) alone, and because the superiority of scripture over perception (*pratyakṣa*) is beyond doubt; for it is not possible for people like us to discern through perception in this case that "the odor and so forth residing in the support of water—which is established by birth—is indeed a quality of earth, and not a quality of water," and so on. Since earth and the other elements are generally intermingled with one another, the appearance of the property of one thing in another is possible; thus, perception is subject to the suspicion of error.

If it is argued that one learns about this from scripture alone, then here too, since Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca) are mutually interconnected through the relationship of material cause and its effect, the appearance of the attributes of one in the other is possible;
thus, perception—consisting of the fivefold aspects of "it exists," "it shines," "it is dear," "form," and "name"—is subject to the suspected defect.
The first three are of the nature of Brahman; thereafter, the two are of the nature of the world.

Thus, it is the same [in both cases] that [the matter] should be established by means of scripture (*āgama*) according to the method stated by the elders. Nor is there a contradiction with that upon which [the scripture] depends; for, while depending on perception regarding the aspect of the essential nature of letters, words, sentences, and so forth—by means of the authority of scripture—the [scripture] does not subvert the truth of those [aspects], they say. ||1||

Now, if scripture (*āgama*) were stronger than perception (*pratyakṣa*), then in the case of the statement "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), one would not have to postulate a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) of the word "sacrificer" to the grass-bundle in order to avoid contradicting perception. Likewise, in the case of "One should sacrifice with Soma," if there were a syntactic connection through three distinct relations (*traiyadhikaraṇyena*), then both the status of being a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) would have to be understood for the sacrifice, and the status of being a means to the sacrifice for the Soma-plant; thus, due to this difference in function, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result.

If it is argued that, when a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) must be asserted, one need not assume a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—namely, "by means of a sacrifice possessing Soma"—in order to avoid contradicting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for even though there is a contradiction with direct perception in both cases, one may disregard it since the identity of the sacrificer with the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) and the identity of the sacrifice with Soma can be established through scripture (*āgama*), which is stronger [than perception]—to this it is replied in the *Bhāmatī-nibandhana*: "Scripture that possesses a specific intended meaning (*tātparya*) is stronger than direct perception, not mere scripture."

However, the mantras and arthavādas do not have their primary purport (*tātparya*) upon the object that serves as the door to their praise, just as they do not have their purport upon the word-meaning (*padārtha*) that serves as the door to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). If it is argued that, in the absence of such a purport, the corporeal form of the deity and other such attributes—which are not contradicted by other means of knowledge—would not be established from them, because it is a rule that a word possesses authority only when it has a purport, we say: no.

The aforementioned rule is not established, because we observe that even in the case of an injunction of a qualified entity—such as, "Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman on the Revatī verses, one desiring cattle should sacrifice with this"—there is authoritativeness regarding the nature of the qualification itself, even though that nature is not within the primary purport of the injunction. For here, the Vāravantīya sāman, which has the Revatī verses as its substratum, serves as the qualification. This is not something established in common worldly experience like the qualification of Soma and the like, such that the sentence's authoritativeness would reside merely in the injunction of a sacrifice qualified by it. Nor is there an implication of the qualification by means of the injunction of the qualified entity.

If the qualification were understood through implication (*ākṣepa*), the injunction would have the qualified [object] as its domain; and if that [injunction] existed, it would imply the qualification—thus resulting in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*). Therefore, it must be admitted that even with respect to the nature of the qualification, there is the authority of the very sentence whose purport is the injunction of the qualified. And yet, there is no primary intention (*tātparya*) directed toward that [qualification]. For if there were intention toward both, it would result in the fallacy of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Thus, even in the case of explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) whose primary purpose is the praise of what is to be enjoined, there is no *tātparya* (final purport) regarding the object that serves as the medium for that praise; because direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is more authoritative than them, one must assume a different mode of operation (*vṛttyantara*) within those passages in order to avoid contradicting it.

In the sentence "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), which is intended as an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), if one accepts that the qualified object—the sacrifice characterized by the substance *soma*—is what is enjoined, then because this enjoined object, unlike the curd (*dadhi*) and other such items enjoined in sentences like "he offers oblation with curd," is not established through worldly means, its establishment must be admitted to occur from the very sentence enjoining it, even without a specific intention [to establish it], just as the qualification consisting of the *vāravantīya* chant based on the *revatī* verses is established.

For a scriptural passage devoid of *tātparya* (intentional meaning) cannot establish a sense that contradicts perception—such as the perception grasping the distinction between the sacrificial oblation and the *soma* creeper; therefore, even in that case, one resorts to the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) in order to avoid such contradiction.

However, the scripture concerning non-duality (*advaita-śruti*), having its intentional focus on non-duality determined by the sixfold marks such as the uniformity of the opening and the conclusion, is more powerful than perception; thus, it is perception itself that is sublated, and not the scripture that is interpreted otherwise to avoid contradicting perception.

In the *Vivaraṇavārtika*, however, it is established that the Veda does not possess greater authority than perception simply by virtue of its intentionality (*tātparya*). For instance, although the injunction "one should cook the *kṛṣṇala* grain" intends to convey that the act of cooking is for the sake of the *kṛṣṇala*, the primary connection of cooking—extending to the point where the original form and color of the *kṛṣṇala* are transformed—is contradicted by perception. Therefore, in order to avoid this contradiction, it is accepted that the word "cooking" (*śrapaṇa*) has a secondary figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) restricted to mere heating.

Even though the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) has as its purport the demonstration of the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, since the non-difference of the denoted meaning of the term *tvam* with the denoted meaning of the term *tat* contradicts direct perception, one must admit that there is a secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) toward the pure consciousness (niṣkṛṣṭacaitanya) in order to avoid that contradiction.

Furthermore, even in the case of explanatory passages (arthavādas), just like the injunctions regarding subordinate parts such as the *prayāja* offerings, when their own meanings have been cognized through their own words without being subservient to another purpose, those very meanings are then understood to serve another purpose by virtue of a specific utility; thus, like the sentences concerning the *prayāja*, these [arthavādas] also certainly possess a purport regarding their intermediate connection, because they form a single syntactical unit with the main sentence.

This is because the Vivaraṇācāryas, in their *Nyāyanirṇaya*, have established that there is no acceptance of a supreme intermediate intention (*paramavāntaratātparya*) when there is syntactic unity within a single sentence; furthermore, even in cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), where a primary literal meaning would otherwise follow, they accept figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) solely for the sake of avoiding contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

How, then, is the authority of scripture (*śruti*) established? It is said: because of its faultlessness and its superiority. It is a general rule that mere scripture possesses greater authority than perception. However, even when perception is sublated by scripture, it must somehow be accommodated by providing it with an appropriate object of its own, since a cognition devoid of an object is impossible. For this very reason, truth—which has been displaced from its status as revealing ultimate reality (*tattva*) due to conflict with the non-dualistic scriptures—is justified by being associated with empirical objects capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*).

In short, even though the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated by the universally established perceptual cognition "this is not silver," it is nonetheless accounted for—out of deference to experience—by accepting that there is silver mixed with the mother-of-pearl in the location directly in front. It is not, however, postulated that the object is silver that is spatially remote, internal, or non-existent, in contradiction to that experience.

And thus, since it is impossible to justify perception—which apprehends a distinction between the sacrificer and the sacrificial grass (*prastara*)—by accepting that its object is merely illusory (*prātibhāsika*), while it persists until the knowledge of Brahman through correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*); and since, if the scripture "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass" were to sublate that perception, it would result in the perception being entirely devoid of an object; therefore, to avoid this, the general rule (*utsarga*) is set aside, and the scripture itself is interpreted otherwise in the manner established in the *Siddhyadhikaraṇa* and other sections.

Furthermore, unlike the case of the non-duality scripture (*advaita-śruti*) and perception, it is not possible here to justify perception by asserting that the scripture and perception have respectively ultimate (*tāttvika*) and conventional (*vyāvahārika*) objects; for it is impossible to establish the ultimate identity of the sacrificer with the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) on the basis of a single explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as this contradicts numerous scriptural passages supported by the six marks of intentionality (*ṣaḍvidha-tātparya-liṅga*) which demonstrate the falsity of everything other than Brahman.

Thus, when the sentence *tat tvam asi* brings about the realization that the referent of the term *tvam* (the "you") has the nature of Brahman—characterized by omniscience, non-enjoyership, non-agency, and so forth—the direct perception of non-omniscience, enjoyership, and the like would become entirely groundless. To avoid this, one resorts to the *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā* (partial renunciation indication) by adopting the following distinction: "Enjoyership and the rest belong to the self as colored by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), whereas the pure self, extracted from that, has the nature of the indifferent Brahman."

Similarly, in cases such as "one should cook a *kṛṣṇala*," where there would otherwise result a total lack of scope for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is applied to the Vedic text (*śruti*) to mean "making warm" in order to avoid that consequence. However, in the case of "here there is no diversity whatsoever," since it is possible to somehow establish a scope for direct perception, the powerful Vedic text is not to be interpreted otherwise; thus, there is no contingency of any lack of systematic consistency.

Alternatively, in cases such as "one should cook a *kṛṣṇala* grain" or "one should sacrifice with Soma," figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*) is not resorted to for the sake of conforming to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but rather due to the impossibility of performance. For indeed, unlike the mere heating [of a grain], the primary act of cooking cannot be performed upon a *kṛṣṇala* grain; nor can a sacrifice identical to that [Soma] substance be performed by anyone, in the same way that a sacrifice having Soma as its instrument is performed.

Nor should it be said that the inability to perform what is intended to be performed is merely another way of expressing "contradiction by perception" (*pratyakṣavirodha*). For in the injunction, "One should make the moon's orb radiant," although there is no contradiction with perception regarding the radiance of the moon's orb—which is intended to be performed—one observes an inability to perform it; thus, that [inability] is distinct from [contradiction by perception]. Consequently, it is precisely in that case that one must resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, there is no sublation whatsoever of the superior strength of the Śruti established by the principle of the "later disqualification" (*apacchedanyāya*) and others.

Now, how does the principle of the "successive severance" (*apacchedanyāya*) operate here? It is said: just as in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, when those proceeding for the sake of the *Bahiṣpavamāna* chant, if the Udgātṛ is severed [from the ritual], the cognition that the performance of the expiation caused by the Udgātṛ's severance must take place arises from observing the Vedic injunction, "If the Udgātṛ should be severed, one should perform the sacrifice again after having sacrificed it without the sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*). Subsequently, when the Pratihartṛ is severed, [one observes]: "If the Pratihartṛ should be severed, one should give away all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*)."

It is sublated by the cognition that the duty to perform the expiation occasioned by the interruption of the opposing priest (*pratihartr-apaccheda*) has arisen through the observation of the Vedic injunction, which is contrary to [the previously established rule].

In this way, the prior perception of the reality of the jar and so forth is sublated by the subsequent cognition produced by the scriptural text regarding their falsity. Nor is there a lack of parallelism with the cited case [of the Udgātṛ's disconnection], where even when the prior cognition of duty occasioned by one cause is sublated by a subsequent cognition of duty occasioned by another cause—whether that be in a case where there is a disconnection of the Udgātṛ alone, or where both disconnections occur simultaneously, or where the disconnection of the Udgātṛ occurs later—the scripture producing the prior cognition of duty still has its scope; however, such is not the case for perception.

One should not suspect a discrepancy by arguing that if perception were sublated by the Śruti of non-duality (advaita), it would become baseless due to the absence of any other object; for in cases such as a jar where perception operates while being sublated by Śruti, that perception has already achieved its purpose by finding a transactional (vyāvahārika) object. Thus, like a prior scriptural injunction that is entirely sublated when a subsequent one occurs, there is no need to seek another object. Furthermore, in this case as well, it can be said that perception finds scope within the existence of Brahman, which is known through all forms of cognition.

However, even in a single performance, because the two respective contingent duties (*naimittika-kartavyatā*) arise sequentially—just as the dark and red colors arise sequentially in a *badara* fruit due to two sequential causes—the two cognitions of those duties are likewise valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), like the two cognitions of color. Therefore, the case of the "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*) is not an example of one cognition annulling a prior cognition.

Therefore, regarding the statement in the *Śāstradīpikā* on the section concerning the "severance" (*apaccheda*): "For this is the meaning of the occasional injunction (*naimittika-śāstra*): although the sacrifice was to be performed in one way prior to the occurrence of the occasion, when the occasion arises, it must be performed in another way"—that is not correct. For [the expiation] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that is to be performed; and in a sacrifice where a subsequent severance of the *pratihartṛ* occurs, there can be no status as an auxiliary for an expiation caused by a prior severance of the *udgātṛ*.

Just as the *āhavanīya* injunction pertains to oblations other than the *padahoma*, so too the injunction "if the *udgātṛ* should be cut off" pertains to a sacrifice in which a subsequent cutting off by the *pratihartṛ* has not occurred;
for it is stated in the *Nyāyaratnamālā*: "By means of a specific subject, etc., [the application] of a general rule..."

"In the analysis of 'sublation by what has been obtained' (*prāptabādha*), whose characteristic was stated as 'contraction is the sublation of that which has been established,' [it is said]: 'This being the case, the meaning of the scripture is as follows: for a sacrifice characterized by the subsequent omission of the Udgātṛ and the absence of the omission of the Pratihartṛ, the giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) is an auxiliary; the same should be understood in the case of the omission of the Udgātṛ as well.'"

As for the statement from the *Śāstradīpikā* that was cited, even that is merely a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*) based on the thought: "Even though the knowledge of the previous expiation has arisen, it becomes false because it is sublated; however, there is nothing to sublate the subsequent one. This is because it is read at the conclusion of the section establishing that the former duty is to be sublated, and [the discussion] assumes that the occasion [for the expiation] has not yet occurred—that is, in the absence of the occurrence of the occasion, even if [the rite] were otherwise to be performed.

However, this does not mean that, prior to the arising of the subsequent cause, the duty associated with the previous cause did not actually exist; for such an interpretation would contradict the context of the preceding text.

Let the boundaries of the Mīmāṃsakas be set aside: what contradiction is there in accepting the production of two successive duties, according to the analogy of a dark color being followed by a red one?

It is said: for what indeed is this "obligatoriness" (*kartavyatva*) that would be set aside by the arising of a subsequent conditional obligatoriness? It cannot be the fitness of the prior conditional act to be accomplished through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatvayogyatva*), because that does not disappear even afterwards. Nor can it be the state of being accomplished through effort as a result-oriented property (*phalamukha-kṛtisādhyatva*), because that was not produced even previously. Nor can it be the state of being that which, if not performed, causes a deficiency in the sacrifice, nor the state of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

Since the state of being a cause—whether as a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the rite through its nature as a specific restrictive rule (*niyamaviśeṣa*) that necessitates a deficiency in the sacrifice upon non-performance, or as a cause through its nature as a specific causal factor by way of either contributing to the fruit (*phalopakāritva*) or as a direct constituent (*sannipāti*)—cannot be merely occasional, it must be established as inherent. Consequently, for the sake of maintaining this inherent character, the subsidiary rite occasioned by a prior interruption (*parvāpaccheda-naimittika-aṅga*) belongs to that sacrifice which lacks a subsequent contradictory interruption; in that case alone is its non-performance the cause of a deficiency in the sacrifice. Thus, [the rule] must be qualified accordingly.

In a sacrifice where there is a subsequent disconnection (*apaccheda*) occurring within it, it is impossible—prior to the arising of that subsequent disconnection—for the ritual subsidiary (*kratvaṅga*) occasioned by the prior disconnection to either exist or to function as the cause of the deficiency of the sacrifice (*kratuvai-kalya*) in the event of its non-performance; for it is neither observed nor logical that any entity should pervade another entity for a certain time and subsequently not do so, or that it should be a cause for a certain time and subsequently not be one.

Nor can there be postulated a distinct property called "obligatoriness" (kartavyatva) that is subject to appearance and disappearance; for there is no evidence for such a thing. Furthermore, since two contradictory injunctions of equal force—such as those concerning the foot-print altar and the Āhavanīya fire—can be reconciled through a system of application (vyavasthā), the claim that two successive obligatorinesses arise is without foundation.

But surely, according to the principle of the section on the opening statement (*upakramādhikaraṇa*), because it is not contradicted by the lack of accumulation [of evidence], should not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself be stronger than scripture (*āgama*)?

It is said in reply: where a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is perceived, there the conclusion must come to rest upon a single meaning; for if there were a difference in meaning, it would entail the destruction of the perceived syntactical unity.

Therefore, when the idea that the giver incurs merit has been established by the arthavāda concerning the deeds of others (parakṛti), which begins with "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa" and so forth—serving as an initial counter-argument—the group of words found in the concluding portion, "As many horses as one might accept, so many four-pot-sherd offerings to Varuṇa should he perform," being contrary to that [idea], cannot achieve syntactic unity with it by conveying their literal meaning because a counter-argument has already arisen. Consequently, for the sake of establishing syntactic unity, [the latter must be interpreted figuratively].

Since a word acquires its own meaning only by incorporating the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇij*) in accordance with it, the initial statement possesses greater force. However, where mutual syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is not perceived, there a sentence that has already acquired its own form and conveys a contrary meaning will indeed communicate its own sense without regard for what preceded; thus, in such cases, the preceding matter does not possess greater force.

For this very reason, disregarding the previously established statement regarding the taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup, it is accepted that the statement regarding its non-taking also conveys its own meaning; however, because there is no other subject for both, one must resort to the performance of an option (*vikalpa*) therein as a last resort.

Likewise, since there is no possibility of the non-dual scripture being in syntactic agreement (*ekavākyatva*) with perception, it can unimpededly convey its own meaning even while disregarding what has been previously established.
And in the production of the knowledge of that meaning...
Because it arises later, the subsequent [cognition] arises without having sublated the prior one;
since the subsequent does not arise otherwise [than through the prior], its occurrence cannot be possible by means of the sublation of the first.
Thus, it is the principle of the later sublation (*apacchedanyāya*) that operates here, not the principle of the initial commencement (*upakramanyāya*).
For this very reason, even in the world, the initial perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated by the instruction of a reliable authority. ||2||

But even so, is it not the case that the primacy of perception itself remains unavoidable due to its status as a foundational support (*upajīvya*)? For in the case of the two rules regarding the "sequential displacement" (*apaccheda*), it is logical that the latter sublates the former because the former is not a support for the latter. Here, however, since perception serves as the basis for apprehending the nature of letters, words, and so forth, it is a support for the scripture (*āgama*) that conveys falsity; therefore, it is appropriate that the scripture alone undergoes sublation in the form of failing to convey a falsity that contradicts that perception.

Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction with the foundational [scriptures], because even if the portion consisting of the reality of letters, words, and so forth is sublated by the hearing of the falsity [of the world], there is no sublation of the portion consisting of its nature as a foundational support; for scriptures such as "There is no diversity here whatsoever" teach the non-existence of the phenomenal world (prapañca) in its very own nature.

On this point, some say: since one who hears a sentence such as "bring the bull" (*vṛṣam ānaya*) may still perceive a verbal cognition even when hearing it in the form "bring the ox" (*vṛṣabham ānaya*) due to a defect in hearing, what is required for verbal cognition is merely the perception of phonemes, words, and so forth—common to both valid cognition and error.
