Therefore, the non-dualist scripture (*advaitāgama*) depends only upon the perception of phonemes, words, and so forth, not upon their validity. Thus, even if the intrinsic nature of phonemes, words, and so forth is sublated, there is no contradiction with that which is depended upon.

Others, however, say that although the validity of verbal cognition does not depend on the establishment of the intrinsic nature of letters, words, and so forth, there is still a dependence on the establishment of the intrinsic nature of compatibility (*yogyatā*), because valid cognition does not arise from an incompatible word. Even with this dependence, there is no contradiction with the foundational source (*upajīvya*). This is because, even though the Śruti text "There is no diversity here" negates [diversity], we nevertheless accept the existence of the world as something distinct from the unreal (*asat*), which persists until the realization of Brahman and is consistent with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Otherwise, it would follow that perception and other empirical means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be devoid of objects.

Nor should it be argued that even if there is a negation of its own nature (*svarūpa*), how can the world-appearance (*prapañca*) acquire its existence? For if the negation were of a nature that does not exclude its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there would be a contradiction. This is because, in accordance with the two cognitions "this is silver" and "this is not silver" regarding mother-of-pearl, we must admit that the absence of the superimposed object residing in the substrate persists until the sublation occurs, and thus it is capable of sustaining a counter-positive that is distinct from the non-existent (*asat*).

By this, the objection that the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in its own nature would result in its non-existence, like a rabbit's horn, is refuted; for there is a distinction, since we accept that its nature is to be sublated by the knowledge of Brahman.

Nor can it be argued that when this superimposed object is negated in its own form within its substrate, its negation in its own form elsewhere is established by itself; for, since its status as the counter-positive of a negation related to all places and times would follow, its non-existence (*asattva*) would be unavoidable. This is because "non-existence" is defined precisely as "being the counter-positive of a negation related to all places and times," and it is impossible to define it in any other way. Thus it must be stated.

They argue that since one who accepts that a non-existent thing is the counter-correlate of negation in relation to all places and times must rely on inference alone—as it would be impossible to establish this through perception (due to the impossibility of perceiving all places and times) and impossible to establish through scripture (due to the non-perception of any such scripture)—then whatever mark (*liṅga*) is stated in that inference which is excluded from everything else (*sarvavyāvṛtta*), that very mark, being the first to be cognized, can appropriately be defined as "non-existence" (*asattva*).

Others, however, maintain that based on the scriptural text "There is no diversity here," the intention [of the scripture] lies solely in the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as something real, and not in [negating it] in its own nature. For if a negation did not sublate the very nature [of the object], it could not be a negation of that object; yet if it were to sublate its nature, there would be a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Nor should it be argued that since reality (*satyatva*) itself is established by perception in such cognitions as "the pot exists," its negation in that form is also improper; for it is logical that perception, in order not to contradict scripture, has as its object only a conventional reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*) which is a mere appearance of reality. Furthermore, this being the case, there is no possibility of the reality belonging to Brahman—which is the ultimate reality—applying to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and thus there is no inconsistency in negating the world in that [ultimate] form.

Just as the very perception of the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is the occasion for the possibility of real silver, and thus its negation occurs—precisely because of this, one understands that what is being negated exists elsewhere, as in: "This is not silver, but that [other silver]"; "This is not my cow, but that very one"; or "Caitra is not here now, but in the inner room"—so too, the very perception of the appearance of reality is the occasion for the possibility of reality, and thus its negation is logically established.

Therefore, they say that since there is no suspicion of subverting the essential nature of phonemes, words, semantic competency (*yogyatā*), and so forth, there is no contradiction with that upon which [the Vedas] depend (*upajīvya-virodha*).

Others, however, do not accept a threefold division of existence—namely, ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-satyatva*) in Brahman; empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*), which is a semblance of reality, in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); and illusory reality (*prātibhāsika-satyatva*), which is even more inferior, in cases such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. This is because the misconception of existence in objects like jars or silver-in-shell is sufficiently accounted for by the permeation of the ultimate existence residing in the underlying substrate (Brahman), and thus the postulation of a "semblance of reality" lacks any basis in valid cognition.

Thus, since there is no perception of reality in the phenomenal world (prapañca), and because the perception of that [reality] in Brahman—which has attained identity with it—is logically extended to the phenomenal world through non-discrimination (aviveka), there is no contradiction with a foundational premise when the phenomenal world is negated as real; nor is there a negation of what was never previously established.

Nor should it be argued: "Why is the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl accepted as something purposeless, when there is no appearance of existence in the phenomenal world apart from the ultimate existence residing in Brahman? For it must be admitted that such an acceptance is necessary to account for the immediate manifestation of that which is remote and not in contact with the senses, since immediate perception is impossible for what is distant. ||3||

But surely, in the case of an illusion of reflection as well, there would have to be the production of an appearance of a face in the mirror that is distinct from the face located on one's own neck; for even if the regions of the nose and so forth in one's own facial face can be perceived directly, it is impossible to perceive the regions of the eyeballs, forehead, and so forth, whereas in the illusion of reflection, the perception of the regions of the eyeballs and other such parts is actually observed. Nor is it a matter of merely accepting what is desired [to avoid contradiction], because if a reflection were admitted to be distinct from the original object (the *bimba*), then the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection of Brahman, would also be distinct from Him, resulting in its falsity (*mithyātva*).

Regarding this, those who follow the *Vivaraṇa* say: since it is possible for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the face being located in the mirror, of its facing backward, and of its appearing as a distinct reflection—all due to the defect of proximity to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of the mirror—while the face remains actually in the neck, one need not postulate a superimposition of the face upon the mirror. This is because such a view involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, there is only a sublation (*bādha*) of the relation, namely, "the face is not in the mirror," whereas if it were a separate false entity, there would result a sublation of the essential nature (*svarūpa-bādha*), namely, "this is not my face.
Finally, there is the recognition of non-difference from one's own face in the cognition, "My face shines in the mirror."

Nor is it impossible for the face located in the neck—the substratum—to be directly perceived. This is because we accept the rule that the rays of the eye, obstructed by an adjunct (*upādhi*), turn back and grasp the reflected image, as in the case of a creeper and the like. If this rule were not accepted, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even an atom, or a large object situated behind a wall or similar obstruction, could produce the illusion of a visual reflection. Nor can it be argued that there is a rule stating, "The illusion of a visual reflection occurs only for that which is unobstructed, large, and possesses manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*), and not for anything else."

For when the production of visual cognition is possible through the postulated function of the image residing [in the eye] and the manifestation of the form [of the object], it is illogical to assume a different mode of operation. Furthermore, if a wall or similar obstacle were to act as a hindrance here by merely obstructing the connection with the ocular rays without destroying them, then that same [obstacle] could likewise act as a hindrance in cases such as the perception of a jar; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total loss of the status of "mere contact of the eye" as a causal factor.

Even for one who maintains that there is a false superimposition (adhyāsa) of the face upon the mirror, the previous experience must be justified by the very assumption that the rays of the eyes sometimes turn back and grasp one's own face, in order to establish the latent impression (saṃskāra) included among the three causes [of memory]. Nor can the latent impression be accounted for solely from a previous experience delimited by regions such as the nose.

To that extent, the superimposition of a reflection of the eyeball and so forth would be untenable; furthermore, in the case of the superimposition of the reflection of a man perched on a tree on the bank in the water of a pond, it is impossible to account for a prior experience in any way whatsoever. Thus, if one must necessarily assert—on the strength of the resulting perception—that the eye-rays, though obstructed by an adjunct (upādhi), reach the object and perceive it, then it must be said that only those rays struck by a mirror and the like reach the object and perceive it, and not those obstructed by stone and such.

Because light rays from copper and other metals that are not very transparent are obstructed by contact with an impure limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), they fail to grasp specific features such as the shape of a face; this is like those who, seeking the sun directly, turn back after reaching the limiting adjunct and thus do not encounter the same obstruction by the solar radiance. Consequently, there is no impossibility in perceiving the reflected sun, as there is in perceiving it directly. Regarding the proximity of limiting adjuncts such as water, while some rays are obstructed by the adjunct and reach the original object (*bimba*), others enter within it and perceive internal things like sand; since such conceptualizations are possible, there is no fault whatsoever.

However, those who follow Advaita-vidyā and accept the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the reflection—namely, the proponents of the threefold nature of the individual soul (*trividhajīvavādin*) such as Vidyāraṇya-guru and others—state their intention as follows:

The reflection of one's face in a mirror, which is clearly perceived by bystanders as being distinct from the face itself and yet similar to it, is different from that face in its true nature and is indeed false—just as the "silver" in a mother-of-pearl shell is false in relation to the silver held in one's own hand. Nor is there any contradiction with the cognition of non-difference expressed in the thought, "My face shines in the mirror," for such a cognition of non-difference is impossible due to its contradiction with the clear perception of difference, duality, and the fact that [the reflection] faces inward.

Furthermore, the designation "my face in the mirror" is figurative, just as one's own face is designated [as such] when it is reflected in a clear surface. Nor should it be suspected that the distinction itself must be figurative simply because it contradicts the cognition of non-difference; for it is impossible to deny that children experience a delusion of another person in a reflection, which culminates in purposeful action such as avoidance or pursuit.

Nor should it be argued that even for discerning people, the cognition of non-difference reaches the point of purposeful action (arthakriyā), because they are seen to employ mirrors and the like to fully recognize the specific features of their own faces. For even when there is difference, the employment of such means is justified precisely by the recognition of the specific feature that the reflection is invariably similar in form to the original object (bimba).

As for the claim that "there is no face here" constitutes a sublation (bādha) only of the connection of the face with the mirror, and not of the face itself—that is incorrect. For in the case of "this is not silver," it would follow [absurdly] that there is a sublation only of the identity (tādātmya) of silver with the object "this," and not of the silver itself.

Furthermore, if it is because of the superimposition of silver upon this "this" (the substrate) by way of identity that there is a sublation of the silver itself by way of identity—expressed as "This is not silver," rather than a sublation of mere identity—then it follows by parity of reasoning that, since the face is superimposed upon the mirror by way of relation, there is a sublation of the face itself by way of relation—expressed as "There is no face here"—rather than a sublation of mere relation.

As for the objection that there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating superimposition even upon the substratum (*dharmin*), that is not a fault because it is supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), just like the complexity involved in postulating the appearance of silver. This is because, in cases of error such as the reflection of one's own eyeball, there is no means to postulate the direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of the original object (*bimba*). For if one were to postulate that the rays of the eye, though obstructed by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), reach the original object, many things would result that contradict what is observed.

For how could some rays of the eye, upon encountering water, enter within after being reflected, while other rays—though likewise obstructed by contact with water and being exceedingly soft—should overcome the entire mass of rays that is impeded and enter the solar disc situated in their midst?

And how could it be that, just as in the case of looking at the moon, there would not also be a refreshing nourishment for the eyes—cool as nectar—through the manifestation of coolness in the eyes due to the specific proximity to its reflection? And how could rays that are obstructed by contact with water not also be obstructed by contact with stones and the like? Or, if they were to turn back upon being thus obstructed, why would they not come into contact with the eyeballs and so forth? Or, even if they did come into contact, why would they not cause that which is contacted to be directly perceived?
For even by way of a defect, it is observed that only the apprehension of the specific attributes is obstructed, but not even the apprehension of the nature of the proximate substratum itself.
However, in the view that there is a superimposition of the face [upon the mirror], nothing need be postulated that contradicts what is perceived.

For instance, since visual superimposition is observed only in the case of gross and manifest form that is not obstructed, it is established that the grossness and manifest form residing in the original object—which are known to be causes for the direct perception of their own substratum—are likewise causes for the superimposition upon the reflection of their own substratum. As for a substance such as a wall that acts as an obstruction, it is established as an impediment to the direct perception of an obstructed object by way of disrupting the contact between the eye and its object, according to the principle of the sense of touch and other senses which function through reaching their objects (*prāpyakārin*).

Even in the case of the superimposition of a reflection on something obstructed, one must postulate an obstructive capacity even without another intervening medium. What contradiction is there in this? For when a certain thing has been established as a cause (or by some other property) in one instance, it may be postulated as a cause (or by that same property) elsewhere as well, provided the evidence of the result warrants it. By this, the objection is refuted that if the visual rays, obstructed by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), are not admitted to reach the object, then there would follow the undesirable consequence of a visual illusion of reflection for things that are obstructed or devoid of manifest color and so forth.

Moreover, the very acceptance of that [position] entails the same aforementioned refutation. How so? Just as when looking directly at the sun without the movement of the eyes, one looks with a lowered head into water, and the rays of the eye, being reflected from there, leap upward and grasp the image of the sun; likewise, when looking into a mirror with straight eyes without lateral movement of the eyes, the rays reflected from it grasp the face situated to the side.

Even in the absence of the turning of the face, it is difficult to avoid the consequence that rays of light obstructed by an intervening object would reach the back of the object; for, setting aside the rule that such obstructed visual rays must turn back, they would simply proceed to wherever the object itself is located.

Likewise, in the case of a reflection of a fair face in a soiled mirror, although the fair color belonging to the original object (bimba) exists, it is of no use for the visual cognition [of the reflection]; thus, following the logic of the error regarding a yellow conch, the visual nature of the reflected face must be accounted for solely through its association with the superimposed color. In that very same way, even though the mirror is itself colorless, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that it becomes the object of a visual illusory reflection precisely through its association with the blackness of the limiting adjunct (upādhi).

For even though the sky is by its own nature formless, it is commonly accepted as being perceptible to the eye due to its association with the superimposed blueness. Therefore, the position that the face is superimposed [in the mirror] in its own essential form is indeed superior.

Nor is there any difficulty regarding the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience in that case; for just as in dreams the superimposition of a person never before seen occurs through the mere impression of a general experience of "person," so too the superimposition of a specific face upon a mirror is possible through the mere impression of a general experience of "face."

However, this is the distinction: in dreams, there is a superimposition of specific human forms in accordance with the perception of causes for good or evil; here, however, there is a superimposition of specific facial features in accordance with the proximity of the original object.

Nor is it a fault that the reflection would be false by its very nature, leading to the undesirable consequence that the individual soul (*jīva*), as a reflection of Brahman, would also be false. For even if the reflected soul were thus [false], liberation remains possible because the delimited soul (*avacchinna-jīva*) is real.

As for the view held by some that a reflection in mirrors and the like is indeed real insofar as it consists of a specific shadow (*chāyā*) of the face—that is not so. For what is called "shadow" is simply darkness (*tamas*) which takes form in a particular location when the light pervading that space has been obstructed by the various limbs of a body or other object. Furthermore, it is not logical that the reflections of pearls, rubies, and the like—which possess forms such as white and red that are contrary to darkness—should be of the nature of shadow, which is darkness.
Nor is it tenable that the reflections of the sun and other luminaries, which are devoid of shadow in the form of darkness, should be so characterized.

If it is argued: "In that case, since it is impossible for the shadow in the form of a reflection to be of the nature of darkness (*tamas*), let it be a distinct substance; for when it is not included among the established substances, its status as a distinct substance can be postulated just like darkness," [we reply: Is that distinct substance endowed with specific properties such as color, dimension, configuration, and facing inward—which are perceived in reflections—or is it devoid of them?

In the latter case, the perception of a reflection composed of specific forms and so forth cannot be accounted for by that other substance; thus, its postulation is useless. In the former case, however, how can there be a justification for the reality of multiple large-sized reflections of faces being perceived simultaneously and without confusion within a single small space?

Furthermore, how could there be the production of another substance within a mirror—which consists of densely packed parts and remains exactly as it was—possessing many depressions and elevations such as the chin, nose, and so forth? Moreover, regarding the production of a reflection possessing various colors such as white, yellow, and red, there exists no such cause situated within or in proximity to the mirror.

If it should be argued that "the cognition of great dimension and the cognition of such depressions and elevations in reflections—which are limited in size and capable of resting within the confines of the limiting adjunct (upādhi)—are merely errors; and that some cause must be postulated which is capable of producing such a reflection without contradicting the prior state of the mirror and its parts," then let even the silver in the mother-of-pearl shell be real!

Even in that case, since the mother-of-pearl remains exactly as it was before, it is possible to explain the matter by postulating some cause capable of producing silver that has attained identity with it; for one can then describe a rule whereby that silver is perceivable by the sense organ only when assisted by a cause considered to be a defect (*doṣa*). Why, then, resort to the "half-lion" logic [of partial truth] by claiming that "silver in the mother-of-pearl is unreal, while the reflection is real"? Moreover, if that were so, there would be no occurrence of the mother-of-pearl—which is perceived as "silver"—melting like silver when thrown into fire.

Just as the reflection of aloe-wood, musk, and so forth lacks heat, fragrance, and the like, it is logically consistent that the silver in a shell-lake lacks the capacity for liquefaction or dissolution. Now, if it is argued that the silver in a shell-lake is not real because there is a sublation (*bādha*) universally accepted by all—expressed as "This is not silver" or "Silver appeared here falsely"—then it is more reasonable to conclude that the reflection is also unreal, given the universally established sublation expressed as "There is no face in the mirror; a face appeared here in the mirror falsely," and so on. Therefore, the doctrine asserting the reality of reflections is untenable.

But surely, even the doctrine of its falsity is untenable, because—just as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—there is no determination of any cause characterized by positive and negative concomitance, such as ignorance (*ajñāna*), nor of any subverting cognition (*jñāna*).

On this point, some maintain that although, even after the knowledge of the substrate in its entirety, the superimposition of a reflection arises—wherein neither the ignorance that veils the substrate (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) serves as the material cause (*upādāna*), nor does the knowledge of the specific details of the substrate (*viśeṣāṃśa-jñāna*) act as its sublater—nevertheless, since it is possible for that very ignorance to persist through its aspect of projective power (*vikṣepa-śakti*) even when its aspect of veiling power has ceased, that [ignorance] alone is the material cause. Furthermore, the knowledge of the substrate, aided by the cessation of the proximity between the original object (*bimba*) and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is what sublates that [superimposition] along with its material cause.

Others, however, maintain that it is not inherent to knowledge to remove only the portion consisting of the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) while leaving aside the portion consisting of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*). For if, through the knowledge of Brahman, the root ignorance were removed, or through the knowledge of a mother-of-pearl shell, the ignorance of its particular state were removed—leaving only the portion of the power of concealment—there would follow the undesirable consequence that the power of projection would persist at all times. Nor can it be argued that this [persistence] is caused by an obstacle to the removal of the portion of the power of projection, which consists in the proximity of the object and its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

For, even before the proximity of the object and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), when it is perceived through direct perception that there is no contact with the mirror in the case of Caitra’s face as the object, or that Caitra’s face does not exist in the mirror, the aspect of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) must necessarily cease; consequently, if those two were in proximity at that time, the absence of the material cause would entail the impossibility of the error of reflection. Therefore, only root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) is the material cause of the superimposition of the reflection. Nor is there an equality of the aforementioned defect in this case.

Although the modifications (*vṛtti*) directed toward external objects act as suppressors of portions of the power of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) that obscures consciousness within the specific regions delimited by their respective objects, they do not remove the portions of its power of projection (*vikṣepaśakti*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the dissolution even of the empirical projections residing in those very same regions.
Nor does it follow that if the reflection were an effect of root-ignorance, it would necessarily be merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*).

Because being not produced by any defect other than ignorance is the determinant of empirical reality (*vyāvahārikatva*); and in the present case, since there exists the defect of proximity to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the reflected object—which is distinct from that [ignorance]—its status as merely apparent (*prātibhāsikatva*) is established.

It should not be argued that, this being the case, there is the undesirable consequence that the knowledge of the substrate—even when assisted by the cessation of the proximity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and the original object (*bimba*)—would fail to remove the superimposition of the reflection, because it lacks the capacity to remove the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that is its root. This is because there is no contradiction [between the two]. Even though it does not remove the ignorance regarding Brahman, the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate, when aided by the absence of obstacles, is logically capable of removing the superimposition of the reflection—which has that [Brahman] as its material cause—because its object is opposed to that superimposition.

Even on the view that the substrate-ignorance (*avasthājñāna*) is the material cause (*upādāna*), it is impossible for that [substrate-ignorance]—whose power of concealment has been removed by the previous knowledge of the substrate—to be sublated by the subsequent knowledge of the substrate occurring at a time when the obstructing factor is absent, because that would entail a loss of the requirement of having the same object (*samānaviṣayatva*). Therefore, it must be accepted that only the superimposition of the reflection (*pratibimbādhyāsa*) is what is sublated by that [subsequent knowledge]. Alternatively, let this superimposition be sublated precisely by the knowledge of Brahman which sublates its own material cause, namely ignorance.
As for its status as "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*), they say it is refuted by the fact that it is produced by a defect other than ignorance. ||4||

Thus, some say that because the superimposition of dreams occurs upon either the undivided consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*) or the consciousness conditioned by the ego (*ahaṅkāra-upahita-caitanya*)— both of which are devoid of cognition in the form of specific states— and because the Teacher [Śaṅkara] stated that "the darkness called deep sleep, which is ignorance (*ajñāna*), is the seed of both dreams and waking," dreams and the waking world are both effects of the same root-ignorance; therefore, being sublated solely by the knowledge of Brahman which removes its own material cause (*upādāna*), they possess only a phenomenal reality (*prātibhāsika*) due to being produced by defects such as sleep, which are distinct from nescience (*avidyā*).

Others, however, maintain that its status as *prātibhāsika* (illusory) is due precisely to its being sublated by knowledge other than the realization of Brahman—since the waking consciousness sublates the superimposition of dreams, as stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Moreover, these chariots and so forth seen in a dream are sublated upon waking," and as seen in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Because it is the opposite of the bondage consisting of ignorance, like the waking consciousness"; and because one who has awakened experiences the falsity of the dream. Thus, the waking consciousness is the remover of the dream-superimposition.

Nor should it be argued: "How can a cognition that does not have the true nature of the substrate as its object, and which does not remove the ignorance that is its own material cause, ever remove superimposition? For they say that the superimposition of a snake on a rope is seen to cease not only by the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate—which removes the ignorance that is its own material cause—but also by a subsequent error regarding a staff arising immediately after that [initial error] upon that very same substrate.

Others, however, maintain that when the vital points (*marmans*) that bestow waking experiences cease, there arises a state of sleep—a particular modification (*avasthābheda*) of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)—which covers both the empirical individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection and the perceiver of the waking world, as well as the waking world itself that is perceived by it; this state is the material cause (*upādāna*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the dream-world, and not the root-ignorance itself. Nor is there a lack of evidence for the fact that sleep is a form of situational ignorance (*avasthājñāna*).

For the empirical individual (*vyāvahārika-jīva*), who perceives the waking world-phenomenon (*jāgrat-prapañca*) while being veiled by root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), and who conceives of himself without doubt or error as "I am a man," "I am a Brahmin," "I am the son of Devadatta," and so forth—due to his long-standing familiarity with that [self], there is for him no concealment at any time of his own grandfather’s death and other such events belonging to the waking world-phenomenon, which are experienced as having a single, unchanging form. Just as in the waking state, even during the time of dreaming, when [the waking world] is absent due to some cause, [he may think]: "I am a tiger," "I am a Śūdra," and so on.

Because this would entail the non-existence of such delusions as "I am the son of so-and-so" and the delusion regarding the living state of one's own grandfather, it is established that sleep itself is a particular state of ignorance (*ajñāna*) produced at that time, which veils the empirical world and the individual soul (*jīva*). Nor does it follow from this that there would be an absence of a perceiver for the dream-phenomenon, since the perceiving *jīva* is also superimposed as being of an illusory nature along with the dream-phenomenon itself.

Furthermore, when the waking experience arises from karma that produces enjoyment, the sublation of the dream-world occurs precisely through the knowledge of the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which removes the ignorance in the form of sleep that constitutes its own material cause. It should not be argued that, if the dreamer—the illusory (*prātibhāsika*) *jīva*—is likewise sublated by that [waking knowledge], there would be no subsequent recollection such as "I experienced an elephant in a dream. For they say that since the illusory *jīva* is superimposed upon the empirical *jīva*, even if the empirical *jīva* is held to recollect based on the experience of the illusory one, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the argument.

Indeed, both of the two positions previously stated—that the unconditioned consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*) or the consciousness conditioned by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra-upahita-caitanya*) is the locus of the superimposition of the dream-world—are untenable. Regarding the first position: since the dream-elephants and other such objects occupy a location distinct from the locus of the witness conditioned by the ego-sense, it is impossible for them to be manifested by that witness without depending on a contact with an internal mental modification (*vṛtti*), as is the case with pleasure and the like; nor is it possible for them to be manifested by depending on such a contact, because the eyes and other sense organs have ceased their activity, making the arising of a [sensory] modification impossible.

In the second case, there would be the undesirable consequence of superimposition (adhyāsa) in the form of "I am an elephant," just like "this is silver," or "I possess an elephant," just like "I am happy."

On this point, some support the first position: they maintain that consciousness unconditioned by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is not accepted as the substratum for the dream-world outside the body, but rather within it. For this very reason, because the requisite space corresponding to the perceived dimensions is absent, it is said that dream-elephants and the like are composed of illusion (*māyāmaya*).

Thus, although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) requires the eyes and other sense organs to produce a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward external objects such as the "this-ness" of a mother-of-pearl shell during the waking state—due to its lack of independence outside the body—there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the fact that the internal organ within the body is independent and can produce a modification by itself; for the unconditioned consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*), manifested through the modification of the internal organ within the body, serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

For this very reason, just as in the waking state ignorance—residing in the consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect of mother-of-pearl manifested through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by sensory contact—undergoes illusory transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of silver, so too in the dream state, ignorance residing in the consciousness manifested within a mental modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that is affected by defects such as sleep, and accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of various objects awakened by past karma (*adṛṣṭa*), may undergo illusory transformation into the form of the manifold world (*prapañca*). Such is the statement of Bhāratītīrtha in the *Vivaraṇopanyāsa*.

Others, however, maintain that the unconditioned consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*), when manifested by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is not the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the dream-world. This is because the arising of a mental modification whose object is the unconditioned consciousness—which is not rooted in verbal testimony—is impossible; for we observe that modifications in the form of "I" arise only with respect to consciousness conditioned by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth. Therefore, the substratum is the unconditioned consciousness, which is inherently immediate (*aparokṣa*) and not limited by the ego-sense and the like.
For this very reason, the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* states: "An erroneous cognition whose object has an immediate nature must depend upon an immediate locus."
Because it is manifested in that way through the mind itself, or through the eyes, as in dreams, delusions, and so forth.

Having stated in this verse that the immediacy of the substrate required for immediate superimposition is sometimes intrinsic, sometimes through a mental modification (*manovṛtti*), and sometimes through an external sensory modification, [the author continues]: "Consciousness is intrinsically immediate; nevertheless, an error arises in the form of a specific appearance. Caused by the mind, as in a dream, it repeatedly manifests its own locus even without an object of the eye."

Just as an error regarding silver and the like, though perceived by the senses, is observed in many ways through distinctions such as white and so forth, so too an error that delineates form in space— though it is only accessible to the mind— is observed in the same way due to the power of its apparent immediacy.

In the immediately following verse beginning with "ityādi," the immediate manifestation (*aparokṣya*) of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in the superimposition of a dream is illustrated by itself. Nor should it be argued that the mere consciousness unconditioned by the *ahaṃkāra* is veiled, and thus its manifestation cannot occur without a mental modification (*vṛtti*); for it is accepted that while the Brahman-consciousness alone is veiled, the individual soul-consciousness (*jīva-caitanya*), which is the reflection of ignorance (*avidyā-pratibimba*), is not veiled even though it is unconditioned by the *ahaṃkāra*.

And thus they say: when an elephant or other object in a dream is superimposed upon the consciousness (caitanya) that is not delimited by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), there occurs for the subject-consciousness (pramātṛcaitanya) the empirical usage "I see this," due to the manifestation of non-difference brought about by a modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) whose objective domain is co-extensive with that [superimposed object].

Others, however, justify [the position] by maintaining that the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is consciousness delimited by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); thus, they do not accept that the ego-sense enters the category of the substrate as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), but rather that the substrate is merely consciousness in the form of its reflection (*pratibimba*) as conditioned by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāropahita*). Consequently, there is no contingency for such experiences as "I am an elephant."

In this way, even the silver in the case of mother-of-pearlor-silver is superposed upon the reflection of consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect of the mother-of-pearlor, which resides within the mental modification (vṛtti) located in that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Some maintain that if it were superposed upon the original consciousness (bimba-caitanya) delimited by the "this" aspect of the mother-of-pearlor—which is common to all—there would follow the undesirable consequence that it could not be known by another person alone, just as pleasure and other such states are not so known.

Some, however, accepting that superimposition occurs upon the consciousness of the reflection itself, establish its non-cognisability by others by arguing: "That which has the ignorance belonging to a particular [reflection] as its material cause is perceptible only to that [reflection], and not to another individual soul. ||5||

Now, how is the experience of visual perception in the superimposition of silver on mother-of-pearl explained—whether directly or by way of depending on the knowledge of the substrate? And how is the experience of visual perception regarding dream-elephants and the like to be accounted for?

It is replied: First of all, it cannot be asserted that for the sake of supporting that [dream experience], the sense organs also undergo an illusory manifestation (*prātibhāsika-vivarta*), just like the dream body and its objects; for there is no such thing as an "unknown existence" (*ajñāta-sattva*) in the case of the illusory. Furthermore, since the sense organs are themselves beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), their existence must be stated as something known. Nor can it be maintained that the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) sense organs themselves emerge from their respective sockets, resort to the dream body, and thereby apprehend their respective objects.

This is because it is heard in scripture that during the time of dreaming, there is a cessation consisting of the absence of activity for those [organs]; furthermore, it is impossible for the empirical organ of touch to pervade the entire dream-body—which is larger in dimension than itself—within the interior of the body, which lacks the attainment of the empirical locations appropriate to it. Moreover, if it were to reside only in a single part of that body, it would fail to account for the sensation of cold touch experienced throughout all limbs resulting from immersion in dream-water.

For this very reason, even the suspicion that one might justify [the perception of dream objects] by claiming that "although the waking sense organs have ceased their activity in a dream, there exist subtle sense organs—which are constituent parts of the subtle body and are employed for the functions of the Taijasa state—and through these, dream objects possess the quality of being perceived by the senses," is also refuted; for such subtle sense organs distinct from the waking sense organs are not established.

Furthermore, because it is difficult to distinguish the self-luminosity of the Self during the waking state—due to the intermingling of lights such as the sun and the movement of the functions of the eyes and other senses—the text, referring specifically to the state of dream, establishes the self-luminosity of the Self therein. Otherwise, the statement "here" would be redundant, since the self-luminosity of the Self exists at all times.

In that regard, if one were to assume that the functioning and movement of the eyes and other senses continues even in dream, then, as in the waking state, its self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) would be difficult to discern there as well; thus, the scriptural passage cited would be contradicted. Now, one might object: "Even if it is assumed that the eyes and other senses have ceased in dream, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) remains unceased; therefore, since the *pariśeṣa* (method of elimination) is not established, the discernment of self-luminosity is not possible. This is not so.

This is because, by the reasoning stated in the section beginning with "The agent [is the self], for the sake of the meaningfulness of the scriptures" (*kartā śāstrārthavattvāt*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) lacks the capacity to be an instrument of knowledge when independent of other instruments such as the eyes; or else, because according to the reasoning stated in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, since that very organ undergoes transformation into the form of an elephant and so forth during a dream and thus exists as the object of cognition, it cannot simultaneously function as the instrument of cognition—therefore, the conclusion follows by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

Nor is there an impossibility of the recollection by one who has awakened of the elephant and so forth seen in a dream, even in the absence of a mental modification (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) during the dream; for that is possible through a modification of ignorance (avidyāvṛtti) postulated for the state of deep sleep.

In the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it is the very nature of consciousness (*svarūpa-caitanya*) as conditioned by that state which is the manifestation of ignorance, pleasure, and so forth; and for one who has awakened, there is recollection (*anusandhāna*) due to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the destruction of the limiting condition (*upādhi*)—the state [of sleep]—as maintained in the *Vedāntakaumudī*. Furthermore, even in this case [of dreaming], since there is no modification of nescience (*avidyā-vṛtti*) during deep sleep according to that school's view, the recollection is established through the mental impression produced by the destruction of the dream-state, which serves as the limiting condition for the consciousness that manifests the elephants and other objects of the dream.

Alternatively, let there be, even in a dream, a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) having elephants and other such objects as its content, according to the method stated by the *Kalpataru* on the basis of scriptural passages such as, "That is the sentient being (*sattva*) by which one sees a dream. Nor does this much [of an argument] fail to establish the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). For, since the internal organ—which is apprehended as "I"—is superimposed as identical with the individual soul (*jīva*) in every respect, its distinction from that [soul] is not established from the perspective of common worldly experience; thus, for the sake of the method of elimination, only the absence of the operation of the eyes and other senses is required.

Because there exists the certainty that "only what is well-known and visible is capable of being manifested by vision," and because this leaves no room for dependence on anything else by way of elimination (*pariśeṣa*),

it follows that in every respect, since the operation of the eyes and other senses is impossible in a dream, the experience of visual quality (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth regarding the elephants and other objects in a dream is nothing but delusion (*bhrānti*).

If it is argued that even in a dream, when the eyes are open, there is the experience of an elephant and so forth, whereas when they are closed there is not—just as in the waking state—the experience of an elephant and so forth is perceived to follow the opening of the eyes and other such conditions; we reply: like the experience "I see silver with my eyes," this too will be a certain dream-delusion (*svapnabhrama*), wherein the conformity to the eyes or the mental modification (*vṛtti*) conforming to it is superposed upon the experience of the dream-elephant and so forth, which is actually of the nature of the pure Witness (*sākṣin*).

For what indeed is too difficult for *māyā* to produce as an illusion, especially when transformed into the form of sleep? By its power, a chariot perceived in a dream becomes a man in an instant, and that very man becomes a cat in another instant; yet the dreamer does not reflect upon the contradiction between the preceding and succeeding moments. Therefore, although the perception of conformity to causal relations (*anvaya*) and so forth is equal in both cases, only the experience of the waking elephant and other objects is produced by the eyes and other sense organs, whereas the experience of the dream-elephant and other objects is not.

However, the proponents of the theory of creation through perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivādin*) maintain that it is logically untenable for an imagined object to have existence apart from being perceived; thus, they accept that the entire waking world-phenomenon comes into being simultaneously with its perception. They justify the apparent observation that the perception of a jar or similar object follows upon sensory contact with the eyes—though this would otherwise be inconsistent given the non-existence of the jar prior to its perception—by treating it as being exactly like a dream. Consequently, they assert that even the experience of a waking elephant and so forth is not visual.

Now, if one accepts the doctrine of "creation-as-perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*) and admits that the entire waking world-phenomenon (*jāgrat-prapañca*) is imagined, who is its imaginer (*kalpaka*)? Is it the Self (*ātman*) devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), or is it the Self conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopahita*)? The first alternative is not tenable; for even in liberation (*mokṣa*), since the imaginer would exist independently of any other means, the world-phenomenon would persist, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that there is no distinction between liberation and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Nor is the second alternative tenable; for since ignorance itself must be imagined, it must be stated that the imaginer is established prior to the imagination of that ignorance.

On this point, some say: that which is conditioned by each preceding imagined ignorance is the creator of each subsequent imagined ignorance. And because the stream of the creator and the act of creation has no beginning in time (*anidamprathamatva*), there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor should it be argued that because the beginninglessness of ignorance is accepted, its status as an imagined construct is untenable—like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—otherwise the distinction between the produced and the unproduced would be impossible.

Just as in a dream, some things such as gate-towers are imagined as already established from before, while others are imagined as being produced at that very moment, so too in the waking state, some imagined objects are conceived as having a beginning, while others are otherwise; by this much, the distinction between the originated (*sādi*) and the unoriginated (*anādi*) is logically established. By this, the distinction between cause and effect is also explained. Others, however, maintain that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like are in reality indeed unoriginated; they say that the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*) is not accepted there, but rather applies only to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) other than that [ignorance].

But even so, what is the basis for imagining the creation of ether and the rest, along with its sequence, which is perceived through scripture alone? None at all. What, then, is the support for such scriptural passages as, "From the Self, ether was produced"? Know that they have as their support the identity of the Self with Brahman, which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*). The declaration of the commentators and others is that the presentation of creation and dissolution in the scriptures is intended merely as a means to realize that [Brahman], since the realization of Brahman devoid of phenomenal expansion occurs through the methods of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*), and not because it is the primary purport (*tātparya*).

If there is no intention [to convey a literal meaning], then is the effort made to resolve mutual contradictions among the scriptural passages concerning the creation of ether and so forth, as well as their sequence, not futile? It is not futile; for that effort proceeds by provisionally accepting an intention for the sake of training in logic (*nyāya*).
As it is said in the *Śāstradarpaṇa*: "This was stated here after accepting that the scriptures have an intention regarding creation."
"But because those [scriptures] are intent upon the identity of Brahman and the Self, that [contradiction] does not exist at all.

Thus, the attainment of results from the performance of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, as enjoined by Vedic revelation, is equivalent to the correspondence with results produced by the performance of rituals enjoined by dream-revelation. Furthermore, since the Jyotiṣṭoma and other Vedic texts have their ultimate purport (tātparya) on Brahman by way of purifying the mind (sattvaśuddhi), they do not lack authority; this detailed exposition of the method for establishing the theory of "creation through perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi) is to be found in the original treatises. This is the doctrine of Dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda, which holds that the creation of the universe is simultaneous with its perception.
Another [view] holds that the creation of the universe is nothing but consciousness itself, because there is no evidence for a difference between the object of perception and the act of perception.
As it is said: "The wise declare this world to be of the very nature of cognition;
those of perverted vision, wandering in delusion, perceive it as having the nature of external objects."

The doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda* (the view that creation is simultaneous with perception) belongs to those who have studied the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* and other such works, based on the phrase "and because of memory.

However, certain teachers, finding no mental conviction in either of these two types of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*, favor the doctrine of *sṛṣṭadṛṣṭivāda* (the view that creation precedes perception). According to this, the entire universe is created by the Supreme Lord in the sequence shown by scripture; it possesses an existence that remains unknown until the application of the respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for each object, at which point its perception is established.

Nor should it be argued that, in the absence of the world's being merely imagined (*kalpita*), one would have to accept its reality—given that it possesses creation, dissolution, and so forth as established by scripture and other means, and that it performs causal functions as perceived through perception and other valid cognitions.

This is because, unlike the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like—which arises from the three causes consisting of sensory contact, mental impressions, and defects, or from the three causes consisting of the cognition of the substrate, mental impressions, and defects—it is not produced by these three causes. Consequently, although it lacks simultaneity with its conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), we nevertheless accept its falsity (*mithyātva*)—defined as being removable by knowledge alone, or as being distinct from both the real and the unreal, or as being the counter-positive of an absolute negation at all three times within the locus in which it is perceived. This is because, on the view that the world is real, such falsity is absent from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and therefore [the world] would be distinct from that [falsity].

If it is objected: "In that case, since the ego (ahaṅkāra) and its attributes also possess the aforementioned form of falsity—despite not being imaginary (kalpita) like space and so forth—the effort in the *Bhāṣya*, *Ṭīkā*, and *Vivaraṇa* to establish the three causes for their superimposition (*adhyāsa*) would be useless"; [the reply is:

Citsukhācārya maintains that the ego and the rest are indeed of a merely apparent nature (*prātibhāsika*), because they are cognizable solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

That is merely a statement made for the sake of argument (*abhyupetyavāda*). For the passage in that [text] which establishes the three causes—beginning with "of consciousness (*caitanya*), which is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the Self as Brahman, the non-dual substrate"—is clearly a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), because if consciousness were the instrument of valid knowledge (*pramākaraṇa*), it would entail the collapse of the conceptual framework that the Vedāntas are the instrument [of such knowledge]. Thus say the venerable Rāmādvayācāryas. ||7||

Now, since both the theory of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*) and the theory of "perception of creation" (*sṛṣṭidṛṣṭivāda*) agree that [the world] is false, how can that which is false possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)?

We reply: it is like a dream. [Objection: But is not the causal efficiency consisting of bathing and so forth, accomplished by water and the like in a dream, itself unreal? Whereas that accomplished by water and the like in the waking state is real? [Response: Some say that in both cases, the capacity to produce causal efficiency of a nature identical to itself is indistinguishable.

The teachers of Advaita-vidyā, however, say that dream objects do not merely possess causal efficiency that is sublated upon waking; for it is observed that dream women, serpents, and the like also produce effects such as pleasure and fear that are not sublated by that waking state.

For even in the case of pleasure, fear, and so forth, produced by objects in a dream, no sublation (bādha) is experienced after waking; on the contrary, since their persistence is observed even after waking through such signs as mental clarity and trembling of the body, it is determined that they existed even prior [to waking]. For this very reason, living beings desire a dream whose object generates pleasure once again, while they feel aversion toward a dream that is not of such a nature.

Moreover, even in a dream, there arises—just like a cognition—a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) in the form of pleasure, fear, and so forth. Nor should it be argued that it is the cognition of the woman and other objects in the dream alone that generates the pleasure and so on, and that such a cognition is itself real; for even that [cognition] is established merely through imagination, being a modification consisting of seeing, touching, and so forth, superimposed upon the witness of the dream-phenomenon. Indeed, for one whose sense organs have ceased to function, the modifications of the eyes and other organs cannot possibly be real.

Nor can it be said that the mere immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of that object is what produces pleasure, and that such immediacy is simply the nature of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). This is because we observe specific degrees of pleasure from seeing versus touching a beloved woman, or from touching her with the foot versus touching her with the hand; and because we observe specific degrees of fear from touching a serpent on a non-vital spot versus touching it on a vital spot. Consequently, even in a dream, it must be admitted that specific instances of pleasure, fear, and so forth are produced by specific mental modifications (*vṛtti*) consisting of imagined seeing, touching, and the like.

Likewise, some maintain that in a room illuminated by light being observed by other persons, where there is the capacity for objects such as jars to be manifested during waking, a man who has just entered perceives a darkness he himself imagines; and it is observed that this [imagined] darkness performs the causal function appropriate to well-known darkness—for instance, it acts as an obstruction to the jar and so forth for him, it recedes when a lamp or similar object is brought in, and it obstructs again when that [lamp] is removed. Thus they argue.

Others, however, maintain that in the performance of purposeful actions such as drinking or bathing, it is merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of water and so forth that is useful, not its "reality" (*satyatva*) residing therein; for since reality lacks both causality and the status of being a limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*), what is the use of it? Nor does this entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the water of a mirage or the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell would perform the same purposeful actions appropriate to well-known water and silver.

According to the view of the author of the *Tattvaśuddhi*, the fact that an error regarding a mirage or similar phenomenon is expressed by the word "water"—even though the universal of "water-ness" (*udakatva*) and so forth does not exist therein—is caused by the production [of that error] from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous experience that was itself expressed by that word; for, precisely because the universals such as "water-ness" that would cause the respective purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) are absent, such an [error] would otherwise not occur.

In that case as well, there exists a universal such as "upwardness" (*udaktva*) and so forth; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the erroneous cognition (*bhrama*) which manifests that specific distinction, and it would follow that those seeking water or the like would not engage in activity toward it. Thus, according to the view of those who maintain that the usage of "being of the same class as what was previously seen" applies even to the illusory (*prātibhāsika*), [superimposition occurs] in some cases through the destruction of the superimposition along with its root by the knowledge of the specific substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-viśeṣa-jñāna*); in some cases through the destruction of the mere superimposition by the cessation of the knowledge of the general substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-sāmānya-jñāna*); and in some cases, such as the locus of the superimposition of fire upon a cluster of *guñjā* seeds and the like, by means of the visual sense organ (*cakṣus*).

Furthermore, because there is no superimposition (adhyāsa) of the hot touch and other qualities that cause burning, cooking, and so forth, it is logically consistent that the specific causal efficacy (arthakriyā) associated with those [qualities] is absent in those cases. Moreover, it is accepted that in some instances, certain causal efficacies are indeed desired. Furthermore, one must state a form of the object that is useful for causal efficacy and serves to distinguish it from things like mirage-water; yet, apart from "unsublatedness throughout the three periods of time"—which contradicts scripture and is difficult to apprehend through perception and other means—it is possible to state that the very nature of being silver (rajatatva), when not produced by a particular defect, is the form useful for the causal efficacy appropriate to silver. Thus, the [alleged] contradiction is resolved.
Therefore, since the capacity for causal efficiency is possible even in the case of falsity, the phenomenal world is indeed false and not real. ||8||

Now, if the falsity (*mithyātva*)—which is a property of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—were real, then the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*) would be compromised; therefore, that [falsity] too must be declared to be merely false. So how could there be a compromise of the reality of the phenomenal world? For, according to your own reasoning, the falsity of something that is itself false does not contradict its reality; thus, the phenomenal world’s being "possessed of manifestation" (*saprapañcatva*), though false, does not contradict Brahman’s being "devoid of manifestation" (*niṣprapañcatva*).

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Advaitadīpikā*: "Falsity (*mithyātva*) has the same ontological nature as the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), such as space and so forth. And that falsity subverts the reality of its substratum (*dharmin*). For, when a property (*dharma*) subverts a property contradictory to itself, what is required is that the property possess the same degree of existence (*samasattva*) as its substratum—a point established by both parties—not ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*). This is because we do not admit the ultimate reality of properties such as 'being cloth' (*paṭatva*) which subvert [the absence of] 'being a pot' (*aghaṭatva*) and so forth. Since the state of Brahman having the phenomenal world (*saprapañcatva*) does not possess the same degree of existence as its substratum, it does not subvert its being devoid of the phenomenal world (*niṣprapañcatva*)."

For this very reason, the objection that "if falsity (*mithyātva*) is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*), then its contradictory—the non-illusory reality of the world (*prapañca-satyatva*)—must be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*)"—is refuted; because if falsity, which has the same ontological status as its substratum (*dharmin*), is empirical, it follows as a rule that the substratum itself must also be empirical.

Alternatively, whatever property is removable by the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of its own object excludes that which is its opposite in that very locus. This is seen from the established distinction: in the case of mother-of-pearl, the identity with mother-of-pearl is not removable by the direct perception of that object, and it is opposed to non-mother-of-pearlhood; whereas in that same locus, the identity with silver is removable by that [perception], and it is not opposed to silverness. Thus, the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), even though it is imagined (*kalpita*), is not removable by the direct perception of the phenomenal world, and therefore it indeed excludes its opposite, namely reality (*satyatva*).

However, since the world-phenomenality (*saprapañcatva*) of Brahman is to be removed by the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*), it does not contradict its being devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañcatva*).

By this, it must be stated that if Brahman, which is accessible through verbal testimony, is real, then the fitness (*yogyatā*) of the words and the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the verbal cognition must also be real. This is because there is no establishment of a conventional object by means of an untrustworthy statement possessing merely apparent fitness, nor of a ultimate object by means of a statement regarding the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth possessing merely conventional fitness; for there is a rule that the meaning of a word is established as possessing the same level of reality as the fitness itself. Furthermore, if the validity consisting in the non-sublation of the object were unreal, the reality of that object would be impossible.

And thus, the argument that because of the existence of real entities other than Brahman, duality would necessarily follow, and therefore the phenomenal world consisting of ether and so forth must also be real, is refuted.

Since causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) has been established as being merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), it is possible for even conventional fitness (*yogyatā*) to exist within the true Brahman; for in the Vedānta texts dedicated to Brahman, such words as "truth" (*satya*) and so forth exist, thereby establishing the truth of Brahman. Conversely, in sentences concerning the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the like, such words are absent; and even if they were present, their meaning would not be established due to contradiction with the more powerful scriptural texts on the non-duality of Brahman. Thus, the distinction between the two cases is logically justified. Furthermore, there is no evidence for a rule that the ontological status (*sattā*) of a word and its referent must be identical.

Furthermore, just as the validity of the cognition of a jar is itself non-jar-like, so too the validity of the cognition of the real Brahman is established as being false, because it is composed of elements other than that [Brahman]. Therefore, by the logic stated in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, the falsity of the entire phenomenal world, beginning with the ether (*viyat*), becomes as indelible as a diamond coating. ||9||

[Objection: Surely, even if the falsity of the insentient phenomenal world consisting of ether and so forth is established by the words "originating" (*ārambhaṇa*) and others, it is not logical that the sentient beings who partake in liberation should be false; therefore, the concordance (*samanvaya*) with the non-dual Brahman is not tenable. Nor is the previously mentioned identity of those beings with Brahman logical, because it is impossible for those who are mutually distinct to be identical with a single Brahman. And their mutual distinction is not unestablished, since it is established by the distribution of pleasure, pain, and so forth. [Reply:
No, for even though they are non-different, the distribution of those [experiences] is possible solely through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). 10.

But surely, even if there is a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), since that [essential] non-difference does not depart, how can there be any systematic distinction? For the non-confusion of contradictory attributes, which must be established by means of a difference in substrata, cannot be accomplished by accepting a difference in something other than those [substrata].

On this point, some say that the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth is indeed established through the difference of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). This is because scriptures such as, "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are merely the mind," and "Consciousness performs the sacrifice," demonstrate that the mind alone is the locus of all misfortunes; and because scriptures such as, "For this person (*puruṣa*) is unattached," and "Being unattached, he is not attached," demonstrate that the conscious self (*cetana*) is entirely indifferent.

And this being so, there is no contradiction with the experience of the bondage of agency and so forth having the same substratum as consciousness (*caitanya*). For, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is superimposed through identity with consciousness, it is logical that its attributes are experienced as having the same substratum as consciousness. Nor should it be argued that if the internal organ were the locus of the bondage of agency and so forth, the conscious self would not be the transmigrating entity (*saṃsārī*).

This is because it is accepted that its very state of being the substrate for the superimposition of identity with the knot of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)—which is the locus of bondage such as agency—is its transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). For by that much alone, just as there is the conceit "this is an ornament" regarding a rope or similar object which is the substrate for the superimposition of identity with a serpent that is the locus of the ornament, the conceit of the Self being the locus of misfortune is likewise established. It is precisely with this intention that we find such scriptural and traditional texts as: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," and "The self, deluded by the ego-sense, thinks 'I am the doer.'"

Nor should it be argued that even so, the systematic distribution of imagined pleasure, pain, and so forth within the Self does not succeed—on the grounds that various internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which serve as the substrates for diverse pleasures and pains, are superimposed upon one and the same Self. For, just as the mass of evils residing in the internal organ—which has attained a state of identity with the Self through superimposition—is regarded by the Self as its own through such conceit, so too is the mutual distinction existing between those [organs] likewise regarded as belonging to the Self; thus, the systematic distribution of those [pleasures and pains] is established by means of that very distinction.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "Even though pleasure, pain, and so forth are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), their experience takes the form of the Witness (*sākṣin*); therefore, because the Witness is one, the distinction between experiences—such as the enjoyment consisting of the experience of pleasure and pain—is not established. [The response is:

Because the Witness itself becomes differentiated through its identification with each respective internal organ, it possesses differentiation according to the distinctions among those internal organs; thus, since the experience of the pleasure, pain, and so forth of each respective internal organ takes the form of that [differentiated] Witness, the establishment of that distinction is indeed possible.

Others, however, argue that since it is impossible for an insentient entity (*jaḍa*) to be the locus of bondage such as agency, the Sūtra—"The agent [is the Self], because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless"—establishes that the locus of bondage is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Furthermore, because this unreal reflection is distinct from its original (*bimba*), there arises a systematic distinction between the learned and the ignorant, or between those who experience pleasure and pain, or those who act and so forth, based on the difference in each respective internal organ. Nor does this lead to the fault of a lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between bondage and liberation, even if the locus of bondage is this superimposed reflection; for liberation occurs when that very reflection is sublated.

They say that bondage consists in the state of being the locus of the superimposition of identity with the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)—which is the substrate for the attribution of agency—because that reflection is superimposed upon the ultimate individual soul (paramārthajīva), which is the substratum underlying liberation, since [the reflection] exists within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) while the [ultimate soul] exists in its own nature.
Others, however, say:
"The wise declare that the self, when joined with the body, the senses, and the mind, is the enjoyer.

Since scripture teaches that the conscious principle (*cetana*)—joined with the body and senses as their auxiliary cause and with the mind through identity—is the enjoyer, there is a distinction between the states [of bondage and liberation] based on the distinctions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the resulting distinctions of the qualified [self]. Nor is there a lack of coordination (i.e., a mismatch between the locus of bondage and the locus of liberation) such that the qualified self is bound while the pure self is liberated; for the bondage residing in the qualified self does not fail to inhere in the substrate (the pure self), since the qualified self is not something distinct from it. Thus they say.

But let it be that the pure consciousness alone is the locus of bondage such as agency; for, according to the analogy of the redness [reflected] in a crystal, since the internal organ—or that which is qualified by it—is the locus of agency and so forth, agency and other such qualities are superimposed upon the consciousness as well due to its proximity. Nor is there any inconsistency in the established distinction of that [consciousness] as being one; for that distinction is established precisely through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). And it should not be argued that the attribution of contradictory properties to one thing on the basis of a difference in another is untenable.

They say this because we observe that in a tree, the distinction between conjunction and its absence is established merely through the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the root and the tip; and because we observe a variety of phenomena—such as the perception and non-perception of sound in various locations, and the perception of sounds that are loud, soft, pleasant, or unpleasant—in the case of space which has attained the state of the sense of hearing (śrotra) through the difference in the limiting adjuncts of the ear-cavities of various individuals.

However, some say: "If the rule for establishing contradictory attributes arises solely from a difference in substrata, then let the conceptualization of difference in the case of consciousness (caitanya) occur precisely through the power of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). For there is no consensus anywhere that a non-conceptualized difference in substratum is the cause of such establishment.

This is because we accept the establishment of attributes such as dark, bright, round, and long in a face through a difference conceptualized by limiting adjuncts like a gem, a mirror, or a sword; and we likewise accept the establishment of attributes such as being behind or in front in a lamp through a difference conceptualized by the limiting adjunct of support by a finger. ||11||

Thus, when the establishment of the distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) has been rendered possible, it remains to be determined: what is the specific limiting adjunct that serves as the cause for the living beings' failure to experience one another's pleasure and so forth?

On this point, some say that the non-difference and difference of the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that cause, respectively, the connection and lack of connection [between experiences]. This is because there is a connection between a sensation delimited by the body and that which is delimited by it, whereas there is no connection between a sensation delimited by the foot and that which is delimited by the hand; for one does not have the cognition: "I, who am delimited by the hand, am experiencing a sensation delimited by the foot. If that is so, how then does the hand function to extract a thorn stuck in the foot? [Response: It is due to the proximity (*sāmīpya*) [of the two parts of the body]. Just as the eye, though distinct from the mind, functions toward objects through its connection with the mind, so too the hand, though distinct from the foot, functions toward the foot through its connection with the mind. Or rather, it is because of the non-difference of the substratum (*āśraya*); for the substratum of the sensation is the self (*ātman*), which is not delimited by the body. Thus, the sensation delimited by the foot is connected with the self, and the activity of the hand is likewise connected with that same self. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the distinction between the locus of experience and the substratum is established by the fact that the former is the object of the notion "my body," while the latter is the object of the notion "I. For the notion "I" does not refer to the body, since the body is perceived as "this" (*idam*), whereas the notion "I" is never perceived as such. Nor is the notion "I" a mere mental construction (*kalpanā*), for it is not sublated by any other cognition. Consequently, the notion "I" refers to something distinct from the body, and thus the self is proven to be eternal. Furthermore, the notion "I" is not a mental construction because it is not produced by the recollection of a previously perceived object, nor is it produced by the perception of a currently present object.
