Therefore, the notion "I" is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And since it is a direct perception, it is not erroneous, just like the perception of color. This is not an operation of the hand, because there is no synthetic awareness [of the pain] as being delimited by the hand; rather, since there is no difference between the part and the whole—the foot and the body—the sensation delimited by the foot is synthesized by that which is delimited by the body in the form, "I am one who feels pain in my foot. It is due to this synthesis [that the pain is felt). Likewise, because there is no identity between the bodies of Caitra and Maitra, the sensation delimited by Caitra’s body is not synthesized by that which is delimited by Maitra’s body.

Nor is it connected by means of another whole (avayavin) that is interwoven through both bodies; for there is no such thing as a whole interwoven through both that could serve as a locus of experience. Thus, there is no consequence of Maitra’s body engaging in activity to extract a thorn lodged in Caitra’s body.

Others, however, maintain that the distinction of separated limiting adjuncts (*viśliṣṭopādhibheda*) is the cause of non-identification. Thus, there is no fault even if one accepts the identification of a sensation delimited by the hand with one delimited by the foot. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an embryo identifying with the mother's pleasure; for the term "separated" is intended to refer to two things that have not entered into a single whole as constituent parts (*avayava*), and such is the case with the mother’s body and the fetal body. So they say.
And it is not the case that "even headless trunks (kabandhas), with their staff-like arms raised in weapons and seeing with the eyes of their fallen heads, struck down enemies here."

It should be stated that even in the case of dismemberment mentioned in the *Bhārata*, continuity is understood; for there too, the head and the trunk have entered into a single composite whole as constituent parts. Furthermore, since either fainting or death is inevitable immediately after the severing of the head, such a statement—which describes a fact contrary to what is observed—is intended, by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*), to praise the extraordinary intensity of the warrior's enthusiasm.

This is because, even though it is a statement of an existing fact (*bhūtārthavāda*) by virtue of having as its object a particular person endowed with such power, there is no obstruction to the general rule that such a statement does not depend upon [the speaker's] personal recollection. For this very reason, in the views stated and those yet to be stated, there is no possibility of fault regarding the recollection of the internal events of the bodies of yogis and those who remember their past lives (*jātismara*).

Others, however, maintain that identity and difference of the body are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that cause the presence or absence of recollection; for we observe that there is recollection of what was experienced in childhood and in another life, while there is no such recollection [between different bodies]. Nor can it be argued that there is a difference of the body even between childhood and youth, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Nor can their difference be understood through a difference in dimension (*parimāṇa*); for just as there is a difference of dimensions at the root and the top of a single tree, so too it is possible for multiple dimensions to coexist in a single entity across different times.

If it is argued that there can be no difference in dimension (*parimāṇabheda*) without an accumulation of parts, and since parts arriving later cannot occupy a body already established beforehand, a difference in dimension necessarily implies a difference in the body—this is not so. For we do not accept the process of atoms (*paramāṇuprakriyā*), as it is impossible for it to conform to such phenomena as the expansion of a circle of light pervading the interior of a palace at the very moment a lamp is lit, or its contraction at the very moment the lamp is covered.

Regarding the theory of illusory manifestation (vivartavāda), they say that just as a body shown by a magician, the growth of the body is possible through illusion (māyā) even without an accumulation of constituent parts.
Others, however, maintain that the distinction between [the self's] recollection and non-recollection is due to the identity or difference of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) with [the self].
And this position has been established previously.

However, some, accepting that "the various ignorances (*ajñāna*) are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual souls (*jīva*"), maintain that the distinction between the experience of unity and the lack thereof is established by the difference or non-difference of those [ignorances]. ||12||

In this regard, some—following the sequence of the sūtras and the commentary in the section beginning with "A part [of Brahman], because of the designation of diversity," namely "Because of the lack of restriction regarding unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)," "And likewise in the case of intentions and so forth," and "If it be said [the distinction is due to] location, no, because of being included within"—state that if one does not accept a systematic arrangement based on the difference of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) within a single Self, then the same impossibility of systematic arrangement applies even to the doctrine of the plurality of Selves according to the system of Kaṇabhuj (Kaṇāda) and others.

For instance, when a thorn piercing the foot of Caitra produces pain in Caitra, why does pain not arise in other selves as well? Since all selves are omnipresent, there is no difference in their inclusion within Caitra’s body. Nor can there be a fixed rule that "pain belongs only to him whose body the piercing occurs, and not to others," because it is impossible to restrict the body—which arises in the presence of all selves—to belong to one person alone and not to others.

Nor is there a rule that "whatever body is produced by a particular unseen force (adṛṣṭa) belongs to that [specific] self," because the restriction of the unseen force itself remains unestablished. For when the mind is conjoined with a certain self for the production of that unseen force, it is conjoined with other selves as well. How, then, could that unseen force be produced in one case alone when the causes are common to all?

If it is argued that—even though mere conjunction with the mind is common to all—distinctions such as "I shall obtain this fruit," the volition (*abhisandhi*), and the effort conducive to the production of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) are established [as specific to each individual], and that the restriction of the unseen merit will therefore arise from those very factors; we say no. For even volitions and the like are not established as restricted, since they are produced by the common conjunction with the mind. If it is argued that the conjunction with one's own mind is the cause of volition and so forth, and thus the conjunction with the mind itself will be non-common (specific); we say no.

Because the mind, being eternally conjoined with all selves, cannot be restricted as belonging to any one self alone; nor can the relationship of ownership between specific selves and the mind be established on the basis of specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), since that *adṛṣṭa* itself cannot be established as having a fixed distribution, as previously argued.

[Objection: "Even if selves (*ātman*) are omnipresent, it is only specific locations (*pradeśaviśeṣa*) of theirs that undergo bondage; therefore, since other selves lack those specific locations within Caitra’s body, the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth will be maintained. [Reply: No. For when Caitra departs from a certain location after experiencing pleasure and so forth there, and Maitra arrives at that very same location, one observes pleasure, pain, and so forth in him as well; thus, a specific location of another self must also be included within another body.

Therefore, even if there were a plurality of selves, the systematic arrangement [of experience] would be difficult to establish. And if it could somehow be established, it is more appropriate to accept a single self in accordance with scripture and for the sake of parsimony, and to establish that arrangement within that very unity. ||13||

"Let it be then that the selves are indeed atomic, if no systematic account can be given for their omnipresence. Not so; for if the selves were atomic, the simultaneous arising of pleasure throughout the entire body, as well as the simultaneous presiding over the hands, head, and feet, would be impossible.

Regarding this, the modern conception is that the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic, because its passing out, going, and returning—as heard in scripture—would otherwise be inexplicable, and because its atomicity is explicitly stated in such scriptural passages as, "For this self is indeed atomic; by which [self] these two are bound, merit and demerit," and "Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair. Even though they are atomic, due to the analogy of the light of a lamp, their qualities such as knowledge and pleasure extend to specific locations beyond their own substrate; thus, there is no lack of perception of pleasure throughout the entire body.

Because individual souls (*jīva*) possess a partial nature (*aṃśatva*) in accordance with such Smṛti texts as "Droṇa is a portion of Bṛhaspati," there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the non-simultaneity of pleasure, pain, and so forth among those [souls] residing in hands, heads, feet, and the like, nor in the diversity of experiences among yogins residing in multiple bodies (*kāyavyūha*). Thus, since the individual souls are atomic (*aṇu*), there is no confusion [of experiences], and the regularity of pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as the distinction from the omnipresent Lord (*īśvara*), is established.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Advaitadīpikā*: "Even so, how can systematic order (*vyavasthā*) be established? For, just as Caitra experiences the pleasure and pain residing in his own distinct parts—as in 'pain in my foot, pleasure in my head'—it would be impossible to prevent him from also experiencing the pleasure and pain belonging to Maitra. For there is no difference between the distinction of Caitra’s own parts [from one another] and the distinction of Maitra [from Caitra]."

In the case of the bodily manifestation (*kāyavyūha*), since those parts capable of spreading elsewhere must necessarily be distinct from the living self (*jīva*), and because you yourself admit both difference and non-difference between the part and the whole; nor should it be argued that "pure difference" is not the cause of the lack of identification (*ananusandhāna*). For what would constitute the "purity" of difference? Would it be its not being accompanied by the relation of part and whole, or its not being accompanied by non-difference? It cannot be the first.

For, since the Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtra passages—namely, "This is indeed a portion of the Supreme," "A portion of Myself alone [is] in the world of living beings," and "A portion [of the Lord], because of the designation of diversity"—establish that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of Brahman, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion of enjoyments between Brahman and the individual soul.

Now, one might object: "Just as the parts of a living being are related to the living being itself, so too the individual soul (*jīva*) is not a part of Brahman in the sense of being a literal portion; rather, its 'part-hood' is merely figurative, consisting simply in being similar to it while being smaller than it—just as Jupiter's disk is said to be a hundredth part of the moon's disk. If this is argued, we ask: apart from that, what is the primary sense of part-hood belonging to the parts of the living being in relation to the living being itself, which is here assigned to the body as the cause of non-recollection? It cannot be the state of being a constituent material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), like threads in relation to a cloth, because the living being is beginningless (*anādi*).

Nor can they be considered as mere spatial divisions (*pradeśatva*) of the Great Space, like the space within a jar and so forth, nor as fragments (*khaṇḍatva*), like pieces of stone split by a chisel; for, being atomic (*aṇutva*), they are partless (*niṣpradeśatva*) and indivisible (*acchedyatva*). If it is argued that "being a part" (*aṃśatva*) is intended to mean being a substance that is both different and non-different [from the whole], we say no; for if that were the case, it would result in the confusion of experiences (*bhogasāṅkarya*) between the individual soul and the Lord, as well as among the individual souls themselves.

For you also accept that there is non-difference among those [individuals] who are distinct from one another by virtue of their sentience and so forth; furthermore, according to your view—which maintains both difference and non-difference between a collection and its members—there exists mutual non-difference among the individual souls contained within a single collection, since it is unavoidable that each soul is non-different from itself by virtue of being non-different from the collection with which it is non-different.

If conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like, as well as genus (*jāti*), were to reside in multiple substrata, then—since quality (*guṇa*) and substance (*guṇin*) would be non-different—it would follow that even a cloth which is non-different from a conjunction non-different from a jar would itself be non-different from the jar; for you yourself have accepted the rule that "what is non-different from what is non-different from X is itself non-different from X."

Nor is there another form of non-difference between the part and the whole—distinct from the non-difference caused by their being included in a single aggregate, their uniformity in properties such as sentience common to other living beings, and so forth—which could serve as the basis for the mutual awareness [of the part] despite their difference, such that it might be intended here to avoid over-extension. For if that were the case, it would follow that this very [non-difference] must be specifically defined. If it is argued that the "distinction" regarding the non-difference of the part and the whole consists in its not being caused by the uniformity of properties and so on, we say no.

Since the soul (*jīva*) and its parts (*aṃśa*) possess a single uniform nature through common attributes such as sentience, they are non-different both when delimited by a single body and when merged in a *kāyavyūha* (multiplication of bodies) by virtue of being a collective whole; thus, there exists the fact that their non-difference is indeed caused by the uniformity of their attributes and so forth. If it is argued that even though other forms of non-difference caused by the uniformity of attributes exist, the non-difference that serves as the cause for the relation of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*) between the soul and its parts is not caused by that [uniformity of attributes], we say: no.

Because, in your view, there is no duality due to the non-difference between those two, and since the locus being one, you do not admit that either difference or non-difference can be manifold based on a difference in counter-correlates or a difference in their forms; therefore, in the first position, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains firmly established. By this very argument, the second position is also refuted. For if difference unaccompanied by non-difference were the cause of the failure to recognize [the identity], then according to the reasoning stated, since non-difference exists between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, as well as among individual souls themselves in your view, the over-extension would be unavoidable.

Now, it might be argued that "the perception of non-difference is the cause of identification," and thus in its absence there is no identification. Since one's own non-difference from oneself and one's non-difference from one's own body are perceptual, the observer of those [states] experiences the identification with pain and so forth; however, although non-difference from another individual soul exists, because that is not perceptual, there is no identification with that other's pain and so forth.

If it is argued that for one who remembers their past lives (*jātismara*), the recollection of events from a previous birth is possible because the non-difference from that former self is perceptually evident, whereas for others it is not due to the absence of such perception—and thus all this is consistent—then, even under the doctrine of a single Self (*aikātmyavāda*), Caitra would have no perceptual experience of non-difference from Maitra’s Self and so forth because of the obscuration of ignorance (*ajñāna*) which veils the state of being the Self of all. Since all practical distinctions (*sarvavyavasthā*) can be accounted for by that very [obscuration], the acceptance of a plurality of selves (*ātmabheda*) is useless and contradicts the Śruti.

Even in this case, your position—which maintains that the nature of reality consists of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)—cannot be sustained. For since the omniscient Lord must necessarily perceive the non-difference between himself and the substantially real individual souls (*jīva*), he would inevitably experience the thought "I am suffering" whenever those souls are in pain. In our view, however, although the Lord perceives the transmigratory state within the soul that is non-different from himself—just as one perceives dirt on a face reflected in a mirror—he does not grieve because of his certain knowledge of its falsity; thus, this undesirable consequence does not arise.

It might be argued: "Let there be no distinction of parts for the hands, head, feet, and so forth, nor for the manifestation of multiple bodies (*kāyavyūha*). Since the lamp of the self possesses an all-pervading radiance of knowledge that never departs, this alone will serve as the substrate for everything. This is not so. For, unlike knowledge, the experience of pleasure and pain—which is a property of the self—cannot arise by depending upon knowledge; consequently, it would follow that there could be no diversity in experience based on the distinction between the parts of the whole (such as hands and feet) or the distinction between different bodies in the case of one possessing a manifestation of multiple bodies (*kāyavyūha*).

If one accepts that "the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth is a property of cognition alone, not a property of the self," then even if a distinction among the cognitions—which are qualities of the self—is established by their diversity, the non-distinction of the self itself remains unestablished; thus, it is impossible to refute the non-difference of the self on the grounds of the diversity of experiences and the like. Furthermore, this position entails an abandonment of [your own] doctrine, for if the self, which is the substratum of experience and the like, were atomic and thus distinct in each body, there would be no occurrence of a confusion of all attributes, as would be the case if one asserted either its omnipresence or its non-difference [from other selves].
Therefore, it is not tenable to establish the systematic order [of experience] by accepting the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Nor is it logical for you to establish a difference between that [Self] and the Lord, because of the scriptural hearing of its departure and so forth, and because of the direct hearing of its atomicity in your own doctrine that "the individual soul (jīva) is atomic. This is because in such scriptural passages as "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," "He has entered within as the ruler of people," and "The two who have entered the cave in the highest, most excellent [place]," the hearing of entry and so forth is evident; and because in the scripture, "This is the subtle one (aṇimā); this is my Self within the heart, subtler than a grain of rice or a grain of barley," there is a direct hearing of atomicity.

If the other [the Supreme Self] were also established as being merely atomic, how could the distinction between the Supreme and the individual soul (jīva) be established on the basis of their being all-pervasive and atomic respectively?

One might object: "Since the scriptures state, 'He is omnipresent and eternal like space,' and 'Greater than heaven, greater than the intermediate region,' and so forth; and since the omnipresence of the Supreme is established by His being the material cause of the entire phenomenal world, those scriptural passages concerning His atomicity must be interpreted as intended for the purpose of meditation, or they should be understood as referring to His being difficult to grasp. Furthermore, the scriptural passages concerning His entry [into bodies] are to be explained by means of limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as the body. And it should not be suspected that the scriptural passages concerning the departure of the individual soul and so forth can likewise be explained away by means of the intellect as a limiting adjunct.

If it be argued that this is because the departure of the individual soul (jīva) is stated to occur even before the departure of what is called the intellect (buddhi)— as in the passage, "When he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him"— and because movement is heard of even after the liberation from name and form— as in, "The knower, freed from name and form, goes to the divine Person who is higher than the high"—

and because of the mention of the analogy of a cart as the basis for natural movement, as in, "Just as a chariot well-equipped moves along when its driver lets go [of the reins], even so this bodily self, mounted by the conscious self (prājña), moves along letting go"— we reply that this argument lacks substance.

"Verily, this great, unborn Self is that which consists of consciousness. Just as when a jar containing space is being carried, it is the jar that is carried and not the space; even so is the individual soul (jīva) comparable to space."

This is because in such scriptural passages as these, the individual soul (*jīva*) is also heard to possess omnipresence; furthermore, in your own system, since *prakṛti* alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world and Brahman lacks the status of being the material cause of the world, it is possible for the soul—even if atomic—to be the material cause of the world, just as it is the material cause of the diverse pleasures and pains experienced within its various bodies in the case of the "multitude of bodies" (*kāyavyūha*). Consequently, its omnipresence remains unestablished. Moreover, if the scriptural texts concerning its "entry" [into the world] are interpreted as being conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the body, then it is equally possible to accept that the scriptural texts concerning the soul's "departure" and so forth are likewise conditioned by the limiting adjunct of the intellect (*buddhi*).

In the commentary on the sūtra, "The one with five functions is designated as the mind," the distinction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established through their difference in function; therefore, when the individual soul (*jīva*), whose limiting adjunct is the intellect, first departs, it is logical that the vital breath follows after it. Furthermore, since the scriptural teaching regarding the attainment of Brahman after the relinquishing of name and form applies to the attainer—the individual soul—it would contradict the omnipresence of Brahman, the object to be attained, were it not so.

Even after liberation from ordinary name and form (*nāmarūpa*), according to the view that Brahman is to be attained through the mediation of a non-material cosmic body (*vigraha*) and so forth, there is no contradiction in the scriptural accounts of attaining Brahman through the mediation of the individual soul (*jīva*), since the soul also possesses a non-material body, senses, and so on. Furthermore, if the soul’s intrinsic movement were established merely by hearing the analogy of the cart as the locus of movement, then by the same token, Brahman would also [be subject to movement], because of its association with the soul—the locus of intrinsic entry—in the passage, "The two have entered the cave."

Because it is possible for there to be an establishment of entry into the essential nature (*svābhāvika*), one must maintain that the single term "entered" (*praviṣṭa*), which applies to both Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*), refers to an entry of a single form. Therefore, since in the opponent's view the distinction between the all-pervasiveness of Brahman and the atomicity of the individual soul is not established, there is no hope of establishing their difference on that basis.

In our view, since the subordinate statements must be interpreted in accordance with the Great Mahāvākya concerning the non-duality of Brahman and the individual soul (jīva), it is clearly explained in the Bhāṣya and other works that the soul is all-pervading in its essential nature (svarūpa), while its limitation is due to its adjuncts (aupādhika); thus, the scriptural texts that appear to establish a difference between the individual soul and Brahman are reconciled.

Therefore, because the insentient phenomenal world (prapañca) is illusory and the sentient phenomenal world is not distinct from Brahman, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the Vedāntas' consistent convergence (samanvaya) upon the non-dual Brahman, which is the sole object to be attained through knowledge.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śāstrāsiddhāntaleśasaṅgraha*.
The Third Chapter.
Now, an objection: how can the attainment of Brahman be through knowledge alone? For it is recorded in the Smṛti that ritual actions (*karma*) are also a cause for attaining it.
"It has been stated by the Great Sage that consciousness and action are the causes for attaining That.

This is true; for according to the Śruti, "There is no other path for going," and because in the attainment of the eternally established Brahman—which is like finding a forgotten necklace of gold already around one's neck—no means other than knowledge is possible. Such a Smṛti text merely intends to show that action is required indirectly in the attainment of Brahman. Where, then, is the utility of actions?

On this point, the followers of the Bhāmatī school say: "The Brahmins seek to know that very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting"—according to this scripture, [the aforementioned duties] are useful for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), which serves as the means for attaining Brahman by way of accomplishing knowledge. Now, one might ask: why could they not be useful for the very knowledge that is desired? It cannot be so, because the meaning of the suffix (the desire) is primary.

And from the commentary on the *Sarvāpekṣā* section: "The means for the realization of knowledge (*vidyā-sādhana*), such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), are proximate due to their application to knowledge; however, sacrifices and the like are remote because they are connected with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

If it is argued that the application of sacrifices and the like to the desire to know is not logical—since for one who performs sacrifices for the sake of the desire to know, the desire to know would already be established once there is a wish directed toward knowledge, and in its absence, a longing for the desire to know (as a means to knowledge) is impossible, making the performance of sacrifices for the sake of the desire to know untenable—we say: no.

Just as one who has become emaciated through an aversion to food may, despite having a desire characterized by longing for food in order to remedy that condition, fail to develop an appetite (ruci) leading to actual engagement with it due to the defect of an imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātu-vaiṣamya) caused by severe indigestion and so forth—therefore, according to the method of administering medicine for such loss of appetite—the Brahman, which is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, is the means of attaining it through knowledge; this is established by the power of the clarity of mind (*citta-prasāda*) produced by the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*) throughout many previous births, performed without desire for their fruits.

Even when a person has attained full confidence and possesses a desire characterized by an orientation toward the realization of Brahman and knowledge, there may still exist numerous defects of evil deeds accumulated through beginningless existence. Due to these, just as in the case of a worldly seeker (*āstikakāmuka*) who is inclined toward prohibited actions, an inclination that culminates in engagement in the means of knowledge—such as hearing (*śravaṇa*)—does not arise because of the obstruction caused by a preoccupation with the enjoyment of sense objects. Therefore, it is logical to enjoin sacrifices and other rites that remove such obstructions and bring about that [inclination].

However, those who follow the *Vivaraṇa* say: "According to the general rule that 'between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix, the meaning of the suffix is predominant,' the connection with being a verbal means (*śābda-sādhanatā*) occurs only with that which is understood through words as the object of desire. This is because, in sentences such as *svargakāmaḥ*, the specific rule already established is more powerful.

In common usage such as "he wishes to go by horse" (*aśvena jigamiṣati*) or "he wishes to kill with a sword" (*asinā jighāṃsati*), the means of action—such as the horse—is understood to be connected only with the object of the desire denoted by the desiderative suffix (*san*). Likewise, in Vedic usage such as "that is to be sought after, that indeed is to be desired to be known" (*tadanveṣṭavyaṃ tadvāva vijijñāsitavyam*) or "it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (*mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), the injunction expressed by the suffix *tavya* is understood to be connected only with the object of the desire denoted by the desiderative suffix. Therefore, because the application of sacrifices and other rites is established only with respect to knowledge—which is denoted by the verbal root—as being the very object of the desire, [the rites are subordinate to knowledge].

If it be objected that, such being the case, since the performance of ritual action would follow until the dawning of knowledge, the fact that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)—characterized by the abandonment of action—is for the sake of knowledge, as established by such scriptural texts as "Indeed, that is to be known through renunciation alone," would be contradicted; we say no. For just as the production of rice and other grains occurs through both plowing and non-plowing—there being plowing prior to sowing the seed, and non-plowing thereafter—so too it is said:
"For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person when he has ascended to yoga, tranquility (*śama*) is said to be the means. (BhG 6.3)

In accordance with such statements, ritual action is to be performed until the arising of an inward inclination toward direct realization—characterized by the desire to know and so forth—within the purity of the mind; thereafter comes renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). This is because it is accepted that knowledge is perfected through both action and its renunciation.
For it is said in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*: "Having brought about the inward inclination of the intellect through purification by means of rituals..."
"Having accomplished their purpose, they set like clouds at the end of the rainy season. Thus [it is said].

If it is asked: "Even in the view that ritual actions (*karman*) are for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārtha*), what is the difference from the view that they are for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣārtha*), since in both cases one performs rituals only until the point of the desire to know?"—the distinction is this: in the view that rituals are for the sake of knowledge, even after the desire to know—which serves as the intermediate means—is accomplished and the rituals have ceased, there remains a rule that knowledge is produced only after one has completed the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), which are preceded by renunciation (*nivṛtti*) and depend upon the acquisition of a qualified teacher.

However, according to the view that [ritual action] is for the purpose of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), one’s aim is accomplished merely by producing an intense desire capable of generating engagement in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; thus, there is no necessary rule that it must produce knowledge. They say this is just like the case in the Smṛti passage, "He who has these forty sacraments," where ritual actions are held to have the purpose of *saṃskāra*—characterized by the removal of impurity and the instilling of qualities—which renders one fit for the knowledge of the Self. ||1||

Now, of which actions is the application (viniyoga) understood through the cited scripture? On this point, some have stated that the phrase "by the recitation of the Vedas" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the duties of the student (*brahmacārin*), "by sacrifice and by charity" for the duties of the householder (*gṛhastha*), and "by austerity and by fasting" for the duties of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); thus, it is the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) alone that are useful for knowledge (*vidyā*). For this very reason, in the *Śārīraka-sūtra*, in the aphorism "And because they are prescribed, the duties of the stages of life also [are to be performed]," the term "duties of the stages of life" (*āśramakarma*) is employed among the actions intended for knowledge.

In the *Kalpataru*, however, there is no application of knowledge (*vidyopayoga*) for the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) alone; for in the section titled "But even in between, because that is seen," the application of knowledge is established even for the rites performed by those such as the widowers (*vidhura*) who are devoid of a stage of life.

Nor should it be suspected that the aforementioned section (adhikaraṇa) is intended merely to establish the eligibility of those such as Vidhura—who, though not belonging to any stage of life (anāśramin), have generated the desire for knowledge (*vividisā*) through sacrifices and other rites performed in previous births—to engage in the means of knowledge such as hearing the scriptures; for it does not intend to establish the utility of those very rites for the sake of knowledge. This is because, in the sūtra and its commentary for that section, "And there is the favor of the distinction" (*viśeṣānugrahaśca*), the utility even of duties belonging solely to one's caste, such as the recitation of prayers (*japa*), which were performed by them, is stated explicitly for the sake of knowledge.

This was stated with the intention that, in the sūtra *vihitatvāccāśramakarmāpi*, the term *āśramakarman* (duties of the stages of life) is also indicative of the duties of the castes (*varṇadharma*). Thus, even those duties distinct from the duties of the stages of life have utility for knowledge; however, this applies only to the obligatory (*nitya*) ones. For it is the fruit of these—the destruction of evil (*durita*)—that depends upon knowledge, whereas the fruit of optional (*kāmya*) rites, such as heaven and so forth, does not.

In this regard, just as when there is an extension (atideśa) of the auxiliary elements whose benefits are already established in the archetype (prakṛti), no benefit other than the archetypal one is postulated; likewise, for sacrifices and the like which are enjoined for the sake of knowledge, no benefit common to both obligatory and optional rites—beyond the destruction of sin, which is the established fruit of their obligatory performance—is to be postulated.

In the *Saṃkṣepaśarīraka*, however, the application of both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites is stated, because there is no distinction in the use of terms such as "sacrifice" (*yajña*) and so forth. The connection of constituent elements (*padārtha*)—which have their utility established in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—with the modified forms (*vikṛti*) occurs precisely through the extension (*atideśa*) of that established archetypal utility; it is not the case that utility is postulated after the extension of the constituent elements. Thus, there is no possibility of postulating a utility in those cases that exceeds the archetypal utility.

But here, in the case of sacrifices and other rites that are enjoined and taught from the very beginning by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), how could an auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*) not be postulated—despite being established for the sake of fulfilling the injunction understood first—which is common to all obligatory and optional rites alike, even though it is conveyed by a general term? For even among the ritualists (*adhvara-mīmāṃsaka*), it is held that "the restriction to a specific postulated benefit applies only when there is a connection of constituent elements (*padārtha*) by way of an auxiliary benefit."

Having reached the consensus that "after the syntactical connection of the constituent parts (*padārtha*) has been established, when a benefit (*upakāra*) is postulated, one must postulate a benefit that, even if not previously established, is indeed consistent with the constituent parts already enjoined," the first section of the tenth book (*daśamādhyāya*) establishes the application of archetypal elements (*prākṛtānvaya*) in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) by way of such a benefit, for the purpose of successfully initiating the definition of sublation (*bādha*).

Furthermore, if one accepts the position that "this application (viniyoga) pertains only to the obligatory rites because of the non-availability of [other] established auxiliaries," then this application is redundant, provided that the destruction of evil (duritakṣaya) resulting from the obligatory rites, and the arising of knowledge from that [destruction], are established through other means. If they are not so established by other means, then the capacity to produce the auxiliaries required for knowledge would not have been previously established for those [obligatory rites]; thus, since there is no distinction, the application common to both the obligatory and the optional would be unavoidable.

Now, even if it is established from other sources that obligatory rites (*nitya*) have as their sole purpose the destruction of evil, it is not yet established that they specifically remove the evil that obstructs the arising of knowledge; rather, when this application (*viniyoga*) exists, for one who performs the obligatory rites with the aim of knowledge, knowledge necessarily arises.

If it is argued that otherwise there would be mere purification and not the certain production of knowledge—thus this application (viniyoga) is meaningful—then even for obligatory rites (*nitya*), the destruction of evil that obstructs the production of knowledge would have to be assumed as something not previously established. Furthermore, an unseen potency (*apūrva*) must be postulated as the means, which brings about the acquisition of a qualified teacher and the performance of hearing, reflection, and so forth, which are the means to knowledge. Since there is no difference in the assumption of an unestablished benefit, the application common to both obligatory and optional rites, which is derived from the general scriptural injunction, should not be set aside.
[Objection: Even so, how can one explain [the statement]: "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone"?

How, then, is the consistency of such traditional texts (*smṛti*) maintained? Nor can it be said that those [karmas] are intended solely for the performance of rites for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārtha-karman*). For, by the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" in the passage concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*), it is understood that only Brāhmaṇas have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for rites performed for the sake of knowledge. Therefore, one must state that the karmas performed by Janaka and others contribute directly to liberation itself. Not so. The mention of "Brāhmaṇas" in the *vividiṣā-vākya* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all three twice-born classes (*traivarṇika*).
As the venerable Vārttikakāras have stated: "And here, the mention of 'Brāhmaṇas' is an elliptical indication of the twice-born."
"Because the qualification [for knowledge] is not distinct for all, [the teaching of the Self applies] to everyone's awakening to the Self. Thus [it is said].

For it is not tenable that, when the injunction regarding the qualification of one who desires knowledge is modified to "one desiring knowledge should perform sacrifices and so forth," the word "brāhmaṇa" can serve to specify the qualified person; this is because a qualification cannot be attached to that which is the subject of the injunction (the *uddeśya*).

Nor is it appropriate to argue that—just as in the injunction for the Rājasūya sacrifice, "A king desiring self-sovereignty (svārājya) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," where the king, though prescribed as a qualifier of the sacrifice by way of being its agent in the sense that "one desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with a Rājasūya performed by a king," is included within the category of those entitled to perform it (*adhikārin*) because a Rājasūya performed by one who is not a king cannot be accomplished; so too here, the Brāhmaṇa, prescribed as the agent of the sacrifice and other rites, is included within the category of those entitled to perform them by implication. [This is because the case is not analogous. In the Rājasūya context, the king is indeed prescribed as a qualifier of the sacrifice through his status as the agent, and since the sacrifice cannot be realized by a non-king, he is logically included among the eligible performers. However, in the present case, the Brāhmaṇa is not prescribed as a qualifier of the sacrifice itself, but merely as its agent. Furthermore, unlike the Rājasūya, there is no inherent impossibility for a non-Brāhmaṇa to perform sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma; therefore, the inclusion of the Brāhmaṇa in the class of eligible performers based on this prescription of agency is not tenable.

In the sūtra, "In every way, they [are the same] because of the dual indicative marks," it was established that in the *vividiṣā* passage, there is an injunction regarding the connection with a specific result for sacrifices and other rites already prescribed elsewhere, and not an injunction for new sacrifices and so forth. Consequently, since both an injunction of a quality in the form of the agent and an injunction of the connection with a result would have to be made in a single sentence by way of restating the sacrifices already established, this would result in the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Nor is it tenable that, as in the case of the *rājasūya* injunction—where, even under the view that the king is not enjoined as the agent, the status of being a qualified agent is obtained merely through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "king"—here, for the sake of avoiding a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the qualification of the Brāhmaṇa as the agent would be established merely through the co-occurrence with the word "Brāhmaṇa," despite his not being enjoined as the agent, such that the injunction would terminate in his entitlement (*adhikāra*).

Otherwise, since sacrifices and other rites—already established as pertaining to the three castes (*traivarṇika*) elsewhere, and here also enjoined for the purpose of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) which likewise pertains to the three castes—it is impossible to restrict their eligibility merely on the basis of the co-occurrence with the word "Brāhmaṇa," which lacks any connection to an injunction regarding eligibility for that specific knowledge; therefore, it is appropriate that the word "Brāhmaṇa" serves as a mere indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those eligible for knowledge as they are already established. ||3||

If it be objected: "But if [the mention of the *kṣatriya*] is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for anyone qualified for knowledge (*vidyā*), then since a *śūdra* could also possess the desire for knowledge and so forth, it would follow that he too would be entitled to perform the rites for the sake of knowledge," we reply: no. For in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, the entitlement to Vedic matters is restricted to one who possesses the knowledge of the meaning of the *svādhyāya* acquired through formal study; thus, the entitlement of a *śūdra*—who is devoid of formal study, the hearing of Vedic texts, and so forth—to knowledge is denied.

Some maintain that because of the Smṛti text, "One should not impart wisdom to a Śūdra," and because there is no possibility of his attaining understanding even through the mere majesty of knowledge, it is impossible for him to have a desire for it; therefore, he has no qualification for knowledge.

Others, however, say that even for a Śūdra there is indeed eligibility for ritual action for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*). Although he lacks the capacity for the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*), the *agnihotra*, and so forth, he is nonetheless eligible for the muttering (*japa*) of the King of Mantras, the venerable five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara-mantrarāja*), and other such means of destroying sin; as well as for austerity (*tapas*), giving (*dāna*), and domestic sacrifices (*pākayajña*), because these are possible for him. This is because of scriptural texts using distinct case-endings for the factors of action, such as "by the recitation of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by giving" (*vedānuvacanena yajñena dānena*), and because the practice of mere muttering and giving for the sake of knowledge is permitted even for widowers and others, without requiring the combination of all [the aforementioned duties] beginning with the recitation of the Vedas. Furthermore, it is not impossible for a Śūdra to have a desire for knowledge.

"One should cause the four castes to hear [the scriptures], having placed the Brāhmaṇa at the forefront. Since this traditional rule (smṛti) records that all four castes possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to hear the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, it is possible for even a Śūdra—who has understood the greatness of knowledge through the *Purāṇas* and other sources—to have a desire for that same knowledge. Furthermore, the prohibition "One should not impart wisdom (*mati*) to a Śūdra" is intended to forbid the transmission of knowledge regarding rituals such as the *Agnihotra*, which are not applicable to his performance; it does not prohibit the acquisition of knowledge itself.

Otherwise, since there would be no means for him to understand even his own class-duties (*svavarṇadharma*), those scriptural statements that differentiate his duties—such as, "The Śūdra is the fourth caste, of a single birth; for him also [there are] truthfulness, absence of anger, purity, sipping water for the purpose of purification, and according to some, the washing of hands and feet, the performance of *śrāddha* rites, the maintenance of dependents, contentment with one's own wife, and service to the higher castes"—would incur the fault of being non-authoritative due to their non-implementation. Nor does this render the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the exclusion of Śūdras) devoid of subject matter. For its...

Because of such Smṛti texts as, "There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve the initiatory rite (saṃskāra)," which aim at prohibiting the eligibility of a Śūdra—who is devoid of the initiatory rite known as upanayana, a limb of knowledge—for the meditations on the qualified Brahman (saguṇa-vidyā) and for the hearing of the Vedāntas and other means for the knowledge of the unqualified Brahman (nirguṇa-vidyā); and because, even in the case of the knowledge of the unqualified Brahman, it is impossible to prohibit the desire for it induced by the inherent beauty of its object; and because, since that knowledge is not something to be enjoined, there is no possibility of eligibility beyond [the aforementioned requirements], making a prohibition of it untenable.

Nor should it be said that, even though the performance of rites for the sake of knowledge is possible for him despite the impossibility of hearing the Vedānta, the performance of those rites for his sake is useless because knowledge does not arise.

For even though he lacks the qualification for hearing the Vedānta, the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, in the concluding commentary on the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, has demonstrated the qualification for hearing the Purāṇas and other texts concerning the identity of Brahman and the Self—which serve as means to knowledge—by stating: "Since it is recorded in the Smṛti that all four castes are entitled to the study of Itihāsas and Purāṇas in the words 'One should cause the four castes to hear [them],' whereas there is no qualification for Śūdras regarding that which is preceded by the Veda, this is settled. Thus, his qualification for hearing the Purāṇas and so forth, which establish the oneness of Brahman and the Self, is clearly shown.

Since it will serve the purpose of liberation by means of producing a pure body of a deity suitable for the arising of knowledge—just as the performance of ritual action for the sake of qualified knowledge (*saguṇavidyā*) results in gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) for those of the three higher castes—it will likewise serve the purpose of generating knowledge by means of producing a body of one of the three castes fit for hearing the Vedānta; and because there is no contradiction in a Śūdra performing rituals for the sake of knowledge, it follows that in the *vividiṣā* passage, the word "Brāhmaṇa" refers simply to whoever is eligible for knowledge as established by other sources, and thus the eligibility of even a Śūdra for performing rituals for the sake of knowledge is indeed established. || 4 ||

Granted that actions may be useful for knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of purifying the mind; but by what means is renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) useful for it? Some say: since the evils (*durita*) that obstruct the arising of knowledge are infinite, some are removable by the performance of sacrifices and other rites, while others are removable by the unseen merit (*apūrva*) of renunciation. Thus, renunciation is also useful for that [knowledge] by way of mental purification through action. Accordingly, for householders and others who perform hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth during intervals in their ritual duties, the attainment of knowledge does not occur in that very life, but rather only after obtaining renunciation in another birth.

However, for those such as Janaka and others who, while remaining householders, possess knowledge, their acquisition of knowledge resulted from renunciation in a previous birth; therefore, there is not even the slightest suspicion of a deviation from the rule regarding renunciation being a prerequisite for knowledge.

Others, however, maintain that because renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is included within the group of four means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) as captured by the word "renounced" (*uparata*) in such scriptural passages as "peaceful, self-controlled, and renounced," and because the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "Injunction of another auxiliary" (*sahakāryantaravidhi*) establishes this: "For the renunciant who possesses that [qualification] and possesses knowledge, this third stage, silence (*mauna*), is enjoined in relation to childhood and scholarship; for in the scriptural passage beginning 'Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa [should practice] scholarship,' there is the qualification for renunciation prior to that in the words 'they lead the life of a mendicant'"; and because it is said:
"Only for one who has abandoned all activities and desires to flee from transmigratory existence..."

And because of the statement in the Vārttika, "Only those who desire to know [Brahman] have the qualification for the Upaniṣads," they say that the unseen potency (apūrva) of renunciation serves as a qualifying attribute for the person entitled to the hearing of the Vedāntas and other means of knowledge, and thus it is useful for [attaining] wisdom.

Others, however, maintain that because of the statement in the *Vivaraṇa*—"the fruit of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) by virtue of its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to hearing [the Vedas] and so forth"—its utility for knowledge lies in the performance of hearing and the rest through the state of having no other activity. For when a visible means is possible, it is improper to postulate an invisible one (*adṛṣṭa*). However, if for an intelligent and diligent person of the highest caliber, even while remaining in another stage of life (*āśrama*), hearing and the rest are accomplished during intervals between ritual duties, then the restrictive rule—that "hearing and the rest must be performed only by adopting the stage of renunciation among the four stages of life"—must be accepted as refuted. || 5 ||

Now, one might object: "In these two positions, how can Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas perform the practice of hearing the Vedānta and so forth? For renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) has Brāhmaṇas as its qualified practitioners, since the injunctions for renunciation—such as 'A Brāhmaṇa, out of detachment,' 'A Brāhmaṇa, having withdrawn from worldly life,' and 'A Brāhmaṇa should go forth into the forest'—specify the Brāhmaṇa. As it is stated in the Vārttika: 'The mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of identifying the specific qualified practitioner; the injunction for renunciation does not apply to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas because of the Śruti. If this is argued, [the response follows].

On this point, some maintain: "Alternatively, one may renounce even from the stage of studentship, or from the house, or from the forest"—according to such scriptural texts that make no distinction, a Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya may renounce from the home;
for all three castes, these four stages of life (āśramas) are prescribed.

Thus, because the status of being supported by Smṛti establishes the eligibility for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) even for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the mention of Brāhmaṇas in other Śrutis is intended as an indication (upalakṣaṇa) of all three classes. For this very reason, in the Vārtika as well, after stating the intention of the Bhāṣya with the verse beginning "of a specific eligible person," it says:
"Renunciation is heard of in the Śruti without distinction for the three [classes];
when the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of indication, then [it applies to all]."

Thus, by means of the immediately following verse, they establish that the eligibility for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is shown to belong to the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well, thereby supporting their accomplishment in the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that because the mention of the Brāhmaṇa occurs in numerous injunctions regarding the rite of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), and because—even though the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is absent in the cited Jābāla-śruti injunction for renunciation—the qualification of the Brāhmaṇa is established by other scriptural passages; furthermore, since there is a reference to the Brāhmaṇa in the statement, "In the state of renunciation, being without the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*), how can he be a Brāhmaṇa?", the qualification for renunciation belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone.

This is because, according to the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*), only that meaning of a Smṛti which is not contradicted by Śruti is to be accepted. As for the statement in the Vārttika regarding the eligibility of all for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), that refers specifically to the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*); it does not aim to establish universal eligibility for the renunciation of the sick or the seeker (*ātura-vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*), as that would contradict the intention of the Bhāṣya. For it is said: "If knowledge is attained, which cuts off the eligibility for all [ritual duties]..."
"How can a restriction of eligibility be forcibly imposed upon one who has risen [from worldly life]?

By this subsequent verse, the restriction of eligibility is refuted for the period of *jīvanmukti* following the dawn of the knowledge of Brahman; specifically, it refutes the restriction that only the *vidvat-saṃnyāsa* (renunciation by the knower) is required. Thus, while *saṃnyāsa* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the performance of hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth for Brāhmaṇas, for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, there is eligibility for hearing and so forth independent of that [renunciation]; this is how their performance of hearing and so forth is sustained. For if *saṃnyāsa* were required for hearing, it could not be restricted to hearing alone as being dependent on it.

They say that because one who has attained the state of a deity through the practice of meditation with attributes (saguṇopāsanā), which results in gradual liberation (kramamukti), must necessarily be declared to have no need for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) regarding hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; and because, since deities have no engagement in the performance of ritual acts (karmānuṣṭhāna), renunciation—which consists of the abandonment of such acts—is impossible for them.

Others, however, maintain that for one whose "establishment in Brahman"—meaning completion within Brahman—is declared by the scripture, "He who is established in Brahman attains immortality," and who possesses that steadfastness characterized by the absence of any other activity, there is primary eligibility for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. For it is said: "Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, he whose mind is not intent upon inquiry is called dead."

"Until sleep or until death, one should pass the time in reflection upon Vedānta"—because such Smṛti texts enjoin inquiry at all times; and that stability in Brahman is not possible for one remaining in another stage of life (āśrama) without renunciation (saṃnyāsa), due to the distraction caused by the performance of duties prescribed for one's own stage of life. Therefore, for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who lacks renunciation, there is no primary eligibility for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth.

However, according to the principle stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the section beginning with "But even for those in the intermediate state, because that is seen" (*antarācāpi tu tad-dṛṣṭeḥ*), which holds that "knowledge has a visible purpose and qualifies one who desires it for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth even by the mere absence of prohibition," there is permission for hearing and so forth for those two [classes]—who, like Śūdras, are not prohibited—by virtue of a merely secondary qualification that brings about the attainment of knowledge in another body, as is the case with widowers and others.

Indeed, it cannot be said that in the section beginning with "But even for those between [the stages], because that is seen," the eligibility of widowers and others for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth is accepted as primary; for the author of the Sūtras himself clarified their secondary eligibility in the sūtra: "Therefore, the other is superior, and because of the indicative marks. Nor should it be suspected that in that context his intention was merely to state that they lack eligibility for hearing and so forth, rather than stating that their specific duties serve to assist their knowledge (*vidyā*).

This is because it would contradict the commentary on that very section which states, "And knowledge has a perceptible purpose. Nor can it be argued that because Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas lack the qualification for renunciation (saṃnyāsa), their qualification is secondary; for by that same logic, the gods' qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth would also have to be merely secondary.

And thus, it must be stated that one who attains a divine body through saguṇa-vidyā—which has gradual liberation as its fruit—and performs hearing [of the scriptures] and other practices, must obtain a subsequent birth as a Brāhmaṇa suitable for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) in order to attain [final] knowledge; only then can there be no contradiction with such scriptural passages and sūtras as "He reaches the world of Brahman," "And he does not return," and "Non-return, on account of the word. This is what must be asserted.

They say that because the gods lack the distraction of duties to be performed, it is possible for them to possess a state of non-engagement in other activities by their very nature; thus, based on the authority of the scriptures which teach saguṇa-vidyā (meditation with attributes) as having the fruit of gradual liberation, they accept that the gods have a primary qualification [for such meditation] even without renunciation (saṃnyāsa). || 6 ||

Now, one might object: how can the inquiry into the Vedānta, performed by a non-primary qualified person for the sake of understanding the meaning of the sentences—which constitutes a visible result—be of use in attaining knowledge in another birth? Indeed, it is not even logical that an inquiry today could be the cause of understanding the subject of inquiry on another day, let alone its being the cause thereof in another birth. Nor should it be argued that even for a wandering ascetic (parivrājaka), who is a primary qualified person, the hearing (*śravaṇa*) performed is solely for a visible purpose, because the resulting comprehension is itself a visible result.

Just as in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Even that which belongs to this life [occurs] when there is no obstruction of what is not currently underway, for that is seen," it has been determined that karma which has begun but does not produce its fruit in this birth will produce its fruit in another birth once the obstacle is removed, so too would it be for that performed by one who lacks primary qualification. For since hearing [the scriptures] devoid of scriptural auxiliaries does not produce the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), how can its utility for knowledge in another birth be established?

For if one were to accept that the operation of a means of knowledge belonging to a previous birth causes comprehension in a subsequent birth without the mediation of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the pot [as a substrate], it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). It is replied: even by one who is not a primary qualified candidate, but who has generated the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), the hearing (*śravaṇa*) performed is impelled by the *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by the performance of sacrifices and other rites for the sake of prior knowledge, which serve as the door to generating that very desire for knowledge. Thus, that same *apūrva*, while functioning until the fruit in the form of knowledge is attained, effects the utility of the hearing performed by oneself even for knowledge in a subsequent birth; therefore, there is no inconsistency.

However, in the view that there is no injunction regarding hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, even for one who has performed hearing preceded by renunciation, since no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is produced, it must be explained in this very way that, when an obstacle exists, that hearing serves as the cause for knowledge in another birth.

The teachers, however, maintain that even under the view that it is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), this same resolution holds: because for one who practices hearing (*śravaṇa*), the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from that restriction generally does not arise prior to the attainment of the fruit; for that [unseen merit] is to be accomplished by the performance of hearing characterized by repetition until the fruit is reached. Indeed, the restriction of hearing which generates the unseen merit of the restriction is not completed merely by the commencement of the hearing that is to be repeated until the fruit is attained.

They say that because the rule (niyama) regarding hearing—even though its result is not seen—would be possible to arise even before the end of the result is heard, [hearing] must be accompanied by repetition just like threshing (*avaghāta*). Since hearing, as qualified by repetition, is the means to the result, a statement intended to establish that rule prior to the completion of the constituent element (*padārtha*) which is the means to the result would be without a basis (*nirālambana*). Furthermore, if the rule were completed merely by the commencement of hearing or threshing, then the performance of the rule-injunction would be accomplished at that very point;
consequently, it would follow that there would be no deficiency even if one did not repeat it. Thus they argue.
However, some [hold] that the hearing of the Vedānta has a perceptible result, as it is said: "Day by day, from hearing the Vedānta with devotion,
obtained through service to the Guru, one obtains the fruit of eighty kṛcchra penances."

On account of the authority of such scriptural statements as these, there exists also the production of an independent unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Just as the act of *ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires), though intended for the consecration of the fire, is also for the sake of the person because it is enumerated among the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the person, so too, by the force of the scriptural statement, its dual purpose is established. And thus they say that the utility of the means—listening, reflection, and so forth—for the knowledge pertaining to the hereafter arises solely through the power of the unseen merit produced by daily listening. ||7||

Thus, while this universally accepted principle—that the attainment of knowledge occurs through the systematic practice of means such as hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana)—stands firm, Bhāratītīrtha, in his *Dhyānadīpa*, states that there is yet another means for the attainment of knowledge.

"That cause is attained through Sāṅkhya and Yoga," for it is seen in the Śruti and Smṛti that "the state which is reached by the followers of Sāṅkhya is also reached by the followers of Yoga. Just as what is called Sāṅkhya—namely, inquiry into Vedānta denoted by the term *śravaṇa* (listening), accompanied by *manana* (reflection) and so forth—is a means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā*), so too is what is called Yoga—the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*). Nor should it be doubted that there is no such thing as meditation upon the attributeless [Brahman].

In the *Praśnopaniṣad*, within the inquiry of Śaibya, it is stated: "But he who meditates upon that supreme Puruṣa by means of the three-measured *Oṃkāra*. Since this teaches the very meditation upon the attributeless (nirguṇa) [Brahman], immediately following that, in the statement regarding the fruit of meditation—"He beholds the Puruṣa dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond this mass of living beings"—that which is designated as the object of the act of beholding (*īkṣati-karman*) is the very same attributeless Brahman that is the object of the act of meditating (*dhyāyati-karman*) in the meditation-injunction; it is nothing else.

This is because the meaning of the principle—"due to the rule that *īkṣati* (contemplation) and *dhyāna* (meditation), which stand in the relation of cause and effect, must have the same object"—has been accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya and others in the section concerning the object of *īkṣā* (*Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*); furthermore, it has been elaborated elsewhere in other Upaniṣadic texts such as the Tāpanīya and Kaṭhavallī.

Furthermore, in the *Sūtrakṛt* (Brahmasūtra), within the section on the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*) which was commenced for the purpose of defining the attributes of the object of meditation, the inclusion of both positive qualities such as knowledge and bliss and negative qualities such as non-materiality (*asthūlatva*) has been demonstrated. This is evident from the sūtra, "Bliss and the rest [belong] to the Principal" (*ānandādayaḥ pradhānasya*), which shows the inclusion of positive qualities like knowledge and bliss, and from the sūtra, "But there is a restriction of the cognitions of the Imperishable," etc. (*akṣaradhiyāṃ tvavarodhaḥ*), which shows the inclusion of negative qualities. If it be objected that, in the case of including qualities such as bliss, the object of meditation would no longer be devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), we say: no.

Because meditation is possible without subverting its qualitylessness by means of [the attributes] such as bliss and non-materiality (*asthūlatva*), characterized by [negations] such as "I am Brahman, which is the undivided single essence. If it is argued that the supreme Brahman is not to be meditated upon because of the scriptural text, "Know that alone to be Brahman, not this which they worship here," then [we reply] that by the scriptural text, "That is indeed other than the known," even its status as an object of knowledge would result in being unestablished.

If, because Brahman is well-known in other Vedic texts as being known, the scriptural statement regarding its unknowability is intended to mean its actual unknowability, then let the scriptural statement regarding its not being an object of worship also be intended to mean its actual non-worshipability, since it is well-known in the Atharva-veda and elsewhere that it is to be worshipped.

And thus, for those who—due to dullness of intellect regarding the hearing [of the truth] expressed in the words, "He who is not obtained even for hearing by many," or due to the non-availability of a qualified guru skilled in the exposition of logic—cannot engage in hearing and so forth, and who have attained a superficial understanding of the identity of Brahman and the Self through the Vedāntas studied during their formal education; for them, even without an inquiry [into the Upaniṣads], there exists [instruction] in the Ārṣa texts such as the Praśnopaniṣad and others, in the Brāhma- and Vāsiṣṭha-kalpas, and in the Pañcīkaraṇa and similar works, wherein all matters scattered across numerous recensions are collected together.

Having ascertained from gurus who know the tradition alone the method of practice for the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman—determined in the Kalpasūtras like that of the Agnihotra and other rites—one attains, through its performance, the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of the attributeless Brahman which is the object of meditation, gradually. This is because, according to the logic of non-contradictory error, even meditation may, in some cases, culminate in valid knowledge at the time of its fruition.

Just as when someone, having concealed five cowrie shells in their hand, is asked, "How many cowrie shells are in your hand?", the speaker of the reply, "Five cowrie shells," possesses a knowledge of that specific number which—though lacking a foundational means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and being of the nature of a mental imposition (*āhāryāropa*)—is nonetheless true; so too is the meditation on the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahmopāsana*), which, though performed by relying solely on the scriptures of meditation like those concerning the "small [space]" (*dahara*) and so forth, is independent of any definitive foundational means of valid cognition that would investigate the actual reality of the object.

In reality, because it is consistent with the facts, the direct realization of its own object produced by the meditation on the *nirguṇa* [Brahman]—just like the meditation on *tadādi*—must necessarily have as its object the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*), exactly like the realization produced through the channel of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.

However, there is this distinction: for a person free from obstacles, the direct realization of Brahman is accomplished quickly through the channel of hearing and so forth; thus, the path of Sāṅkhya is the primary method (*mukhya kalpa*), whereas the path of Yoga, which proceeds via meditation, is the secondary method (*anukalpa*). || 8 ||

Now, in both of these two views, what is the instrument for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman? Some say it is *prasaṅkhyāna* itself, which consists of the repeated practice of mental impressions (*pratyaya*). This is because such [practice] exists in the path of Yoga from the very beginning in the form of meditation (*upāsanā*), and in the path of Sāṅkhya in the form of contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) following reflection (*manana*). Nor is there a lack of evidence for its being the cause of the direct realization of Brahman; for it is heard in scripture: "But then, meditating upon Him, he sees Him who is partless" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.1.8). Furthermore, the causality of *prasaṅkhyāna* is established in the case of a person afflicted by desire having a direct realization of a beloved woman who is spatially remote.

This is because, in the section beginning with "Until departure, for that too is seen," and in the section beginning with "An option [exists], because the fruit is not distinguished," it is accepted that those who meditate on the "I-grasp" (ahaṃgraha) of the small ether (dahara) and other such objects attain direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of the qualified Brahman through contemplation (prasaṅkhyāna). Now, an objection may be raised: since contemplation (prasaṅkhyāna) is not included among the enumerated means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), the direct realization of Brahman arising from it would not be a valid cognition (pramā).

Nor can its status as valid knowledge (*pramātva*) be established through the non-sublation of its object—like the illusory cognition of a specific number of cowrie shells that coincidentally matches the truth—because that which is not rooted in a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) cannot be valid knowledge. Furthermore, since a mental operation (*vṛtti*) produced by volition (*āhārya*) is, like the operation of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), a mental activity distinct from [ordinary] cognition, it is not accepted as valid knowledge even when its object is unsublated, just like desire and other such states. This is not so. For even though it is not rooted in the well-known instruments of valid knowledge, its status as valid knowledge is possible—just like the mental operation of the Lord’s *māyā*—due to the equality of the non-sublation of its object.

In both paths, since the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self is rooted either in the Vedānta texts that have been deliberated upon or those not so deliberated, and because the direct intuition of Brahman produced by *prasaṅkhyāna* is itself rooted in a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not erroneous. As stated by the authors of the *Kalpataru*: "The immediate cognition born from the cultivation of the knowledge arising from Vedāntic sentences does not incur the status of error, owing to the firmness of its foundational source."

"And there is no contingency of falling into the position that validity is extrinsic (*paratastva*), because [the scripture] follows the purity of the source in order to eliminate exceptions. Others, however, maintain that based on such scriptural passages as "This subtle Self is to be known by the mind" and "But it is seen by a sharp intellect," the mind alone is the instrument for the direct realization of Brahman. This is because the mind is established as the instrument for the valid cognition (*pramā*) consisting of the mental modification (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*) regarding the Self when associated with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is also demonstrated by texts in the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa* such as: "of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the means of knowledge for the cognizer and so forth, contrary to the world-appearance of a dream."

Furthermore, since the mind is acknowledged as the instrument even in the direct realization of Brahman during dreamless sleep—as stated in the Śruti: "He thinks, 'I am indeed all this, I am everything'—this is his supreme world"—and because at that time no other instrument exists, *prasaṅkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) is nevertheless useful by way of being an auxiliary to the mind.

This is because of the statement in the *Bhāmatī*: "The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), accompanied by the ripening of the cultivation of the meaning of the sentence, manifests the nature of the referent of the word *tat* (the Absolute) for the immediate referent of the word *tvam* (the individual self), by negating the forms of its respective limiting adjuncts. Furthermore, in the Śruti passage: "But with the clarity of knowledge, one whose being is purified sees Him, the partless, through meditation," meditation is prescribed specifically as a cause for the one-pointedness of the mind—which is designated by the term "clarity of knowledge"—and not as an independent instrument (*karaṇa*) in itself.

They say that because no instrument of knowledge (jñānakaraṇa) has ever been postulated for it [prasaṃkhyāna], and because even in cases such as the direct perception of a beloved woman by one afflicted with passion, it is possible for the mind alone—assisted by prasaṃkhyāna—to function as the instrument, it is improper to postulate another, unestablished instrument of knowledge.

Others, however, maintain that it is the great Upaniṣadic sentence alone [that brings about realization], because in such scriptural passages as "He understood it from him," "The teacher leads him to the further shore of darkness," "The man who has a teacher knows; for him there is delay only so long [as he is not released]," and so forth, we hear of the arising of the direct intuition of Brahman immediately after the teacher's instruction, which implies the attainment of liberation while living (jīvanmukti); because in the passage "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta," we hear of the absence of any further need for other forms of knowledge; and because in the passage "That person who is known through the Upaniṣads," we hear that Brahman is accessible solely through the Upaniṣads.
