The instrument for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman is not the mind (*manas*), because its status as the instrument for the direct realization of Brahman is denied in the passage: "That which one does not think with the mind. Nor is this [denial] restricted to an immature mind, because the supplementary statement, "That by which they say the mind is thought," refers to the mind alone. Furthermore, one should not suspect that, in this manner, the status of speech as an instrument for that [realization] is also denied by the passage: "That which is not expressed by speech."

Even for those who maintain that the mind (*manas*) is the instrument [of cognition], since it is admitted that sound (*śabda*) is the cause of indeterminate and mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), one must state that the purport of the scripture—“from which words turn back, not having reached it along with the mind”—is to deny that sound is the instrument [of that knowledge] by way of its power (*śakti*) consisting in the attainment of the word’s meaning. However, there is no contradiction in sound being the instrument of that [knowledge] by way of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), which consists in a relation to what is possible [to be expressed].

Nor should it be argued that the status of the mind as an instrument for that [perception], established by the scriptural text "It is to be seen by the mind alone," cannot be rejected; for even in the production of verbal direct realization (*śābdasākṣātkāra*), one-pointedness of the mind is required, and thus the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is justified on the basis of its being merely an instrumental cause. This is seen in such passages as "For with the mind one sees, with the mind one hears. They say that the statement by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) regarding the mind being an instrument in his *Gītā-bhāṣya* was made with reference to another philosophical view (*matāntara*). || 9 ||
If it be objected that even so, it is not consistent for a word—whose inherent nature is to produce indirect knowledge—to produce immediate knowledge;

to this some reply as follows: although the word is inherently incapable, it produces immediate knowledge when assisted by the mirror of the mind’s one-pointed concentration on Brahman, which is acquired through the accumulation of impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from the repeated practice of direct perception preceded by hearing and reflection upon the scriptures. This is postulated just as a sacrifice performed in a fire consecrated by scriptural impressions produces the *apūrva* (unseen potency). This is established by the authority of the scripture: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow."

They say that since the immediate superimposition of agency cannot be removed without the knowledge of its immediate substratum, and since no other means of knowledge applies to the Brahman taught in the Upaniṣads, liberation would be impossible if immediate knowledge did not arise even from the Word (śabda).

Others, however, support [the view] by following the analogy of experience, arguing that since it is observed that the mind—even when externally incapable—can produce the direct perception of a lost beloved when accompanied by the accumulation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is likewise logical that the Word (*śabda*) can produce immediate knowledge when accompanied by meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*).

Others, however, maintain that the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of cognition consists in its having an immediate object as its domain. This is because no other definition [of immediacy] can be provided. Furthermore, the immediacy of an object does not consist in its being the object of an immediate cognition—which would result in a circular dependency—but rather in its non-difference from the consciousness (*caitanya*) belonging to a particular person. This is because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its attributes, being superimposed upon the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), exist in non-difference from it.

Since there is no non-pervasion (avyāpti) anywhere—because jars and other objects imagined within the internal consciousness (antaḥcaitanya) possess that non-difference [from the Self] through the manifestation of their respective non-difference from the consciousness belonging to a particular person, which is effected by the mental mode (vṛtti) within external consciousness (bāhyacaitanya)—nor does it follow that merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), and latent impressions (saṃskāra) would become directly perceived (āparokṣya), just like knowledge and so forth; for although these too are equally imagined in the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), we maintain that direct perception belongs only to that insentient object which is manifested (udbhūta) and possesses non-difference from consciousness, whereas those [merit, etc. are unmanifested (anudbhūta).

And thus, because it is always non-different from the consciousness of all persons, Brahman is directly and immediately manifest by its very nature according to the scriptural text, "That Brahman which is immediate and direct. Therefore, they say that the expression "immediacy" is appropriate even for the verbal knowledge of Brahman, since its object is an immediately present reality.

The teachers of Advaita-vidyā, however, maintain that the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of knowledge does not consist in its having an immediate object as its domain. This is because such a definition would fail to encompass the self-luminous nature of the essential bliss (*svarūpa-sukha*), which is itself of the nature of immediate consciousness, and because it would preclude the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) characterized by being its own object. Rather, just as the immediacy of an object consists in its non-difference from the consciousness that is conducive to its own empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), so too the immediacy of knowledge consists in the non-difference of the consciousness conducive to its own empirical usage from that respective object.

And thus, immediacy (*aparokṣya*) is indeed a property of consciousness (*caitanya*) itself, and not a property of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) as is the case with inferentiality (*anumititva*) and the like. For this very reason, there is immediacy in the Witness (*sākṣin*), whose nature is the manifestation of pleasure and so forth, and in Consciousness, whose nature is the manifestation of the bliss of one's own essence (*svarūpasukha*). Nor is there any contradiction with experience regarding the modifications of the senses directed toward jars and other objects; for it is logically consistent that experience has as its object the immediacy residing in the consciousness delimited by such a modification.

If it is objected: "Has it not been stated that the immediacy (*āparokṣya*) of both cognition and its object—pertaining to verbal cognitions whose objects are the heart and so forth—is over-extended? For in those cases, when by chance there occurs a conjunction between the mental modification (*vṛtti*) and its object, the manifestation of the non-difference between the consciousness delimited by the modification and the consciousness delimited by the object is unavoidable. We reply: No.

Because a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that functions mediately (*parokṣavṛtti*) is incapable of removing the ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the object, there is no manifestation of the non-difference between the consciousness of the object—which is veiled by ignorance—and the witness-consciousness delimited by the modification, which is unveiled; consequently, immediacy (*āparokṣya*) does not arise. For this very reason, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is in reality identical with Brahman during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no such immediacy of Brahman for it, because the difference created by the veil of ignorance still exists. Nor does it follow from this that Brahman would become non-omniscient due to the impossibility of its being immediately perceived by the individual soul.

Because ignorance does not conceal the Lord, it does not bring about a difference between Him and the individual soul (jīva). For that ignorance which conceals a particular subject brings about a difference in its own substratum only with respect to that subject. Therefore, when Caitra’s ignorance regarding a jar is removed by his knowledge, Maitra’s unremoved ignorance brings about a difference in the consciousness of the object only with respect to Maitra; thus, there is no impossibility of Caitra’s experience of the direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of the jar.

If it is argued that, in this case, since immediacy—characterized by the manifestation of the non-difference between the consciousness of the object and the consciousness of the mental mode—is dependent upon the removal of the ignorance residing in the consciousness of its own object, it would be impossible for that [manifestation] to be the cause of the removal of ignorance; and thus, knowledge alone would be the remover of ignorance: we say no. This is because of the qualification: "Only that knowledge which, as it arises, arises already in contact with its object through the power of its own causes, is the remover of ignorance. This is because sensory cognitions possess such a character.

And thus, even though the knowledge of Brahman arises from the word, it arises as being already connected with its own object, Brahman, who is the material cause of all; therefore, its capacity to remove ignorance is fully established, and upon the removal of ignorance, its immediacy (aparokṣya) is also established through the dissolution of the distinctions rooted in that ignorance.

[Objection: But in that case, why should there not be immediate intuition (*aparokṣya*) through the knowledge of Vedānta produced even by the study [of the texts], since that would also remove the root ignorance? Nor should it be said that it does not remove ignorance because it lacks the nature of a certainty regarding its existence; for even so, since the ignorance would be removed by the doubt-free verbal knowledge of one who has completed the hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*) and the rest would become useless. [Reply: No.

They say that even when knowledge free from doubt has arisen from hearing, because it is obstructed by the defect of mental distraction (*cittavikṣepa*), ignorance is not removed; therefore, the performance of the injunctions for reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) is purposeful for the sake of dispelling that [ignorance]. Furthermore, they maintain that for one whose mental distraction has been eliminated through the practice of reflection and so forth in previous lives, the direct realization (*aparokṣya*) of Brahman is desired to arise from mere instruction (*upadeśamātra*). || 10 ||

Now, even for one who has thus performed *nididhyāsana*, why should the cessation of ignorance regarding Brahman not occur through the cognition of a jar and so forth, just as it does through the knowledge of Brahman produced by the Vedānta? Nor should it be argued that because such [cognition] does not have Brahman as its object, there is no cessation of ignorance regarding Brahman from it; for it is accepted that the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) in the form "the jar exists" (*ghaṭassan*) has as its object Brahman, which is of the nature of Being (*sadrūpa*).

Nor should it be argued that when the ignorance regarding that [pot] is removed by a mental modification (vṛtti) having the form of a pot, the consciousness delimited by it shines forth as "existent" solely through its own self-manifestation, and thus that [consciousness] does not have the pot-form modification as its object. For in the absence of such [self-manifestation], since knowledge of the pot would have as its object the consciousness delimited by it, and ignorance would likewise have as its object that same consciousness delimited by it, it would be impossible for that ignorance to be removed by a knowledge whose object is different; furthermore, because there is no function of veiling with respect to an insentient thing, the pot cannot be the object of ignorance.

Nor should it be argued that, although the function [of the internal organ] regarding a jar or the like has as its object the consciousness delimited by that [jar], the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) is not removed from it because it lacks the form of partless bliss (*akhaṇḍānanda*). For even in the case of the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) produced by the Vedānta, that [partless bliss] is absent; for in that [intuition], there exists no qualifier such as "partlessness" or "bliss," since that would entail the loss of the defining characteristic of the Vedāntas as having an "indivisible meaning" (*akhaṇḍārtha*), which consists in their producing a valid cognition whose object is a relation. Nor should it be argued that there is an invariable rule that the removal of that [ignorance] occurs only through the knowledge produced by the Vedānta.

For it is impossible to restrict [the removal of ignorance] in that manner, since the specific characteristic that serves as the cause for removing a postulated ignorance exists in other cognitions as well. Nor should it be argued that because the limited consciousness (avacchinna-caitanya) which is the object of a mental modification (vṛtti) such as that of a jar is itself illusory (kalpita), there is no established causal factor—namely, the sharing of the same object as the ignorance to be removed—for cognitions like those of jars; this is because they lack as their object that true, unlimited (anavacchinna) consciousness which is the object of the root-ignorance.

In that case, even if the limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) is imagined (*kalpita*), the limited aspect (*avacchedya*) consists of consciousness (*caitanya*) which is the object of the non-imagined root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). If that [limited consciousness] were also imagined, it would be insentient like a jar; consequently, it could not serve as the object even for the state-ignorance (*avasthājñāna*). Thus, one must admit that the state-ignorance has as its object that non-imagined consciousness which is the object of the root ignorance. Since the knowledge of a jar or similar objects, which removes that [state-ignorance], would necessarily have that same [non-imagined consciousness] as its object, the undesirable consequence remains unavoidable: that the root ignorance would be removed by such knowledge.
Regarding this, the teachers say: consciousness is not an object of the mental modifications (vṛtti) produced by the eyes and other senses.
As it is said: "Its form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees it with the eye.
The Self-existent One pierced the sense-apertures outward; therefore, one looks outward, not at the inner self."

This is because such scriptural passages teach that it (the Self) is unfit for perception by the eyes and other senses—just like atoms and the like—and because of the qualifying term "known through the Upaniṣads. Nor is it the case that [Brahman] is established as the form of Brahman cognizable by all means of knowledge.

This does not contradict the Vārttika and other such texts. For when a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of a jar or the like arises, the veil [of ignorance] is overcome; consequently, Brahman—which is self-luminous and of the nature of existence—becomes capable of being treated as "the jar exists" (*ghaṭaḥ san*), just like the jar itself. This is because those texts intend to show that [Brahman] is knowable through modifications such as "jar," in a figurative sense. Furthermore, the capacity of the cognition of a jar or the like to overcome the veil is established precisely by its having the jar or the like as its object.

Since even a jar and the like are objects of ignorance—as evidenced by the experience that the state of ignorance regarding a jar has as its object the jar itself, through such cognitions as "I do not know the jar," "by the knowledge of the jar, the ignorance of the jar [is removed]," and "the ignorance of the jar has perished"—it cannot be argued that the postulation of ignorance is unjustified there because it lacks the function of veiling; for the non-manifestation of that [jar] is established precisely by the veiling of the consciousness delimited by that very [jar], which is the illuminator of it.

Although, by the manner stated above, the direct status of the insentient (*jaḍa*) as the object of ignorance is rejected, there is nevertheless an obscuration of the light of consciousness delimited by the insentient by means of ignorance. Consequently, even though there is a connection with the light of eternal consciousness, the insentient is fit for such empirical usages as "it does not exist" or "it does not manifest. Thus, since the status of being an object of ignorance is accepted through this indirect succession, knowledge has as its object precisely that which is to be obscured by ignorance, whether directly or indirectly.

This is because [the definition] is included within the body of the causal factors that necessitate the removal of that ignorance. Nor does it follow that, by the aforementioned reasoning, objects such as jars would also be the objects of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), thereby leading to the undesirable consequence that the root-ignorance would be removed simply by the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a jar; for, on the strength of the observed result, what is essential for its removal is precisely the state of having as its object something other than the effects of that ignorance.

Alternatively, the insentient object is not the domain of primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) itself. However, for the various states of ignorance (*avasthājñāna*), which reside in the limited consciousness (*avacchinnacaitanya*), that very insentient object is their domain. Otherwise, when the consciousness of a piece of sandalwood is manifested by a visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*), its fragrance—which is in contact with it—would also necessarily become directly perceived (*aparokṣya*). Conversely, if that [consciousness] were not manifested, even the sandalwood and its color would fail to appear.

Nor should it be argued that the manifestation of both the sandalwood and its color occurs through the visual modification (cākṣuṣavṛtti) by means of the manifestation of the consciousness delimited by them, while the non-manifestation of the fragrance occurs because the consciousness delimited by the fragrance is not manifested due to the absence of a modification in the form of fragrance; for since consciousness cannot undergo a doubling of modifications, it is impossible for the qualities of a single substance—which exist pervading their entire substratum—to serve as distinct delimiters of consciousness, just as they cannot serve as distinct delimiters of space.

For those [objects], since they are manifested by the very consciousness delimited by their own substrate-substance—just as nacre-silver is manifested by the consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect of the nacre—it would follow that if that [consciousness] were manifested, the fragrance too would be manifested, and if it were not manifested, even the silver and so forth would not be manifested.

Nor is there a rule that odor manifests only when consciousness is colored by a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of that odor; for the meaning of the word "manifesting" is simply the contact with light (prakāśa), and thus it is contradictory to imagine non-manifestation when the contact with unobstructed light exists, even in the absence of a modification in that form. Furthermore, it is impossible to say that the consciousness which is the material cause of the manifested odor lacks contact with that odor.

Therefore, just as in the case of Caitra’s cognition of a jar, there is the cessation of only that ignorance which veils it, and thus only for him is there the manifestation of the object, not for anyone else; so too, through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of this or that particular object, there is the cessation of only the ignorance veiling that specific object, and not the immediate perception (*aparokṣya*) of another object, because it is accepted that "immediate perception belongs only to an object that is unobscured, due to its non-difference from consciousness."

Since it must be stated that even within a single consciousness, there are distinctions among the states of ignorance (avasthā-ajñāna) corresponding to the distinctions among objects—just as there are distinctions based on the differences among cognizers—it follows that these states of ignorance have their respective inert objects as their domain. Consequently, there is no inconsistency in the fact that mental modifications (vṛtti) directed toward jars and other such objects do not remove the state of ignorance; nor does it follow that they would remove the root ignorance (mūlājñāna).

Even so, it does not follow that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "I," which has the individual self (*jīva*) as its object, must remove the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). This is because such a modification has as its object only the non-conscious (*acid*) aspect conjoined with the self-luminous consciousness (*cit*), and not consciousness itself. Furthermore, even in the case of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "That is I," there is no taking of consciousness as an object; rather, its object is merely the qualification by prior and subsequent times along with the qualification by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) within the self-luminous consciousness.

However, some maintain that since the cognitions of jars and other objects have as their object the consciousness delimited by those very [objects], there is no possibility of the removal of ignorance through such cognitions. They argue that, in accordance with the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding the meaning of the statement "the Vedānta is to be heard"—as stated in the *Vārttika*: "And when all means of knowledge would apply, [the scripture] says 'it is to be heard' because it is the locus of the fruits of all means of knowledge, desiring to introduce the Vedānta"—it is only the knowledge of Brahman produced by the Vedānta, conjoined with the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the restriction, which removes the ignorance of Brahman by obstructing it; thus, there is no contingency of removing ignorance through the cognition of a jar or similar objects.

Others, however, maintain that only the knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which has the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman as its object, is the remover of fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*); for fundamental ignorance has that very non-difference as its object. Thus, there is no contingency of its removal by the cognition of a jar or similar objects, which have only the nature of pure consciousness (*caitanya*) as their object. Nor should it be argued that since non-difference—being cognized by a means of valid knowledge that reveals reality—is not distinct from consciousness, duality would result [if it were], and therefore non-difference must be "pure consciousness alone," so that even the cognition of a jar would have non-difference as its object. This is because non-difference, being something to be known by a pramāṇa that reveals reality, would entail duality if it were distinct from consciousness. Therefore, it must be said that "non-difference is pure consciousness alone. Consequently, even the cognition of a jar has non-difference as its object.

For we do not state that "non-dual knowledge" is distinguished by its object; rather, its status as non-dual knowledge consists precisely in its having consciousness as its object through a specific internal relation (svarūpa-sambandha) that depends upon specific causes, such as the reflective awareness of the two substrates denoted by the words *tat* and *tvam*.

For just as, although there is no difference in the fact that [cognitions] have as their objects the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and their relation (*sambandha*), the nature of a "qualified cognition" (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)—which is distinguished from a "cognition grasping a collection" (*samūhālambana*)—consists precisely in its having those three as its object by virtue of a specific relation whose nature depends on specific causes such as the cognition of the qualifier; or just as the nature of "doubt" (*saṃśayatva*), which is distinguished from "volitional mental activity" (*āhāryavṛtti*) such as "one who possesses both pillar-ness and person-ness," consists in the lack of determination of a distinction regarding the object; so too, in the case of a jar and the like, regarding a cognition such as "this is that very jar."

The state of being a cognition of non-difference—distinguished from cognitions produced by the word "pot" alone—is simply the objectivity (viṣayatva) of the pot and so forth, characterized by a specific *svarūpa-sambandha* (essential relation). Since no separate non-difference can be established, we must accept that just as there are internal distinctions within *svarūpa-sambandha*, such as the specific *svarūpa-sambandha* consisting of the relation of locus and located between an absence or a similarity and its substratum or counter-correlate, or the relation of counter-correlate and sub-stratum between a counter-correlate and its correlate; likewise, in this case, there is a specific *svarūpa-sambandha* [between the pot and its non-difference].

They argue that since the relations of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and identity (*tādātmya*) would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*) even regarding objects, it is impossible to establish a specific object for those mental states (*vṛtti*) which possess an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) with objects in the form of the subject-object relationship; furthermore, because the mutual distinction between them—such as being a cognition of non-difference—is maintained by postulating internal sub-varieties within the already established essential relation itself. Thus, they maintain that there is no loss of the "indivisible meaning" (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) of the Vedāntas, because the knowledge of Brahman is not admitted to have as its object some relation called "non-difference."

[Objection: But surely, just like the cognition of a jar or the like, the cognition of Brahman also cannot be what removes the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), because removal depends upon a contradiction consisting in the inability of the two to coexist; and there is no such contradiction between an effect and its material cause. [Reply: This is not so.

Even though such a contradiction is not observed elsewhere between cause and effect, here there exists a contradiction induced by the cognition or non-cognition of a single object; furthermore, such a contradiction is indeed seen even between cause and effect, as in the case of fire-contact and cloth. Nor should it be argued that the destruction of the cloth results solely from the destruction of the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) through the process of the disjunction of parts initiated by fire-contact, rather than from the fire-contact itself.

Even in the case of a burnt cloth, since the persistence of its previous configuration is observed, and because no separation of parts is seen—as is the case with a jar pulverized by a mallet—the postulation of a separation of parts therein lacks any basis in valid cognition. Nor is it correct to maintain that the destruction of the cloth occurs there due to the destruction of its inherent cause (the threads) through their burning; for since the cloth is observed to burn simultaneously with the yarns and other constituent parts, it is impossible to postulate a sequential process.
This is because the destruction of the parts does not occur prior [to the whole], as the destruction of the part must be said to result from the contact of fire with that very part. ||11||

Now, it may be granted that this is so; nevertheless, one might ask: how can this knowledge of Brahman, which destroys ignorance along with its manifestations (*savilāsājñāna*), itself be destroyed, given the absence of any other destroyer?

To this, some reply: just as the powder of the clearing-nut (*kataka*) combines with water and, while producing the separation of previously combined impurities, also produces its own separation [from the water], so too the knowledge of Brahman, when superimposed upon the Self, removes the entire previously superimposed phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and also removes itself.
Others, however, citing the analogy of molten iron quenched in water, maintain that when one thing has been negated, the negating cognition itself also ceases.

Others, however, offer here the example of the burning of a heap of straw. Nor is there a rule that destruction must be produced by something distinct from its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), for such a rule lacks a logical warrant (*aprayojakatva*). Furthermore, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the destruction of a fire that has run out of fuel. It should not be argued that, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), one must necessarily posit another cause for destruction if it were produced by the counter-positive alone—claiming that even in the destruction of a fuel-less fire, other causes such as time, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), or the will of God exist; for this fails to address the nature of the over-extension.

Nor does it follow as an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that the destruction of a jar or similar objects must also be independent of other causes; for we do not assert that all destructions in general are independent of other causes. Nor can the example of the destruction of a jar be used to prove that the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman depends on another cause; for by that same example, one could equally prove that it depends on the falling of a mallet. Furthermore, there is no over-extension in claiming that because of the commonality of being a "destruction of knowledge," the destruction of the knowledge of a jar and so forth must also be independent of other causes.

Just as the destruction of a fire with fuel depends on visible causes such as sprinkling water, whereas the destruction of a fire without fuel does not depend on them; and just as the destruction of waking cognition depends on another specific counteracting quality, whereas the destruction of the cognition preceding deep sleep does not depend on it, so too it is logically consistent that the destruction of the cognition which brings about [the state of liberation] does not depend on such a cause.

Nor is it independent of other causes, because it is admitted that in the very moment following its own production, those [causes] themselves—by burning away the entire phenomenal world superimposed upon Brahman—burn away that [knowledge] as well, which is included therein. Furthermore, there is no contradiction even if the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman is produced by other causes such as time, destiny, or the will of the Lord, according to the maxim of the extinction of a fire without fuel.

This is because it is not accepted that the cessation of the knowledge of Brahman—which remains as the sole survivor immediately after the cessation of all conceptual proliferation—occurs simultaneously with the burning away of everything; for at that preceding moment, other factors still exist, such as time (which consists of the relationship between consciousness and ignorance, or which takes the form of a distinct substance), the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) consisting of a particular quality of the internal organ in the form of the Lord’s grace, and others.

Nor should it be argued that if [the destruction of ignorance] were to depend on a cause other than the knowledge of that [object], it would follow that the knowledge of Brahman is not false; for it is accepted that falsity consists in being removable by knowledge alone. This is because the meaning [of falsity] is "being removable by knowledge while not being removable by a causal complex that does not include knowledge. Furthermore, the purport of the scriptural text "There is no other path" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8) is precisely this. Therefore, the analogy of the fire burning the fuel that has already been consumed is indeed appropriate.

However, some maintain that knowledge of Brahman in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) does not destroy ignorance or the phenomenal world rooted therein. This is because ignorance, by the rule of being removable only by light, cannot be removed by a modification that is insentient in nature. Rather, it is the light of consciousness reflected in that modification which is its remover. Although consciousness in its own nature, as the witness of ignorance and the rest, is not a remover of them, it is logical that it becomes a remover when mounted upon a modification of the nature of the undifferentiated whole (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*). As it is said: "This solar radiance, though merely illuminating grass and the like, may burn the grass by ascending the sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*); one should apply that same principle here."

Thus, as stated by the learned: "Just as fire, having ascended a certain piece of wood while burning a village, a city, or the like, burns that very wood as well; so too, the light of non-dual consciousness (akhaṇḍacaitanya), having ascended the final mental modification (caramavṛtti) while uprooting the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), is capable of its own cessation as well. Therefore, they say there is no inconsistency whatsoever in its destruction.

Others, however, maintain that the knowledge of Brahman is the remover of ignorance alone, because knowledge and ignorance are directly opposed to one another. As for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), its destruction occurs through the destruction of its material cause; thus, even the knowledge of Brahman, being included within the phenomenal world, is destroyed for that very reason. Nor does it follow that the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the phenomenal world is untenable if it is not removable by knowledge; for although the cessation of the phenomenal world is not produced by knowledge directly, it is nevertheless produced by the destruction of ignorance, which is itself produced by knowledge.

This is because it is accepted that "falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being removable by knowledge alone, whether through direct perception or through traditional instruction. And thus, even upon the arising of the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*), the appearance of the body and so forth for one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is logically established. For, despite the arising of the direct realization of reality, there is the persistence of the appearance of the body and its effects—which are the results of *prārabdha* karma—due to the obstruction posed by that *prārabdha* karma; and consequently, the persistence of a trace of the ignorance that serves as the material cause (*upādāna-avidyā-leśa*) is logically justified.

They say that if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), like ignorance (*ajñāna*), were to be directly sublated by the direct realization of Brahman, this [state of residual impressions] would not be possible; for when the opposing direct realization of Brahman exists, it is impossible for *prārabdha*-karma to persist on its own, and thus it cannot serve as an obstacle to the cessation of the remnants of ignorance.
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, what is this "residue of ignorance" (*avidyā-leśa*) by whose persistence there is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*)?

Some say it is that portion of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) belonging to root ignorance—which possesses both the powers of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection—that causes the persistence of the body and so forth during the period of *prārabdha* karma.
Others say that the formative force of ignorance is like the lingering odor of garlic in a vessel even after the garlic has been washed away.
Others maintain that it is simply the root ignorance (mūlāvidyā) that persists according to the analogy of a burnt cloth.

Some maintain the following position: since it is impossible for even a trace of ignorance to persist once the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) that contradicts the reality of the omniscient Self has arisen, the scriptures on "liberation while living" (jīvanmukti) are merely explanatory praises (arthavāda) for the injunctions regarding hearing [the Vedanta] and so forth; for there is no purpose for the scripture in establishing liberation while living. Therefore, they say that for one who has performed nididhyāsana, the cessation of ignorance along with its manifestations and latent impressions occurs simply through the arising of the direct realization of Brahman. ||1||
Now, what is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
The followers of Brahmadatta maintain that it is the Self (*ātman*) itself.

Nor is knowledge useless because the Self is eternally established; for if knowledge were absent, the Self would remain in a state of misfortune due to the presence of ignorance, which is the cause of misfortune, and therefore one seeks that [knowledge]. Furthermore, in accordance with the definition—"that whose existence follows immediately upon the existence of something else, and whose absence follows upon its absence, is produced by that"—even the cessation of ignorance, though consisting of the nature of the Self, is produced by knowledge.

When knowledge exists, there is the existence of the cessation of ignorance in the form of the self in the subsequent moment; whereas in its absence, there is the non-existence of that [cessation] in the form of ignorance, which is its counter-correlate, because it possesses the aforementioned definition of existence.

The cessation of ignorance is indeed distinct from the Self. It is not existent (*sat*), for that would entail the loss of non-duality (*advaita*). Nor is it non-existent (*asat*), because that which is non-existent cannot be accomplished by knowledge (*jñāna*). Nor is it of the nature of both existent and non-existent (*sadasad-rūpa*), due to contradiction. Nor is it indeterminable (*anirvācya*); for since it is a rule that whatever is indeterminable and has a beginning must have ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*), it would follow that even in liberation (*mukti*), ignorance—the material cause—would persist, and it would further follow that it could be sublated by knowledge. However, the teacher Ānandabodha maintains that it transcends these four aforementioned modes and is of a fifth kind.

The cessation of ignorance, like ignorance itself, is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). Nor does it follow that there would be no liberation because, as long as that [effect] persists, its material cause—ignorance—must necessarily persist; for there is no evidence for such persistence. Just as origination is a modification of being (*bhāva-vikāra*) that pertains only to the very first moment, so too cessation is logically established as a modification of being that pertains only to the final moment.

For this very reason, although cessation is conventionally designated as "will cease" or "has ceased" by means of its future or past states respectively before and after [the present moment], the designation of the present tense—such as "ceases," "perishes," or "is destroyed"—occurs only at the final moment of the cessation. If, however, cessation were to persist [throughout time], then even for a jar that has long since been shattered, there would be such usage as "it ceases now," because verbal suffixes denote meanings such as the presentness inherent in the meaning of the verbal root.

But [one might object]: let it be that those [suffixes] express meanings such as the present tense residing in the agent or object, which are the referents of the base (*prakṛti*) and the number inherent in what is expressed by themselves; or alternatively, let them express meanings such as the present tense residing in the activity conducive to the referent of the base as expressed by themselves. And thus, since the pot—which is the agent of the action of cessation and has long been reduced to powder—and the activity conducive to the cessation residing in it are not present, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not occur. If this is argued, we say: no.

In the first case, even when a jar has already been produced, there would be the undesirable consequence of the linguistic usage "it is being produced," because the jar, which is the agent of the action of production, is present. In the second case, for one whose body has been rendered inert by rheumatism (āmavāta) yet who possesses an effort conducive to rising, there would be the undesirable consequence of the linguistic usage "he is rising" even though rising does not occur, because the operation in the form of effort—conducive to rising—which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), is present.

Therefore, since [grammarians maintain] that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is precisely the presentness and so forth residing in the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it would be impossible to avoid the linguistic usage "the jar ceases" even when the jar has long since ceased to exist, provided that its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is considered to be permanent. Furthermore, if one were to accept that when a jar is shattered by a mallet or similar object, there exists some non-existence called "destruction" which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that jar, permanent, and subsisting in the ground or other substrates, then why would that destruction not be perceptible when the collection of shards has been removed—even if they have not been removed—given that one does not perceive the specific configuration of the shards that distinguishes them from those of a water-jar (*maṇika*), a bowl (*śarāva*), or other such vessels? It ought to be perceptible.

If it is argued that the destruction of a jar and the like is not perceptible but must be inferred from specific features such as the shape of the potsherds, then—just as with the production [of an effect] at the time of the falling of the hammer—it is possible to infer through that [shape] a destruction that is a modification of an entity (*bhāvavikāra*) and which resides in its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); therefore, the establishment of a destruction that is an absence (*abhāva*) residing in the locus of the counter-correlate and persisting thereafter is not achieved by that means.

The linguistic usage "there is the destruction of the jar on this ground" is appropriately explained as having for its object the locus-hood of the counter-positive (the jar) as characterized by a positive modification—just like the usage "the jar has arisen on this ground. Furthermore, since the linguistic usage of the absence of the jar on the ground immediately after its destruction can be explained as being based upon an absolute absence related to a specific time, just like the usage of its absence immediately after the jar has been removed, it is unnecessary to postulate that such usage has destruction (dhvaṃsa) as its object.

If it is argued that this being the case, since the usage of the term "non-existence" for the potsherd prior to the production of the pot is already accounted for by absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), then antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) would also not exist, we reply: let even that not exist. But then, since it would be impossible to define time such that "the time supporting antecedent non-existence is the prior time" and "the time supporting destruction is the posterior time," upon what basis would the usage of terms like "prior" and "posterior" with respect to time rest? [We reply: Let it have as its object some undifferentiated property (*akhaṇḍadharma*), just as the usage of terms like "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*) is applied to things such as pots.

Even if one accepts that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is a persisting entity of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), one must still assert that "destruction-ness" (*dhvaṃsatva*) and so forth, as an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) property, resides within those [destructions]. Nor can destruction-ness consist of the delimited (composite) property of being a produced absence (*janyābhāvatva*); for then a jar, which is itself the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of its own destruction, would result in having that very destruction-ness. Nor is it intended here that destruction-ness is the nature of non-existence as the seventh category (*padārtha*); because this would entail that a jar lacks destruction-ness even with respect to its own prior absence, which would result in the conventional usage of the phrase "the time subsequent to the prior absence" at the time of the jar's existence being rendered groundless. Furthermore, the prior absence and the destruction are not distinct from the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

That being the case, by parity of reasoning, even the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of destruction would have to be distinct from its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Consequently, there would be another prior absence of that destruction's prior absence, yet another for that, and another destruction for that, and yet another prior absence for that—leading to the fallacy of postulating an infinite series of unauthoritative absences of destruction and prior absences. Furthermore, it is impossible to define "destruction-ness" (*dhvaṃsatva*) in any other way that is free from defects such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). The same applies to "prior absence-ness" (*prāgabhāvatva*); this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Therefore, there is no prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) before, nor is there a non-existence through destruction (*dhvaṃsābhāva*) after. In the interim, for a certain period of time, there exists the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of jars and so forth, characterized by the modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*)—namely, origination, subsistence, and destruction—which are themselves indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). Thus, the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) is also a certain modification of being occurring at the moment immediately following the dawning of the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*); since it does not persist in liberation (*mukti*), there is no fault whatsoever in its indeterminability. This is the view of the teachers of Advaita Vedānta. || 2 ||

If it be objected that, in this way, since the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) is momentary, liberation would not be a stable human goal (*puruṣārtha*), you are mistaken. For the cessation of ignorance is not itself accepted as the human goal simply because it is accomplished by knowledge; this is because it is neither pleasure nor the absence of pain. Rather, when ignorance—which is the cause of the suffering of saṃsāra and the veil over indivisible bliss—is destroyed, there occurs the manifestation of indivisible bliss and the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra. It is for the sake of this utility that its being accomplished by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is accepted.

The teacher Citsukhācārya, however, maintains that even the absence of suffering is not an end in itself (*svataḥ-puruṣārtha*) in liberation; for in all cases, the absence of suffering is subordinate to happiness because it merely removes the obstacles to the manifestation of innate bliss (*svarūpa-sukha*). Thus, happiness alone is the end in itself.

Since all other [objects] are subordinate to that [pleasure], and since it is possible for the cognition of being a means to pleasure alone to be the motivator, it is improper to postulate that the absence of pain is an end-in-itself (*puruṣārtha*) and then assume that the cognition of being a means to a desired object—which incorporates the desire for that end—is the motivator, as this would involve a cumbersome construction.

Nor is the mere absence of suffering itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by its own nature; otherwise, it would follow that pleasure is desired merely as a subordinate element (*śeṣatayā*) of that [absence], which is a reversal of the truth. This is because we observe engagement in such things as censurable sexual intercourse—which produces a momentary pleasure even though it is accomplished through long-lasting suffering. In that case, if the absence of suffering coexisting with the momentary pleasure were the human goal, it would be impossible for one to undergo long-lasting suffering for the sake of that [absence]. Nor is there any parity of fault in the view that the momentary pleasure itself is the human goal in those instances.

Since increase and decrease are established by experience in the case of happiness that is a positive entity (bhāvarūpa), it is logical that one might undergo suffering for a long time for the sake of a moment of extremely superior happiness; however, such increase and decrease are impossible in the case of the mere absence of suffering. Therefore, they say that in liberation, even the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra is a residual part of happiness—just like the cessation of ignorance—and thus the attainment of uninterrupted bliss alone is the self-evident human goal (puruṣārtha). || 3 ||

"But surely, unconditioned bliss is eternally attained by virtue of its nature as the inner self. True. Although eternally attained, that unconditioned bliss was led away by being veiled; thus, there arose the state of not having achieved one's purpose (*akṛtārthatā*). And when that [veiling] has been removed, with all distractions of evil dispelled, it is "as if" attained—like a golden ornament forgotten though already upon one's own neck—and thus, according to some, its status as something to be attained is merely figurative.

Others, however, maintain that because the cognition "I lack unsurpassed bliss"—which is produced by the veil of ignorance consisting in the state of being unfit for the empirical usage "it does not exist" or "it does not manifest" during the condition of saṃsāra—is not established for everyone, there exists some conceptual absence of the bliss of Brahman that serves as its objective support and persists as long as ignorance lasts.

Upon the cessation of ignorance, that absence ceases because it is rooted therein; thus, in accordance with the definition beginning with "when this exists, in the subsequent moment," they say that its status as something to be attained is indeed primary.

Others, however, argue that because that which is not experienced lacks the status of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), even though unconditioned bliss exists during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), it is not a human goal due to the absence of its manifestation (*āparokṣya*). Nor can it be said that manifestation occurs then through the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*), since that [essential nature] is always non-different from the bliss of the essential nature. Furthermore, it should not be argued that manifestation occurs through the knowledge of a mental modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*) even in liberation; for manifestation is not merely non-difference from consciousness that is conducive to its own empirical usage.

[The opponents] say: "If consciousness delimited by a jar were manifested, then the fragrance of the jar—which is non-different from that [consciousness]—would also necessarily become directly perceived (*āparokṣya*). Rather, it is the non-difference [of consciousness] with an object that is not veiled [by ignorance]. Thus, since the aspect of being un-veiled occurs only when there is the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), it is logical that the supreme human goal—the direct perception of unsurpassed bliss—is attainable through knowledge (*vidyā*)."

Others, however, maintain that immediacy (*aparokṣya*) consists merely in the non-difference from consciousness that is conducive to empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). Nevertheless, due to the power of ignorance (*ajñāna*), just as there is an apparent difference between individual selves (*jīva*), so too is there an apparent difference between consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*). Thus, in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), just as one person does not have immediate awareness of the consciousness of another person, there is likewise no immediate awareness of unconditioned bliss. But upon the cessation of ignorance, because the difference between consciousness and bliss is dissolved, there is immediate awareness of it; therefore, they say that this [immediacy] is to be accomplished through knowledge (*vidyā*). ||4||

Now, it must be examined whether, upon the arising of knowledge, for one who has abandoned the state of being a *jīva* due to the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there occurs an attainment of the state of the Lord (*īśvara*), or rather an abiding in the form of pure consciousness alone. It is said in reply:

according to the doctrine of a single *jīva* (*ekajīvavāda*), because the entire phenomenal world of distinctions—including the division between *jīva* and *īśvara*—is imagined by that single ignorance (*ajñāna*), its dissolution upon the arising of that knowledge results in abiding solely in the form of non-differentiated consciousness.

Even if one accepts the doctrine of a plurality of souls (*anekajīvavāda*) and acknowledges the established distinction between those bound and those who have experienced liberation, although the phenomenal world produced by the ignorance of a particular soul may persist even after that soul’s knowledge has dawned, nevertheless—according to the position that "the Lord (*īśvara*) is also a specific reflection just like the individual soul (*jīva*)"—the liberated soul abides solely in the form of the pure consciousness that constitutes its source-reflection (*bimba*).

Since a single [consciousness] can have multiple reflections in multiple limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), when one adjunct dissolves, it is logical that its reflection should persist in the form of the original object (*bimba*); consequently, it would be unavoidable for that reflection to become another reflection [of the same consciousness], leading to the undesirable consequence that even for one who is liberated, bondage would recur—just as in the theory of spatial limitation (*avacchedapakṣa*). For this very reason, the theory of spatial limitation is not accepted in the doctrine of the plurality of souls (*anekajīvavāda*), because if liberation occurs through a particular limitation, then upon contact with another internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) within that same limitation, bondage would necessarily follow once again.

In the view that "the individual soul (jīva) is the reflection, the Lord (Īśvara) occupies the position of the original object (bimba), and pure consciousness (śuddhacaitanya) is the thread woven through both," it is maintained that until the liberation of all souls, the liberated one attains the state of the Supreme Lord, characterized by qualities such as omniscience, omnipotence, universal lordship, and the possession of true desires.

Just as when the reflection of a single face appears in many mirrors, upon the removal of one mirror, that reflection remains in the form of the original object (bimba) and not merely as a face—because even then, the status of being the original object (bimbatva) residing in the face, which was produced by the proximity of the other mirrors, has not departed—so too, when the reflection of the single consciousness of Brahman (brahmacaitanya) occurs in multiple limiting adjuncts (upādhi), upon the rise of knowledge (vidyā) and the subsequent dissolution of that particular adjunct, that reflection [remains].

This is because it is necessarily established in the form of a reflection (*bimbabhāvena*). Nor is there any impossibility of the liberated one possessing the status of the Lord of All, characterized by qualities such as having true desires, on the grounds that ignorance (*avidyā*) is absent in him; for even though his own ignorance has ceased, at that time the ignorance of other bound persons still exists. Indeed, the Lord’s lordship and his endowment with qualities such as having true desires are not produced by his own ignorance—since he is stainless (*nirañjana*)—but rather all of that must be accepted as being produced solely by the ignorance of bound persons.

Nor does it follow that there is no distinction between the fruits of saguṇa-vidyā and liberation, on the grounds that even for those who meditate on the Lord with attributes, the Śrutis—such as "As a person's resolve is in this world, so he becomes after departing from here," and "In whatever way they meditate upon Him"—declare their attainment of union (*sāyujya*) with the Lord. For, because those who meditate on the Lord with attributes lack the direct realization of the undivided [Brahman], there is no cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), nor is there the dissolution of the ego and other factors rooted therein. Due to the non-cessation of the veil, there is no manifestation of undivided bliss.

"Excluding the activity of the world, because of the context and because of their non-proximity," and "Because of the indication that there is equality only in respect of enjoyment"—according to the reasoning stated in such sūtras, although they possess equality with the Supreme Lord in respect of enjoyment, and although they have the capacity to create divine bodies, sense organs, women, and so forth for the sake of their own enjoyment by mere volition, they do not possess unimpeded sovereignty characterized by independence in the creation, dissolution, and so forth of the entire universe.

But for those who are liberated—having attained the state of the Lord free from all bonds—all that [bondage] has ceased; thus, there exists a great distinction between them. Nor does the liberation of souls entail a recurrence of bondage upon attaining the state of the Lord, because we hear of the Supreme Lord’s association with darkness, suffering, and so forth during incarnations such as Raghunātha. This is because the Lord, like an actor, merely enacts those states in order to maintain the boundaries He Himself established, such as the infallibility of a Brahmin’s curse, thereby demonstrating the truth of the curse of Bhṛgu and other such events.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with scriptural passages stating that he is eternally liberated, possesses unimpeded sovereignty, and is devoid of equals or superiors. Therefore, until the liberation of all beings, the state of the Supreme Lord belongs to the liberated one; thus, there is no fault whatsoever in his assuming the nature of the Lord within the reflected image (bimba).

This very position is consistent with the Śruti, the Sūtras, the Bhāṣya, and other authoritative texts. To explain: in the section beginning with "The small [space] because of the subsequent [statements]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1) within the Chapter on Concordance (Samanvaya-adhyāya), it is established that the "small space" (daharākāśa) mentioned in such scriptural passages as "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space"—neither the elemental ether nor the individual soul (jīva), but rather the Supreme Lord—on account of the subsequent supplementary statements.

Having determined this based on the reasons consisting of the attributes characterized by being the locus of heaven and earth and so forth—as established in passages such as, "Both heaven and earth are contained within him; as vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart; this is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, without hunger, without thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true"—it is concluded by means of another sūtra: "If it be said [that the individual soul is meant] because of what follows, [we reply] no, for its nature is manifested."

Immediately following the Dahara-vidyā, in the dialogue between Indra and Prajāpati, after introducing the Self to be taught as endowed with the eight qualities beginning with freedom from sin—starting with the words, "That Self which is free from sin"—the text identifies: "This person who is seen in the eye, that is the Self," referring to the one present in the eye as the seer during the waking state; "This [Self] who moves about in dreams, being honored, that is the Self," referring to the one in the state of dream; and "Now, when he is sound asleep, composed, serene, and knows no dream, that is... [referring to the one in deep sleep].

Because of the teaching that even the individual soul (jīva)—who has entered the state of deep sleep and who, having transcended the three states, is described as "this serene being, rising up from this body, attaining the highest light, appears in his own true form; he is the supreme person"—possesses the eight qualities such as freedom from sin, these [qualities] do not determine that the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is the Supreme Lord.

Raising the objection that—given the hearing in each successive section of the passage beginning with "He who is in the dream state," namely "I shall explain this very same one further to you"—the subsequent sections clearly possess the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva) such as dreaming and so forth, and thus belong to the jīva, while the first section alone belongs to Brahman; [the author] anticipates this by stating that what is to be established there, in the fourth section, is the individual soul whose true nature has become manifest through liberation from all bonds.

But it is not [the Self] as defiled by the distinctions of the various states of *saṃsāra*, because in that case there would be a sublation of qualities such as "having true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). The author of the Sūtras, providing a resolution by noting that the presentation of the three states serves to indicate the purity of the teaching in the fourth stage through the mention of the defects of each respective state, clearly states in the fourth stage that the liberated one attains the state of being the Lord (*īśvarabhāvāpatti*).

For if that were absent, even for the liberated one, qualities such as "having true resolve" would be impossible; furthermore, if the eightfold set of qualities mentioned in sequence were present in anyone other than the Lord, the removal of the doubt raised would not be achieved.

In that very Sūtra, the Commentator also states with extreme clarity that the liberated one attains the state of the qualified Lord: "Therefore, by means of knowledge, one realizes the supreme form of the Lord—which is the opposite of that [individual soul]—as having qualities such as freedom from sin, through the dissolution of that individual form which is non-ultimate, produced by ignorance, defiled by defects such as agency, enjoyership, passion, and hatred, and joined with manifold evils."

Furthermore, in the *Avirodhādhyāya*, within the section titled "Aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt," which was introduced for the purpose of defining the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) as that of part and whole—a relationship understood through the mutual roles of benefactor and beneficiary based on such scriptural passages as, "For He alone makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead upward from these worlds; and He alone makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead downward"—it is stated: "In the *Avirodhādhyāya* as well, in the section 'Aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt,' which was introduced for the purpose of defining the relationship between the individual soul and the Lord as that of part and whole—understood through the mutual roles of benefactor and beneficiary based on such scriptural passages as, 'For He alone makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead upward from these worlds; and He alone makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead downward'—"

"If it is admitted that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of the Lord (*īśvara*), then by virtue of the individual soul's experience of the suffering of *saṃsāra*, the Lord himself would also become subject to suffering. Just as in the world, Devadatta—the whole (*aṃśin*)—becomes subject to suffering through pain occurring in any one of his parts, such as the hand or foot, so it would be here. Consequently, those who have attained [liberation] would incur even greater suffering; therefore, it would follow that the previous state of *saṃsāra* itself would be better, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is useless. This is clearly explained in the *Bhāmatī* and other works by way of this passage of doubt.

Relying on the non-confusion between the original object and its reflection, the commentator, while in a state of meditative concentration, clarified that the liberated one attains the state of Īśvara.

In the *Sādhanādhyāya* as well, in the section beginning with "The creation in the intermediate state [is real], for so [the scripture] says" (*sandhye sṛṣṭirāha hi*), having established that the phenomenal world of dreams is illusory, an objection is raised regarding the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) within that illusory dream-world. This is addressed by the sūtra: "But [its power] is concealed by the meditation on another; for from that [concealment] come its bondage and its opposite. [The commentary explains: Since the individual soul is non-different from the Lord, qualities such as the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) do indeed exist [in it], yet they are concealed due to the defect of ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, it is not possible for the soul to be the creator of the dream-world.

Stating this, the author of the Sūtras [intends to show] that "that [Self], though concealed, becomes manifest—like the power of vision obscured by cataracts being restored through the efficacy of medicine—to some person alone who has attained perfection through the grace of the Lord, who meditates upon the Supreme while striving and whose darkness has been dispelled; it does not manifest by its very nature for all beings. Describing the intent of that Sūtra, the author of the Bhāṣya also clarified the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord by accepting the manifestation of the liberated soul's *satya-saṅkalpatva* (the power of true resolve) and other qualities necessary for the creation of dream-objects and so forth.

In the *Phalādhyāya* as well, regarding the scripture concerning the one being liberated which states, "He manifests in his own form," when the inquiry arises—"In what form is this manifestation intended?"—the sūtra "Jaimini [holds that it is] the Brahman-form, on account of the introductory passages and so forth" (BrSū 4.4.5) establishes that the Brahman-form consists of qualities beginning with freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and ending with the fulfillment of true resolves (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), as well as omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) and omnipotence (*sarveśvaratva*). Manifestation occurs through that form, as shown by the introductory passage, "The Self which is free from sin... and the subsequent description, "There he moves about, laughing, playing... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).

Jaimini’s view is that [the soul's existence] is established by the declaration of lordship, such as "delighting with women or with vehicles," and so forth. Then, having introduced the following view through the subsequent sūtra—"By consciousness alone, because its nature consists of that"—and having presented the understanding from such scriptural passages as, "Verily, my dear, this self is without interior or exterior, an entire mass of consciousness," namely that "the very nature of the self is pure consciousness," and thus that "its manifestation is by means of that alone," [the author states: "Even so, because of the introductory statement and because of prior existence, there is no contradiction."

By means of the concluding sūtra, "Bādarāyaṇa [holds this view]," the author of the sūtras declares there is no contradiction, stating: "Even though, from the perspective of ultimate reality, [the Self] is pure consciousness alone, there is no conflict between the two scriptural passages because the previously mentioned collection of qualities—understood through [texts concerning] meditation and so forth—is possible from the perspective of the worldly dealings of bound souls, being composed of māyā. By commenting on these three sūtras as having the aforementioned meaning, the commentator also clearly accepted that the liberated one attains the state of the Lord (īśvarabhāvāpatti).

The Bhāmatī-nibandha and other works followed this very same path regarding this collection of Sūtras supported by Śruti, as well as the collection of statements cited from the venerable Bhāṣyakāra; nor did they say that the sovereignty [of Brahman], which was not obscured by ignorance, becomes manifest through meditation for such an extensive collection of Sūtra and Bhāṣya statements supported by Śruti.

It is appropriate to describe this as a *abhyupetyavāda* (a concessionary argument), according to the method stated in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "That which was said by the author of the Sūtras [regarding] the embodied soul, having accepted that very [position], because of the reason already stated.

Therefore, since it must necessarily be admitted that liberated souls attain the state of the Lord (*īśvara*), the impossibility of this is precisely the defect in the theory of the Lord as a reflection (*pratibimba-īśvara-vāda*). As the authors of the *Kalpataru* have said: "The reflection of Māyā cannot be approached by those who are liberated. And this impossibility is a defect even in the theories of the single Jīva (*ekajīvavāda*) and the ultimate plurality of Jīvas (*pāramārthika-jīva-bheda-vāda*).

As for what is asserted by certain dualists—that because difference is ultimately real, even though the individual soul (jīva) does not attain the state of being the Lord (Īśvara) in liberation, there is no contradiction since qualities such as freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva) can exist there separately for the soul just as they do for the Lord—this is worthless. For if that were so, one could raise the objection that since the soul possesses freedom from sin and other such qualities, these are not marks of Brahman; thus, the intended resolution of that doubt would not be achieved, which contradicts the Sūtra: "If it be argued that [the soul is different] on account of the subsequent [text], [we reply] no, for its true nature is manifested."

Furthermore, there is a contradiction in designating as "Brahmanic" the qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) residing in the individual soul (*jīva*)—which are accepted by others as being included under the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the sūtra "On account of the mention and so forth" (*upanyāsādibhyaḥ*)—as well as the eating (*jakṣaṇa*), playing (*krīḍana*), and rejoicing (*ramamāṇa*) mentioned in the scripture "Eating, playing, and rejoicing. This is because these would conflict with the designation [of the soul] as Brahman in the sūtra "Jaimini [thinks it is] on account of the Brahmanic [nature]" (*brāhmeṇa jaiminiḥ*).

Furthermore, this would contradict the acceptance—stated in the Siddhānta-sūtra beginning with "evam api"—of the fact that liberated souls consist of pure consciousness (*caitanyamātratva*), as taught in the sūtra "by mere consciousness" (*cititanmātreṇa*) on the grounds that those qualities are real even when distinct; it would also contradict the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "the manifestation upon reaching" (*sampadyāvirbhāva*). For in that context, regarding the scriptural text "he manifests in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*), it is not said that he manifests by means of some adventitious form, because that would render the word "own" (*svena*) redundant.

Since it is inexpressible that the adventitious form by which [the entity] itself is manifested belongs to its own nature, it has been established that—by virtue of employing the word "own" (*sva*) as a synonym for "self" (*ātman*)—what is intended is manifestation through its own essential nature, which is eternally established, and not through any [adventitious] attribute.

If this quality of being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth were adventitious to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the state of liberation, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts: first, with the denial of adventitious forms in liberation in the passage "attaining [Brahman], its true nature manifests" (*sampadyāvirbhāvaḥ*); and second, with the teaching that qualities such as freedom from evil are concealed during bondage and manifest in liberation in the passages "But [the soul's power] is hidden due to meditation on another" (*parābhidhyānāttu tirohitam*) and "If it be argued that it is from the subsequent [text], then [we reply] its true nature has indeed manifested" (*uttarāccedāvirbhūtasvarūpastu*). Therefore, these qualities must be declared to be eternally established, and thus the falsity (*mithyātva*) of bondage is unavoidable.

For "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) is indeed the state of being eternally devoid of evil. And in that which is in reality always devoid of evil, neither a connection with evil nor a connection with agency and enjoyership rooted therein can possibly exist as ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*). Consequently, the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from the Lord (*īśvara*) is also unavoidable; for bondage, which contradicts that non-difference taught by the scriptures, lacks any true existence. Otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of the concealment of the eternally established and real power of will (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) in one who is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*).

For even by opponents, it is not accepted that there exists some unrealized, unerring resolve (*avitatha-saṅkalpa*) belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) which persists during the state of transmigratory existence and has some object as its domain; rather, it must be established that it is precisely that eternal, unrestricted, and true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) which belongs to the Lord (*īśvara*), but which—due to the non-manifestation of the soul's non-difference from the Lord during the state of transmigratory existence—is not perceived as its own and is thus "concealed" (*tirohita*) for it. This is the "dawn at the gatehouse" (*ghaṭṭakuṭī-prabhāta-vṛttānta*) argument.

If it is argued: "The state of being 'free from evil' (*apahatapāpmatva*) does not mean the absence of evil, but rather the possession of a power that prevents the arising of evil even when performing actions that cause it; since this [power] is eternally established, there is no consequence of bondage being illusory. Likewise, 'truthfulness of resolve' (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) must also be explained as a form of power, so there is no consequence of identity with the Lord," we say: not so. For there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a construction of the meaning of the words.

Indeed, a power that prevents the generation of sin need not be postulated for the sake of ensuring the non-arising of sin during the state of wandering through the forms of saṃsāra; for at that time, the arising of such sin is accepted. However, from the moment of enlightenment (*vidyotpatti*) onwards, the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) [of sin] occurs solely by the majesty of knowledge (*vidyāmāhātmya*), as demonstrated by the sūtra: "Upon the attainment of That, there is the non-clinging and destruction of both subsequent and previous sins, because of the scriptural declaration thereof. For this very reason, the non-clinging [of sin] is also logically established in the state of liberation (*mukti*); thus, the postulation of a [separate] power is redundant.

Therefore, it is established that those who follow the cited scriptures and aphorisms must accept that for liberated souls—until the liberation of all—is attained the state of the Supreme Lord, which is characterized by an unimpeded sovereignty produced by the knowledge of the bound soul (baddhapuruṣa-vidyā), which is not inconsistent with their being essentially pure consciousness, and which is enriched by the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss distinguished by a multitude of qualities corresponding to that [sovereignty], and which is a seamless and indivisible attainment of His nature.

To the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Makhin—the son of the learned preceptor who performed the Viśvajit sacrifice, the son of one who performed the Śarvatomukha and Mahāvrata sacrifices, and the devotee of the Moon-crested Lord—there was a son renowned as Appadīkṣita. || 1 ||

Having studied all the tantras, which have been clarified by his constant skill in the art of pure exposition, and having followed the tradition rooted in the sacred scriptures, he composed this compendium of the various points of established doctrine. || 2 ||
If, due to being corrupted by delusion regarding the methods of established tenets, I have written anything else [than the truth] here;
May those with refined hearts be compassionate toward this critical edition, being free from doubt through their thorough study of the authentic tradition. ||3||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṃgraha*.
This work is completed.
